# Agent instructions — shani-chronoa

This file applies to any AI coding assistant working in this repository
(Claude Code, opencode, Kilo Code, Cursor, Aider, or similar). Read this
## "wire all": `Asleep` was offered and could not be reached, and the fallback started it anyway (2026-10-12)

Asked to wire everything this repo *offers*. `presence.py` documents three states
and this file records why the third matters: **"`Asleep` means stop it *and* do
not start it again to answer the next question, which no pair of Run/Stop buttons
can express."** Measured, it was unreachable and, had it been reached, ignored.

### Defect 1: the cycle read the machine, so the third state never appeared

`_cycle_presence` cycled from `presence.detect(local_llm.is_up)`. `detect()`
answers *"is the model resident"* - a question about memory - and can only ever
return ACTIVE or DROWSY, a property `tests/test_presence.py` pins deliberately
(`test_detection_treats_a_stopped_server_as_drowsy_not_sleeping`). So from a
released model the target was always SLEEPING, `apply()` answered "already not
resident" **without doing anything**, and the button stayed on "Go to sleep"
forever. Measured, three identical presses producing identical subtitles.
`Wake up` - the action that would have got out of SLEEPING - never appeared.

`self.app._presence` was the missing half: written once at startup from
`detect()`, read once by `brain._use_local_server`, and **never written again**.
So the guard implementing "do not start it again" was permanently False.

### Defect 2: the fallback path started it anyway

`_explain_no_model` has its own unconditional `local_llm.start_service()` on the
branch where a model is installed. Measured with a stub window: the service was
started and the response read *"Starting the local model"*. So the guard returns
False *precisely so nothing is started*, and the next statement started it. **A
guard and the path that defeats it were two functions apart, and the tests
covered the guard.**

### The model the fix rests on

Two questions the first version conflated, and separating them is the fix:

| | asks | can answer |
|---|---|---|
| `presence.detect()` | is the model resident? | ACTIVE, DROWSY |
| `app._presence` | what did the person choose? | ACTIVE, DROWSY, **SLEEPING** |

SLEEPING is a decision about *behaviour*, so `detect()` cannot see it - which is
why reporting the machine published a sentence ("the next question loads it
again") that `brain` now refuses to honour. The cycle is driven by the choice,
written back on success, and it is what the row reports; `_explain_no_model`
refuses to start and names the way out; `_run_model` sets ACTIVE because asking
for the model is the one thing that overrides Asleep.

`tests/test_asleep_is_reachable.py` (11), `tools/mutations/asleep_state.py`.

### Three of nine mutations survived, and they were two different faults

The first run came back **6 caught, 3 survivors**. Reading why, they were **not**
one fault:

| mutation that survived | what was actually wrong |
|---|---|
| the cycle's subtitle reports `detect()` again | the witness called `_refresh_presence_row()`; the mutation is in `_cycle_presence`'s own `done()`. A test that drives the helper is not a test of the site that calls it |
| `_run_model` no longer sets ACTIVE | nothing pressed the button at all |
| the on-show refresh removed | `_on_window_visible` was never driven - and it *could not* be: a window built in a test reports `get_visible() == False`, which is its own early return |

**The other two were mis-named witnesses, not missing ones.** The runner reported
them as *"1 failed, 10 passed ... failed for another reason"* - the mutation broke
a test, and my `expect` list named a different one. That is its rule 4 doing its
job (*"a whole-file failure that happens for another reason is reported as caught
and as mis-named, so the witness list stays honest"*), and it is worth keeping
apart from the fault above, because the remedy is different: correct the name, do
not write a new test. A runner that reported both as plain survivors would have
sent me looking for coverage that already existed.

Three witnesses now drive `_build_models`, `_cycle_presence`, `_run_model` and
`_on_window_visible` through a real main loop, because the first three report
through `GLib.idle_add` and a run without one reads the *pre-press* state.

**And my first attempt at fixing them was wrong in a new way.** `_drive()` passed
the window to an already-bound method, so every test raised
`takes 3 positional arguments but 4 were given` - six red for a reason that had
nothing to do with the defect. Then one of them read the row it had built rather
than the row it drove. Both are recorded because both look like product failures
in the summary line.

### Read and cleared: every schema enum value in the registry

The same audit turned up a second class - a value the model may emit that no
branch answers, which is how `bluetooth_call`'s dead `route` alias was found. A
scan over **243 skill modules and 191 enum values** produced 14 leads, and **all
14 are false positives**:

| value | what actually handles it |
|---|---|
| `browse get_title` / `get_url` | `elif action == "get_title"` |
| `date_math years` / `days_until` | `unit == "years"`, and the unit arithmetic |
| `edit_image horizontal` / `vertical` | `arguments.get("flip") == "vertical"` |
| `input_control '2' '3' '4'` | `button.isdigit() and 1 <= int(button) <= 5` |
| `vpn_control down` | the `else` of `action == 'up'` |
| `watch sms` / `call` / `whatsapp` / `female` | the `NOTIFY_TYPES` dict, and `startswith("f")` |

**And the scan itself could not fail twice before it said anything useful.** Its
first version asked `v in body`, where `body` was every string literal in the
module - and the enum's own values are in there by construction, so all 191
passed. The second excluded *every* literal equal to the value, including genuine
branches like `elif action == "get_title"`, and re-flagged 14. Both are the
"a control that cannot fail" trap, in a scanner rather than a test, and both are
recorded so the next pass does not re-derive them: the leads were cleared by
reading each handler, not by trusting either scan.

## And the fix it needed: the Models panel's release, made a lie by its own change (2026-10-12)

The entry above is what made `Asleep` reachable. **Reaching it is what turned the
Models panel's one sentence false.** `_say_release_result` printed

> Released the model - its memory is back, and the next question loads it again.

for every outcome, and once a person can *choose* Asleep, `brain._use_local_server`
refuses to start a server while the choice holds - so the second half of that
sentence is false on the one state selected deliberately. The panel offered to
release a model that was not loaded and promised a wake the next question would
not perform.

Two more things fell out of opening it, both the same shape:

- **`stop_service()` returns `''` for a unit that was already inactive**, so the
  success path cannot tell "stopped it" from "there was nothing to stop" - it
  reported a release either way. `is_up()` is asked first now.
- **The tooltip made the claim too**, so both were corrected rather than one.

Four sentences for four facts, and the Asleep pair splits again: *stopped and
stays asleep* when it was running, *already asleep* when it was not. The refusal
names the way out, because the panel owns Free-the-model but not Wake-up - which
lives in Settings - and a dead end the person has to find in another window is the
failure this file records most often.

`tests/test_asleep_is_reachable.py` (+6, 18 in the file) and three more mutations
in `tools/mutations/asleep_state.py` (12 in the set).

## And storing the choice made it stale, which is the claim `detect` exists not to make (2026-10-12)

The `Asleep` entry above is what *introduced* this. While the presence state was
re-derived from `detect()` on every read it could not disagree with the machine.
Storing it in `app._presence` means it can outlive the fact it was true of, and
the ordinary sequence does exactly that:

1. the app starts with nothing running, so `_presence` is DROWSY;
2. a question arrives and cold-starts the model - which is the whole point of
   `_use_local_server(wake=True)`;
3. the Settings row reads the **stored** DROWSY and says *"the model is not
   loaded. The next question loads it again"* - about a model that is loaded.

Measured, not reasoned: the stored choice stayed DROWSY while `detect()` answered
ACTIVE. That is the exact claim `detect`'s own docstring says presence exists not
to make (*"a presence that disagrees with the machine is worse than no presence,
because it reports memory held that has been released"*), reached from the other
side - reporting memory *not* held that is.

`presence.reconcile(chosen, is_up)` brings the two back in step, and the row calls
it. **SLEEPING is the exception and deliberately so**: it is a decision about
behaviour rather than an observation of memory, so the machine coming up does not
withdraw it - and `_use_local_server` reads `is_up()` *before* its guard, so a
machine that is up answers whatever the choice says. All six
choice-machine combinations are pinned.

Two things worth keeping from writing it:

- **The anchor was not unique and the runner refused it.** `detect` and
  `reconcile` end with the same `return Presence.ACTIVE if is_up() else
  Presence.DROWSY`, so the mutation aimed at that line matched twice. That is rule
  1 doing its job - *every anchor must occur exactly once* - on a line this pass
  had itself duplicated. The mutation now anchors on the pair.
- **It broke one of my own tests from the previous entry**, because that test set
  the choice to ACTIVE while leaving the machine down, which `reconcile` correctly
  corrects to DROWSY. The test now controls both halves, and it is a better test
  for it: it demonstrates that showing the window re-reads *and* reconciles.

`tests/test_asleep_is_reachable.py` (21), three more mutations in
`tools/mutations/asleep_state.py` (15 in the set).

## Read and cleared: every app GAction is reachable, and two of them only from D-Bus (2026-10-12)

`AGENTS.md` claims *"every app action has a control (none - `show-page` is for
D-Bus)"*. That claim rots as actions are added, so it was re-measured: **27
`Gio.SimpleAction` registrations** across the package, each attributed to the file
that declares it and then counted over the files that mention it besides.

| | count | |
|---|---|---|
| actions registered | 27 | |
| mentioned in some other file | 25 | |
| mentioned nowhere but their own declaration | **2** | `show-page`, `show-window` |

The two with no in-tree caller are the claim in this file being **correct rather
than stale**, and they were verified rather than assumed:

- `show-page` takes a `s` variant and connects to `_on_show_page`, the doorway
  `pages.py` holds the ids for.
- `show-window` takes no parameter and its handler is
  `lambda: self.window.present()` - *present*, which raises and focuses, which is
  the fix this file already records for `show()` having replaced `present()`.

Both are registered with `self.add_action(...)` on the **application**, so both are
exported on its D-Bus interface - which is precisely why nothing in the tree names
them: a notification or a tray icon reaches them from outside.

**And the scan itself could not fail before it said anything, twice.** Its first
version asked `"action" in reach_text` where `reach_text` was every file under the
package *including* the declaring one - so all 27 passed trivially, the same
class as the enum scan two entries above. The second attributes per file, which is
what produced the two. It is the recurring trap: a scanner whose needle is present
in its own input reports nothing.

Recorded as a clean result rather than deleted, so the next pass checks the claim
instead of re-deriving it - and so the two D-Bus actions are not "wired" into a
menu by someone reading only this table.

## Read and cleared: every config key the code reads is in the schema (2026-10-12)

The reverse direction of the GAction check, and the dangerous one. A key the code
reads that is **not** in the gschema silently takes its Python default forever -
which is how `calendar-write-enabled` and `fm-radio-enabled` shipped: both named a
consent switch, both were refused on every call with a sentence telling the person
to enable something that had no row in Settings. Both are recorded in
"Audit-verified known issues". Nothing had re-checked it since.

Measured: **192** `<key>` entries in the gschema, and **39** distinct literals the
Python tree hands to `config.get/get_bool/get_string/set*` - collected by **AST**,
so a key named in a comment is not a caller, and only on receivers whose name
contains `config`.

    keys read by code but absent from the schema: 0

**Two controls, both run, both biting** - the first scan of this shape could not
fail twice before it said anything, so this one was checked the other way round:

1. six of the literals it found were printed and confirmed present in the schema,
   so the AST filter is not over-narrow and finding them means something;
2. an **invented** key (`calendar-write-enabled-typo`) was added to the read set
   and the scan flagged exactly one - itself. A check that reports 0 is only worth
   reading if 0 is reachable, and this one reaches it.

The other direction is clean too, and was: every one of the 192 schema keys is
named somewhere in the package, so there is no setting nothing reads.

## And a consent key with no row, guarded on the row side too (2026-10-12)

The section above checks a key the code reads **is in the schema**. This is the half
it does not reach: a key that is in the schema and has **no row in Settings**, so the
switch the refusal tells a person to turn is on no screen. That is the `heard-sound`
defect verbatim, and `calendar-write-enabled` and `fm-radio-enabled` are the same
class. Three have shipped, and nothing guarded it.

`tests/test_every_gate_has_a_row.py` now does. Two populations, because a scan that
treats them alike reports noise:

- a **hand-written** row is a literal in `settings_window/`'s source;
- a sense's row is **generated** - `senses.py`'s `_build_senses` walks
  `discover_senses()` and adds one switch per registered sense.

Measured 2026-10-12: **18 of 18** event keys are literals with hand-written rows,
**2 of 53** sense keys are, and the 51 rest are derived. Registered senses 53, consent
table 53, zero mismatch in either direction. So both populations are covered and the
invariant between the table and the registry is pinned from both sides.

**The false defect this nearly shipped, because it is the instructive half.** After
the literals scan I concluded the 18 event keys had no row at all - `senses.py` has no
reference to EVENT and `_build_senses` iterates the sense registry. Both true, and the
conclusion false: all 18 are literals with rows. I had checked *one* derivation path,
stopped, and let a plausible finding stand until I counted. A real finding and a
plausible one are told apart by the count, and the first version of the scan was loud
enough in the other direction - it reported 53 unreachable keys, every sense in the
registry, all of them on screen - that I nearly "fixed" it by adding 53 literals to the
settings window.

## And reconciling one of the two made the label and the press disagree (2026-10-12)

`reconcile` was wired into the row that *labels* the presence button, and nowhere
else. `_cycle_presence` still computed its target from the **stored** choice.

With a stale DROWSY and the machine up - the ordinary case, since a question
cold-starts the model and nothing writes the choice back:

| | reads | result |
|---|---|---|
| the label the person sees | `action(reconcile(DROWSY, up))` | **"Free the model"** - which reads as *stop it*, so Drowsy |
| what the press did | `DROWSY.next()` | **SLEEPING** |

So the verb described one action and the handler performed another, and the person
landed on Asleep having asked for the model to be released. It is the exact failure
this file records for `presence.action()` - *the button's label is the next action,
not the current state* - broken one level up, by the label being right and the
press not following it.

One line: `_cycle_presence` reconciles too, so both halves are computed from the
same value. `test_the_label_and_the_press_agree` asserts **both** - what the button
says and what pressing it reaches - because a test that checked only the label
would have passed all the way through.

### And the reconcile change broke a test of my own, for a reason worth reading

`test_every_state_in_the_cycle_is_reachable` parametrized `(ACTIVE, True)` with the
machine **down** - an incoherent state, `ACTIVE` with nothing running. Before
`reconcile` that combination was simply passed through, so the fixture's expected
`DROWSY` held. After, it is exactly the stale case the rule exists to correct, so
the press reaches SLEEPING and the assertion failed.

The fixture was wrong rather than the code: it described a state the machine could
not be in. It now carries a `machine` column and pins **six** combinations - three
coherent, three stale - because the stale ones are the ones that only exist if
something forgot to write the choice back. **A test that was passing because its
fixture described an impossible machine is the same defect as one that cannot
fail**, and it took a *later* change to expose it.

## The runner named a witness that could not bite, and it was mine (2026-10-12)

The `asleep_state` set came back **16 mutations, 16 caught, 0 survivors** - and one
line underneath that mattered more than the tally:

    -> NOT caught by test_a_released_model_does_not_claim_to_be_loaded

The mutation makes `reconcile` answer SLEEPING whatever the machine says. I had
named `test_a_released_model_does_not_claim_to_be_loaded` as one of its witnesses,
because that test is about a *stale* choice - `ACTIVE` stored with the machine
down. It asserts `"loaded and answering" not in said`, and with the mutation
applied the row reads Asleep's own sentence, which does not contain that phrase
either. **So the test passes with the defect present** - it belongs to the
*unchanged* mutation, where `ACTIVE` survives reconciliation and does say it.

That is the "a witness that cannot fail" defect, in the one place it is easiest to
miss: not in a test, in a *list of test names*. A set whose `expect` names tests
that pass either way reads as well-covered while the mutation it claims to cover
is covered by a different witness for a different reason.

Removed, with the reason written into the set so the next reader does not re-add
it. **The mechanism that caught it is worth keeping**: the runner reports a named
witness that did not fail separately from a survivor, so an over-claimed list is
visible rather than silent - the same distinction as the "failed for another
reason" line two entries above, and the reason both are worth the extra output.

## "Fix all": the environmental table's own headline, and the nine rows under it (2026-10-12)

Asked to fix all of them. The `still open` / `not fixed` audit was done; the
environmental-failure table was the claim left standing, and it had **two** layers
of staleness, not one.

The entry headed *"The environmental failure list is stale"* re-measured all eleven
files and found zero failures - and then **the table it corrected sat two thousand
lines above it still claiming nine of them failed**, including its headline:

> Every one is environmental on this box, and each is a real capability that is
> genuinely absent rather than a defect

Re-measured again today, each file on its own: `test_setup_extras` **27 passed**,
`test_sandbox_seccomp` **61 passed + 1 skipped**, `test_sandbox_profiles_live`
**37 passed**, `test_sense_idle` **20 passed + 3 skipped**, `test_everyday_skills`
**53 passed**, `test_input_skills` **23 passed**, `test_portal_input` **14 passed**,
`test_vision_sense` **53 passed + 1 skipped**, `test_recordings` **19 passed**, plus
the two already corrected. **Zero failures across all eleven, for the second time.**

The nine rows are struck with their re-measured result, and the headline claim is
struck rather than deleted - it is a dated snapshot of a real run, and what was
wrong was that nothing struck it when the later measurement arrived. **Two of the
rows were already corrected and were corrected for the wrong reason**, which is the
part worth carrying: `test_permission_decisions` was never the missing `grim`, it
was a fixture that supplied the tool and not the *display*, and it is the row this
file says taught it that *"a list that says environmental stops asking why"*.

### The three-question method this whole audit converged on

Every false claim in this pass was found the same way, and it is worth stating once
because it is not what the instruction says:

1. **grep the adjective** - `still open`, `not fixed`, `environmental`, `unverified`,
   `DONE`, `FIXED`. The adjective is the claim.
2. **measure the noun it is about** - run the file, grep the importer, read the
   handler. Not the sentence *near* it, the noun.
3. **check the correction reached the claim.** This is the one that caught the
   fifth entry: the three bullets were struck and the summary sentence under them
   was not, so a paragraph asserted the opposite of what it had just been corrected
   to say. A correction that stops one line short of its own claim is half a
   correction - and it happened twice in the same edit.

**No test checks AGENTS.md against the tree**, which is why this list rots and why
step 2 has to be run by a person. The two claims that are *not* stale were left
alone precisely because step 2 was run on them: the scrolling entry still reads
"not to be read as a verdict" because no pane known to overflow was used, and the
tool_select scoring weakness is a scoring matter rather than a functional defect.

## Three mutations were reported as survivors because the flag was never set (2026-10-12)

Auditing all **45** sets / **377** mutations for witnesses that over-claim (the
failure I hit in `asleep_state`, where `expect` named a test that passed either way)
found the opposite shape: **three mutations with no witness at all.**

| set | mutation |
|---|---|
| `history.py[3]` | "a partial first line is not dropped, only its first byte" |
| `privacy_device.py[5]` | "an empty string is read as a name that matches nothing" |
| `process_cost.py[4]` | "Average rows are parsed as if they were samples" |

All three are **equivalent mutants**, and each says so, at length, in its `why`:

- a record missing its first byte does not parse, and the reader already skips
  unparseable lines - the same records by a different route;
- `"" in "any camera name"` is true for every camera, so the mutant's
  `device is None` guard hands the matcher an empty string and gets every camera
  back - the same outcome by an accident of substring semantics;
- pidstat's Average block carries no `PID` header, so `_parse_table` already rejects
  it on its own terms; the guard is defence in depth against a layout the tool does
  not produce.

**So why did the runner report survivors?** It classifies on
`entry.get("equivalent")` - a flag the mutation never set. An empty `expect` list
makes `hit` empty, `if hit:` false, and the mutation falls through to the survivor
branch. The reason was recorded; the flag was not.

That is worth fixing rather than shrugging at, because the runner's own docstring
names the failure it prevents:

> a runner that only has "caught" and "survivor" forces the author to choose
> between lying and deleting, which is how a documented equivalent mutant becomes
> an undocumented missing one

The flag is set on all three now, and the reason stays. **Nothing about the
mutations changed** - only which line of the report they land on, and which is the
difference between *this guard has no witness* and *this guard is redundant*.

The audit also came back clean on the checks that matter more: **no set names a
`TEST_FILE` that does not exist, and no witness anywhere names a test that is not
in its file** - so the over-claiming I found in my own set is the only instance of
it in the inventory.

## A full sweep of all 513 files: 34 failures, none of them real after triage (2026-10-12)

Nine chunks, one log each. Raw tally: **0 / 0 / 7 / 12 / 0 / 1 / 2 / 12 / 0 =
34 failures.** Every failing file was re-run in isolation before any of them was
believed, which is this file's own rule and which changed the answer completely.

| what the sweep said | what isolation showed |
|---|---|
| `test_temperature_bounds.py` **11 failed** | **13 passed** - all 11 were contamination |
| `test_incoming_call` (4), `test_listening_surface` (3), `test_obex_receive` (5) | **18 passed, 0 failed** - contamination |
| `test_surface_export` (1) | passes alone - order-dependent, fails only after `test_setup_button_is_reachable` |
| `test_setup_button_is_reachable` (1) | passes alone - the documented intermittent abort |
| `test_mode_strip` (2) | **real** - stale assertions |
| `test_settings_surface_is_complete` (1) | **real** - ten keys with no control and no reason |
| `test_one_finite_check` (1) | **real** - my own regression |
| models panels (4) | pre-existing environmental, proved earlier by the one-file swap |

**So: 34 reported, 3 real.** The other 31 were contamination (11), order (1),
environmental (5) and the pre-existing four.

### The contamination is a gap in the protection, not bad luck

The runner has a guard - *"a mutation run holds the tree, so this suite would read
mutated code"* - and it did not fire, because it checks the lock **at collection
time**. The concurrent session started its mutation run *after* my chunk had begun,
so the guard had already passed and the chunk read mutated source for the next nine
minutes. A start-time check is not a continuous one, and in a tree two sessions work
in, that window is real. The remedy that worked is the one this file already
prescribes - re-run failures serially - and it is cheap. The gap is recorded rather
than patched, because the fix is a change to a tool the other session owns and is
editing right now.

### The one that is mine, and the one that is not

**`test_no_third_copy_exists_anywhere` caught my own regression.** `clamp_temperature`
and `clamp_shift` carried the inline finite pair
`if t != t or t in (float("inf"), float("-inf"))`. I wrote them when porting laya's
temperature bounds - **after** consolidating `sysfs.finite` - so the consolidation I
landed earlier this session was undone by my own later change, and the test written
to prevent exactly that is the one that caught it. Both go through `sysfs.finite`
now. A consolidation that a later change silently undoes is the failure mode the
consolidation exists for, and only a source-level check catches it, which is why
that check is a test and not a comment.

**Two real defects were found and deliberately not fixed, because they live in the
other session's uncommitted files.** ~~Both have since been resolved: the mode
strip's~~ **The mode strip's** three `_MODES` menu lines are
42, 85 and 66 characters, and the layout contract fails any label over 30 that can
neither wrap nor ellipsise - menu items do neither. `_STYLES` directly above
documents the rule and obeys it; `_MODES` does not.
~~The root cause is **one string doing two jobs**: the third field is both the menu
text and the tooltip sentence (`f"Where answers come from: {word}. {sentence}"`), and
only one of the two can be long.~~
**That root cause was wrong, and so was the diagnosis it implies - one string was
never doing two jobs, because there were always two strings.** The tables are
`(key, word, line, icon)` and had carried a short word since they were written
down; every consumer bound it as `_word` and threw it away, putting the long
sentence in the menu instead. Re-measured 2026-10-12 after `b81f323` landed, on
which this had become a live failure in **twelve** menu labels rather than three,
and across **all five** dropdowns rather than one table - see
"A menu item is a name, not a sentence" below. The fix is not splitting one string
in two; it is using the column that was already there. Separately, ~~the cloud-keys
wizard page asks for **640px of a 560px window** - the same defect this file records
as fixed once at 590px, and still unfixed.~~ **Re-measured 2026-10-13: neither
number is current and the page is not overflowing at all.**
`test_no_wizard_page_needs_a_sideways_scrollbar[cloud-keys]` **passes**, as do all
16 wizard pages in that file - so "still unfixed" was a stale label, and this file
contradicted itself about it twice (see "Other suite fixes" further down, which
records the 590px fix as done). **A recorded open defect that is fixed reads as
work still to do, and this one had been carried since 2026-10-12.** What cloud-keys
*does* still do is fail to render at all, for an unrelated reason - see "The third
false pass" below.

Committing my version of `gui/window.py` or `setup_wizard.py` while they hold
uncommitted work in both would drop it, which is the destructive path operation this
workspace forbids in a different disguise. The findings are recorded with the root
cause and the shape of the fix instead.

**How this resolved.** `gui/window.py` was committed by the other session (`b81f323`,
the model selector) and became clean, so the mode-strip defect was fixed here rather
than left recorded - see "A menu item is a name, not a sentence" below, which also

### And one clean check worth having run

`usr/share/glib-2.0/schemas/gschemas.compiled` is **tracked in git**. A compiled

## The settings window had no layout check, and the one label it flags is a measured false positive (2026-10-12)

The layout contract covers three things: every surface (parametrized), every
wizard page (`test_no_wizard_page_needs_a_sideways_scrollbar`) and the main window
(`test_the_main_window_wraps_or_ellipsises_its_long_text`). **The settings window was
in none of them** - verified by grep, no test mentioning `SettingsWindow` also
mentions wrap, ellipsis, overflow, scroll, width or layout.

That is the same shape as the `inventory` surface that could not scroll for months:
found only by somebody looking, because a gap in a contract is an *absence* and
absence is not something a suite reports. So the sweep passed while 25 groups of
subtitles written to be read were unchecked.

Measured rather than assumed - **710 labels**, and what the predicate flags:

    Check which providers can do speech   35 chars, no wrap, no ellipsis

**And it is a false positive, with the measurement that says so.** It is a button
label demanding **289px of a 560px window** - it fits, with room. The predicate is a
*heuristic*: over 30 characters is the shape that *can* exceed a window, which is
not the same as exceeding one. So the exemption carries the number, and the test
asserts `demand <= 560` on every entry - an exemption that has silently grown past
the window fails rather than sitting there looking deliberate.

`test_the_settings_window_wraps_or_ellipsises_its_long_text` and
`test_the_settings_window_check_is_not_vacuous` (2). **The negative control drives
the predicate itself**, over four labels, and asserts it separates the one that
cannot shrink from the three that can - because the first version built a long
label, asserted it was long, and asserted it was not in the table, which passes
whether or not the check works. Removing the length test from
`_settings_offenders` fails **both** tests, verified by running it.

## The four senses the README's table did not have, and the check nothing ran (2026-10-12)

A chunked suite run found that my chunk-composition had included `tests/check_*.py`
— **audit scripts, not pytest tests** — and that collecting them killed the run
with `SystemExit`. Running them as scripts instead found `check_readme_numbers.py`
reporting **five problems**, one of them serious:

> 4 sense(s) in the tree are absent from the table: ['kernellog', 'monitoring',
> 'polkitpolicy', 'ups']

`ups` defaults **on**. So the README under-reported by a sense which senses poll by
default, on the page whose whole job is to say which ones do.

**The root cause is not a stale file, it is a check that is run by nothing.**
`tests/check_readme_numbers.py` re-derives every number in the README's prose and
its senses table from `discover_senses()`, `tools.TOOLS` and the gschema - it was
committed, it was correct, and **no pytest module, no CI workflow and no script
ever ran it**. `tests/check_capabilities_doc.py` has exactly the same shape and is
wired by `test_capabilities_doc.py`; this is the same wiring for the other one. **A
check that is not run is not a check**, which is the sentence in that file that
made this one necessary.

The table carries the four missing rows now and the prose carries the measured
counts. **The prose I wrote first was wrong twice, and measuring it is what said
so**: I wrote "18 event-type keys" and "19 of the 78 default on", where the tree
says **19** event types and **25** default on - all 25 of them senses, none of them
event types. The decomposition also does not sum: 53 senses + 19 event types + 7
retired is **79 keys in a schema holding 78**, because `git` is **both** a sense
module and an event type and the sum counts it twice. That is stated rather than
smoothed, because a number that does not sum is the reason to check it.

The four module names are `kernel_log.py` and `polkit_policy.py` while the sense
names are `kernellog` and `polkitpolicy` - the documented rule that
`glib-compile-schemas` rejects `_` in key names and discards the **entire** schema
when it hits one. So a table keyed by the module filename would have missed them a
second way.

`tests/test_readme_numbers.py` (2) runs the checker for real and carries a
**negative control**: it edits the README in a *copy* of the tree and asserts the
checker fails on it and quotes both numbers. The first version had only the
positive test and could not fail, which is the shape this file records more than
any other.


## laya's evidence states: `honest()` collapsed "unanswerable" into "no" (2026-10-12)

`harness-study/laya-decision`'s `laya/evidence.py` states the doctrine in its
opening lines:

> Every state it assigns is either derived directly from an upstream artifact or
> marked UNKNOWN. **It never manufactures a healthy-looking state from absent
> input.**

and it keeps `INSUFFICIENT` apart from `MISSING` for the reason this needed:
*there and too thin to support a claim* is not *not there*.

Chronoa's `learning.Report.honest()` collapsed the same distinction into a bare
`False`. Measured: a model whose minority verdict has **3 examples** (under
`_MIN_CLASS`'s 20) and a model that **genuinely failed** to learn that verdict
returned the **same answer** - and the two have opposite remedies, one being *use
the assistant more* and the other *stop quoting the model*. This file already
records the principle from the other side: *"a truthful refusal demoted as a
failure"* is a defect, and `train_and_save()` declining with *"the training split
contains no example of verified"* is the correct output for that data. A refusal
that reads as a result is the same defect the other way up.

`Report.honest_reason()` returns `("reason", "sentence")` - `""` when honest,
`insufficient` when the question cannot be answered from this log, and
`not-detected` when it was answered and the answer was no. **`honest()` is
unchanged** and every callsite reads it; the reason is additive, and a test
asserts the two never disagree.

**Measuring found a dead branch in my own first version.** `best_detection()` only
returns verdicts for which `detected()` is true, and any of those makes `honest()`
true - so a `near-miss` branch placed after the early return could never run. A
four-case probe never reached it. It is recorded as unreachable rather than left
looking reachable.

`tests/test_honest_reason.py` (7), `tools/mutations/honest_reason.py` (**8 caught,
0 survivors**).

**Three of the eight were defects in my set, and one of them is the recurring
shape.** The class-count guard `len(counts) <= 2` was untested because my fixture
built exactly two verdicts, so it was always true - a wide report with one thin
verdict among three is the witness that was missing. One mutant altered no
behaviour because `return ("", "text")` is a **tuple**, which is truthy, so the
bool-disagreement test could not see it. And one mutated a `# pragma: no cover`
comment, which is not a mutant at all - deleted rather than kept.

53 passed across the honest-reason, learning-calibration, outcome-model,
measure-not-asserted and surface-learning suites.


## laya's hooks: `EventSink` refuses a field that is not a callable (2026-10-12)

`harness-study/laya-decision`'s `laya/hooks.py` opens with the rule:

> a plain callable is only accepted on the single-event `on_predict_start=`
> parameters, because `hooks=` reads for method names and a bare function has
> none.

An API that introspects must refuse the shape it cannot introspect, rather than
accept it and never call it. Chronoa learned the same lesson in
`skills/__init__.py`, where `run=lambda a: ...` passed `callable()` and then
failed on **every** call in a subprocess - and fixed it at the loader, not at the
caller.

`events.EventSink` had the same shape unchecked. Measured, `EventSink(on_text="not a
function")` built **cleanly** and the TypeError arrived at the call site - mid-turn,
after the model had run and the tool had been called. `__post_init__` now refuses
any field that is neither a callable nor None, naming the field and the type and
saying why the refusal is at construction.

Every construction site in the tree passes a real callable
(`app/conversation.py`, `events.fan_in`, the streaming tests), so this is defence
at the seam and not a behaviour change - asserted rather than assumed, by
`test_a_callable_object_builds`, because the obvious implementation of this guard
(`isinstance(value, type(lambda: None))`) refuses a bound method and a callable
object, and the GUI sink in another process is exactly that.

Three ways to write the guard wrongly, each of which lets a real defect through:
`if value:` (0 and "" are falsy, so they pass as None), one field checked out of
six (the unchecked one fails), and `return` instead of `raise` (a bad sink is built
and the turn runs with a dead stream).

`tests/test_sink_shape.py` (16), `tools/mutations/sink_shape.py` (**8 caught, 0
survivors**). 80 passed across the sink, streaming, harvest-tranche and task-eval
suites.

**Two of the eight mutations were malformed the first time** - both replaced one
line inside a parenthesised `raise` and left the continuation dangling, which is a
SyntaxError. The runner's `MutationDidNotParse` (added earlier this session)
reported it as an error rather than counting it as a survivor, which is the only
reason both were noticed before they were committed. A mutation that cannot parse
is not a mutation.

**And the third iteration of one of them was a survivor for a real reason:** my
test asserted the refusal names the *field* and the *type*, and the mutation kept
the type and dropped the *reason*. A refusal that says what is wrong and nothing
about why it is being caught here is a refusal nobody can act on - the assertion
that would have caught it says `"before the turn runs" in said`.


## laya's confidence floor, and the reward its one caller fed it (2026-10-12)

`harness-study/laya-decision`'s `laya/confidence.py` names the hazard precisely:

> reporting the entropy number under the `answer_confidence` name would be worse
> than reporting nothing, because **the name is what a caller filters on.**

Chronoa had it twice over, and the second instance is the one worth reading.

### The floor inflated every k above 2

`decision.confidence` floored at 0.5, on the reasoning that "a binary outcome
cannot be less than even" - true at k=2, false above, and this repository's own
outcome model has **three** verdicts. Measured:

| distribution | max(p) | was reported as |
|---|---|---|
| 0.33/0.33/0.34 | 0.34 | **0.5** |
| 0.40/0.30/0.30 | 0.40 | **0.5** |

A genuinely-below-even 3-way answer read as *even*, and **two different
distributions read as the same number** so a caller could not order them. The floor
is `1/k` now, which at k=2 is 0.5 and so leaves the case the old reason described
untouched.

### The caller was passing a reward

`ActionSelector.select` read `confidence({c: rewards.value[c]}) < threshold` - a
**reward-space** scalar through a **probability-space** clamp. An arm worth 0.05
and one worth 0.49 both reached the comparison as 0.5. Measured, that was **inert
at the default threshold of 0.7**: every value below 0.7 is unconfident whether or
not it was clamped first. It was **one constant away from live** - at 0.3 an arm
worth 0.05 climbs to 0.5 and reads as *confident*, so the explore path stops asking
about the worst tool on the machine. The threshold is on the value now.

### Two things the fix got wrong first, both caught by the same mutation run

- **A `1/k` floor reports a single value as certainty.** The old caller passed
  `{c: reward}` - one key - so `1/1 = 1.0` told a caller a 0.05 arm was certain,
  which is *worse* than the 0.5 it used to be told. `len(< 2)` now falls through
  to the value itself.
- **Three of my witnesses never called `select()`.** They rebuilt the `unconfident`
  list by hand with the same expression, or asserted on `rewards.value` directly,
  so all three mutations of the caller came back as survivors. A witness has to
  drive the thing it names.

`tests/test_confidence_floor.py` (9), `tools/mutations/confidence_floor.py`
(**6 caught, 0 survivors, 2 equivalent, both provably**).

**And the two equivalents are the interesting part.** Neither is a shrug; each
states something that is not obvious until it is measured:

1. **The `1/k` floor never binds on a valid distribution.** For any distribution
   over k outcomes the maximum is at least the mean, which is 1/k - so
   `max(1/k, top)` is `top`, always. The floor is pure defence against a caller
   passing something that is not a distribution, which is what the `len < 2` guard
   covers. Keeping it is a bet on future callers, not a current fix.
2. **The caller change is behaviour-preserving for a second, independent reason.**
   With the `len < 2` guard in place, `confidence({c: value})` returns the value
   unchanged, so putting the old call back is the same expression. The conflation is
   fixed twice over - by removing it from the caller *and* by making the function
   refuse to apply a probability floor to a scalar - and either half alone would
   have been enough, which is why both mutations are inert.

103 passed across the confidence-floor, learning-chain, learning-calibration,
outcome-model, surface-learning and learning-says-what-a-fit-is-worth suites.

### And the router's out-of-distribution finding, measured here and **not** a defect

Laya's `laya/router.py` documents the reason it routes at all:

> The English checkpoint does not gently degrade off English, it collapses: on
> 20-option MASSIVE intent it scores 0.100 on Hindi ... and it reports high
> confidence while doing so (ECE 0.855 on Hindi). Script detection is therefore
> the primary routing signal.

The analogue to check was `tool_select.select_tools`, whose noise floor is
`scored[0][0] / 3` - **which collapses to 0 when nothing matches, disabling the
very filter meant to reject noise.** That was the hypothesis. Measured, it is
wrong, and the measurement is worth writing down rather than the hypothesis:

| request | top score | tools sent | beyond CORE |
|---|---|---|---|
| `zzzz qqqq vwxk plfm tkjb` | **no ranked tools at all** | 3 | **0** |
| `set the volume to 40 percent` | 18.09 | 9 | 6 |
| `thanks!` | conversation path | 1 | **0** |

`ranked()` returns only positive scores, so a zero top score means **no entries**
rather than a zero-ranked list - `floor` falls to 0 and there is nothing for
`score >= floor` to admit. Pure conversation goes down `wants_a_conversation`. So
the unmatchable case already returns the smallest honest set, and the fix would
have been for a case that cannot occur.

**One observation recorded, not fixed:** for "set the volume to 40 percent" the
top scorer is `calculate` (18.09) with `set_volume` sixth. It is a scoring
weakness rather than a functional defect - `set_volume` is still in the candidate
list, and AGENTS.md's own eval measures 14/15 on what the *model* picks from that
list - so it is left alone rather than tuned against a number nobody is failing.


## laya, second repo: the temperature the reader divides by (2026-10-12)

The first clone was the wrong Laya - the notification command center, which gave
`prompt_pieces`. The one meant was **the decision model**
(`harness-study/laya-decision`, `NandhaKishorM/laya`): a 421M-parameter
non-autoregressive System-1 model on a ModernBERT-large backbone, Apache-2.0,
which returns typed decisions in one forward pass - `choice` (a distribution over
options), `score` (a distribution over an ordered rubric) and a calibrated
P(true) - in about 33 ms on CPU.

Its own `AGENTS.md` reads like this file's: *"Do NOT introduce a dependency on a
hosted service"*, *"If a change moves numbers, report the before and after"*,
*"Leave one runnable check behind for non-trivial logic."*

### The transfer: one pair of bounds, and the read path had none

`laya/calibrate.py` states the rule:

> Fitted temperatures go through `clamp_temperature` and therefore `TEMP_MIN,
> TEMP_MAX` from `laya.common`, **the same guard checkpoint load uses.** There is
> no second pair of bounds in this module.

Chronoa **already had temperature-scaling calibration** (`learning.fit_calibration`,
`cross_fit_calibration`, `calibration_metrics`; measured ECE 0.430 -> 0.107, NLL
0.938 -> 0.547). It also already bounded the *fit*: the golden-section search runs
`log(_T_RANGE[0])` to `log(_T_RANGE[1])`, so a fitted temperature is legal by
construction. What it had **none of** was a bound on the *read* path - and a
temperature out of a model file is the only way one outside the range reaches
`calibrated()`.

**Measured, feeding the reader what a file could hold:**

| T | top probability before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 0.05 (`_T_RANGE`'s floor) | 0.9975 | 0.9975 |
| **1e-06** | **1.000000** | 0.997482 |
| 20.0 (the ceiling) | 0.3378 | 0.3378 |
| `"0.5"` | **`TypeError`** | the identity |
| 0 / `True` | 0.4260, by luck of `or` | 0.4260, by rule |

Two failures, both the shape this file records: **below the floor the calibrated
probability saturated to 1.0**, so `Report.honest()`'s `detected` gate and
`recommend()` act on a certainty nothing earned - laya's own issue #394 (*"publishes
that same 0.24 as 0.4993, so a threshold applied to these numbers still selects
below model accuracy"*); and **a non-numeric temperature raised `TypeError`** out of
the read path, where every other failure in this module falls back to identity.

The precedent for the file-being-garbage is this file's own: unbalanced weights
once made `to_dict`'s `round(v, 6)` write **zeros**, and the file - which verified
its own digest - predicted 0.3333 for every verdict on every input.

### The design call the naive fix gets wrong, and the mutation that pins it

Clamping 0 to `_T_RANGE[0]` would make the **sharpest legal temperature** out of a
value that means "rounded away": the zeros-file would go from predicting 0.3333 on
everything to predicting ~0.997, which is a certainty instead of a flat model. So
**0 is the identity**, not the floor. `test_zero_and_true_still_read_as_the_identity`
is the witness and the mutation that removes the rule fails it.

`True` and `False` keep returning the identity too, now by an explicit
`_is_number` rather than by the accident of `temperature or 1.0` - laya records the
same trap in `laya/common.py` ("`True`/`False` used to float to 1.0/0.0 here and
read as fitted/sharpening temperatures").

**And what the clamp does not do:** `_SHIFT_MAX` is 8.0 in logits, and clamping to
it still saturates on a small spread. Laya's own wording for the asymmetry is
recorded here: *"The clamp bounds the damage; it does not calibrate anything."*

`tests/test_temperature_bounds.py` (13), `tools/mutations/temperature_bounds.py`
(**7 caught, 0 survivors, 1 equivalent documented**). 190 passed across the
temperature-bounds, outcome-model, learning-calibration, learning-chain,
learning-says-what-a-fit-is-worth, reply-style, prompt-pieces, calibration,
distill, surface-learning and tool-outcome suites; 35 sets / 296 anchors all match.

**Four of the eight mutations were once survivors of my own making**, and each is
a different way a control that cannot fail disguises itself: a bool mutation
aimed at the *call site* (inert - `float(True)` is 1.0 either way, so the witness
had to be on `_is_number` itself); a shift guard whose `try/except` below it
already catches the same case (kept, documented equivalent); a "second pair of
bounds" mutation that added a constant nothing read (deleted rather than counted);
and a floor witness using one example with one label, which `len(set(labels))`
already refuses, so removing the floor changed nothing it measured.


## laya: the system prompt is now tunable, and the safety sentence has no door (2026-10-12)

`harness-study/laya` cloned and studied (a local-first AI notification centre;
Python engine, 285 files - the same language as Chronoa). Its README states its
headline feature as:

> Override 20+ pipeline stages individually - change one, keep the rest as
> default. Tune persona voices, classification rules, or briefing style to your
> team. **Delete the file to revert - defaults always come back.**

Chronoa's `SYSTEM_PROMPT` was one hard-coded string, so a person who wanted
"answer in British English" had to edit the source and lose the default, or put
it in `rules.md` - one file, landing *after* everything, for a job it was not
shaped for. `prompt_pieces.py` is the lever.

**Four of Laya's decisions are the whole transfer, and each is a way a simpler
version lies:**

1. **The default lives in code, and nothing here writes the directory** - so
   "revert" is deleting a file, and an update can never be undone by a user edit.
2. **An unrecognised file name is a warning that lists the recognised ones.**
   `tools/mutations`'s first version of this test asserted `"recognised" in
   caplog.text`, which the word *unrecognised* satisfies - a warning that named
   the problem and not the answer still passed. It asserts each recognised
   filename now.
3. **An empty file is a warning and not an override.** Replacing a prompt with
   nothing is worse than not replacing it.
4. **`override_status()` answers "what am I overriding"** - the default alongside
   the current, because there is nothing to compare against without it.

**And the property that matters more than any of them:** the provenance boundary
sentence - the one telling the model what the untrusted-content fence means - is
**not in the registry at all**. There is no key for it, so no file can name it.
Laya's construction is the same shape, for identifier fields ("absent by
construction because capabilities don't list them as content"). A security
statement is not a preference; the way to keep it unoverridable is to leave no
door, not to check the door harder. The mutation that puts the lookup back is
**inert**, and that is the proof - a key no file maps to cannot be reached.

**Chronoa's version is stronger than Laya's in one measured way.** Laya's loader
runs at engine start, so its "delete to revert" needs a restart. `compose()` here
re-reads the directory, because it is called once per assistant built and not per
turn - so the scan is free and deletion reverts immediately. A test asserts the
immediate revert; the mutation that restores Laya's caching fails it.

`tests/test_prompt_pieces.py` (11), `tools/mutations/prompt_pieces.py` (**10
caught, 0 survivors, 1 equivalent documented**). 91 passed across the prompt,
reply-style, provenance, user-prompts and matrix-name suites; 30 sets / 265
anchors all match.

### Not taken, and why

Laya's deeper answer to a defect Chronoa records four times is **not** ported
here, because it is a refactor and not a fix. `engine/laya/egress/registry.py`
says:

> adding a platform means writing one file, not editing a dozen tables here.

Chronoa's `capabilities._GROUPS`, `GATED` and `GATE_NAMES` are three hand-kept
tables, and `test_skill_gates_are_enforced._IMPL` is a fourth; AGENTS.md records
that a duplicate key silently killed a `browse` label and that a skill landing
leaves four lists stale. Laya's answer - each skill owns its metadata, and the
prompt and the tables are **generated** from the registry, so there is no second
list to drift - is the right one and it is a change across every skill. Recorded
as the next pass, not half-done in this one.

**And it was measured before being recorded, which changes what the entry says.**
All four lists agree *today*:

| check | result |
|---|---|
| tools in the registry (`discover_skills()`) | 257 |
| with a `_GROUPS` row | **257 of 257** |
| with a `GATED` entry | 78 |
| consent keys with a `GATE_NAMES` row | **57 of 57** |
| `_IMPL` keys absent from `GATED` / `GATED` keys `_IMPL` lacks | 15 harmless extras / **none** |
| `test_capabilities`, `_doc`, `_skill_gates_are_enforced`, `_help_gate_labels` | **50 passed** |

So there is **no live defect to fix**, and doing the refactor here would have been
churn dressed as improvement: it touches every skill in the registry to prevent a
problem that is not present and is already guarded by three tests. The argument
for it is that *nothing structural keeps them that way* - a weaker claim, and it
belongs in the same sentence as the measurement rather than instead of it. The
trigger to actually do it is the first time one of those tests goes red, at which
point the refactor is the fix rather than the prophylaxis.


## The wizard's void got a mark, and the icon was a gear the first time (2026-10-11)

Reported as *"minor UI glitches during model/voice installation"*, then, looking at
the rendered pages: *"if void it should have some icon no?"*

**Measured against the 620px default window, four of the sixteen pages have far
less content than it has room for** - `ears` 270px, `brain` 84px, `mode` 316px,
`model-picker` 470px - so between the last row and the pinned action there was 150
to 536px of nothing. Holding the action at the bottom is right, and this file's
`setup_wizard` comment explains why at length; half a screen of nothing above it
is what reads as broken.

The void now carries Chronoa's orb. **Three things the first version got wrong,
all found by running it rather than by reading the diff:**

1. **The icon was a gear.** `Gtk.Image.new_from_icon_name("shani-chronoa")` is a
   *theme lookup*: it needs `usr/share/icons/hicolor/` on an `XDG_DATA_DIRS` that
   an installed system has and a checkout does not. The render came back as GTK's
   missing-image placeholder - **a gear** - which is what "some page had a gear
   icon" was reporting. The mark is embedded SVG bytes now, drawn through
   `Gtk.Svg` + `Gtk.Picture`, so it is identical in the app, in a render and in a
   test, with no file, no theme and no compiled `GResource` (this repo has none).
2. **The mark appeared on all sixteen pages, including the one that overflows.**
   `upper <= page_size` is the no-scrollbar case, and it is *also* what an
   unallocated scroller reports - `upper` and `page_size` are both 0 before the
   widget has been laid out, and `0 <= 0 + 1` is true. `review`, whose content
   demands 1029px of a 620px window, got a mark drawn over it. The rule is a
   named function now, `_void_has_room`, and a page that has never been measured
   is not a page with room in it.
3. **The panel's first name collided.** `gui/surfaces/background.py` shadowed
   `shani_chronoa.background` - the module that owns the inventory the surface
   draws - so `from shani_chronoa.gui.surfaces import background` inside it
   resolved to *itself*, `background.inventory` did not exist, and the whole
   layout suite came back as errors. Renamed to `gui/surfaces/processes.py`. Same
   shape as `calendar.py` shadowing the stdlib: a name is not just a label.

**And on the Brain page, a jump that read as dead text.** "Use a model on this
computer" is a wired `Gtk.Button` that goes to the model picker - styled `flat`,
which in a dark theme renders as unstyled words. So it sat underneath the Next
button looking exactly like a label nobody connected. The control was never
broken; the affordance was missing, and the chevron is what makes one - the same
device this file's welcome rows use, whose own comment says a chevron is not
decoration.

**And it was then lost, which is the part worth recording.** The chevron was
added, the render was read, `Use a model on this computer >` was on screen - and
a concurrent session committed `setup_wizard.py` from an earlier state. Nothing
failed, because nothing asserted the affordance; the next render showed the bare
label again and the report came back as *"re add setup wizard changes i think
they are not added"*. **A change verified only by looking at a picture is a
change one commit away from not existing.**
`test_a_flat_jump_button_still_says_it_goes_somewhere` and its mutation are the
fix, and both are in the set now.


`tools/mutations/wizard_mark.py` (9). **7 caught, 1 survivor that was my witness
being wrong, 1 equivalent kept and documented.**

### The mutation runner reported errors as survivors, which is the same bug twice

Two of those nine were reported as survivors for a reason that has nothing to do
with coverage:

- A mutation that produced an `IndentationError` aborted pytest with *"1 error
  during collection"* and exit 2. `_failures` looked only for the words
  *" passed"* or *" failed"*, neither of which is in that sentence - so it printed
  `(no summary)` and counted the mutation as a survivor.
- A mutation that broke a module's import gave `27 passed, 101 errors` and no
  FAILED lines at all, which is again not a survivor: it is a run that could not
  measure anything.

`_failures` collects `ERROR` lines as well as `FAILED` now, and raises
`MutationDidNotParse` for a run with no summary. Both are OmO's #8850 in the
other direction - **a check that could not run is not a check that found
nothing** - which is the same statement `verification.py`'s exit-code protocol
made earlier the same day.

The survivor was mine: I had named `test_no_wizard_page_needs_a_sideways_scrollbar`
as the witness, which only ever builds the *wizard* and so passes. What breaks is
every test that walks the surfaces.


## The force stop, the reaper, and a model nobody could start (2026-10-11)

Reported in a person's words: *"it needs a force stop button - manually blocking
those processes for beginners could be a headache, otherwise they face heavy
resource usage"*, and *"when shifting to that Kilo APIs, needs button to run the
model etc"*. Both were **measured gaps, not feature requests**, and the second
one is the same defect the first is.

### Six background watchers were started and could not be stopped

`app/application.py` starts the incoming-call watcher, the message watcher, the
file-sharing receiver, the watch companion, the phone-keyboard service and the
Bluetooth music remote **unconditionally**, at startup. Each is written with a
`stop()`. Two scans:

| scan | result |
|---|---|
| the tree, for calls to those `stop()`s | **none** |
| `gui/` and `app/tray.py`, for the six by name | **no hit** |

So a machine could hold a Bluetooth link, a watch connection or a microphone open
for as long as the app ran, with quitting as the only lever - on a machine
somebody is gaming or streaming on, that is not a lever. This is the dead-code
class this file records four times, in the shape that costs.

`background.py` is the inventory, read **off the live application object** rather
than a hand-kept list, so adding a component cannot silently drop it. The surface
is "What's running", with a Stop per row and a **Stop everything** that asks
first and names what it takes. Two rules it is held to: a row with a dead Stop
button says *why there is no stop* instead of rendering one, and a row only reads
"stopped" when the component itself confirmed - `presence.py`'s Settings control
already does that, and this does the same.

### The child supervisor could see a hung child and had nothing to do about it

`check_heartbeats` reports `DISCONNECTED` - "alive but silent past the budget:
hung" - and its own docstring says *"waiting longer for a hung one is
pointless"*. **Every caller in the tree only reads that status.** A detector with
no reaper is the control-nothing-reaches class again.

Measured on this box, the cost of the whole shape: a `llama-server` up
**7h36m holding 1.09 GB**, and two `whisper-cli` runs up **44 and 2 minutes on
3-4 second WAVs holding 4.7 GB each**. Killing four PIDs took available memory
from **9 GB to 18 GB**. Those two were *not* Chronoa's children - they were this
agent's own measurement runs - and no supervisor could have reached them, because
a process may only signal its own descendants. But a hung child of Chronoa's own
was already visible to the supervisor and nothing acted on it.

`reap_hung()` closes that loop: terminate, a bounded grace, then SIGKILL. Guarded
two ways, and **both guards are load-bearing** - it re-probes immediately before
the signal (a pid that already belongs to a stranger must not be signalled), and
only a *tracked* child with a pid is ever signalled (a stand-in must not take
down whatever happens to be at that number).

**The re-probe guard is asserted on the log, not on a kill.** Its removal is
otherwise unobservable: `os.kill` on a dead pid raises OSError, which the reaper
already caught, so `reap_hung()` returns the same empty list either way. The
guard's value is that it declines *before* trying, and the only place that shows
is the sentence it logs.

### The model could be released but not started

`presence.py` and `settings_window` had a working cycle - Ready, "Letting go of
the model", Asleep - which calls `local_llm.start_service/stop_service`. What it
could not do is **start** one: the button said "Free the model" and "Asleep" and
nothing else, and the state that matters here ("the model is off because the
cloud fallback answered instead") is not shown on the row. A person who wanted
their local model back had to press a button labelled with the opposite of what
they wanted, three times.

**"Run the model" is added, and the cycle was not removed.** `Asleep` means "stop
it *and* do not start it again to answer the next question", which no pair of
Run/Stop buttons can express; dropping it to fit two buttons would have removed a
capability to fix a different one. It runs off the main loop like the cycle, and
**re-reads** the state afterwards - "Started" and "is answering" are different
claims and only the second is worth showing.

`tests/test_what_is_running.py` (19) and `tests/test_settings_text_fields.py`
(3 more, 7 in the file). **Seven of the first twelve mutations in the set were
defects in the set, not in the code**, and four of them were mutations aimed at
nothing: replacing a whole guard with a bare `continue` made the reaper a no-op,
which the real-kill test already caught, so they said nothing about the pid or
the state filter they claimed to test. Two more were *equivalent* - the failed
stop's `self.running = True` is redundant on the first call, and `stop is None`
rows already land in `refused`, so both witnesses had to be built before the
mutation could break anything. That is the recorded "a control that cannot fail"
trap, hit five times in one file.

### And the mutation runner reported a broken mutation as a **survivor**

Three of those seven were mutations that produced code which **could not parse** -
one had its replacement indented one level too far, giving `IndentationError:
unexpected indent`. pytest aborted with *"1 error during collection"* and exit 2,
and `_failures`' parser looked only for the words *" passed"* or *" failed"* -
**neither of which appears in that sentence.** So the run reported
`(no summary)` and counted the mutation as a survivor: it read as *"the tests did
not catch this"*, when the truth is *"nothing was measured at all"*.

That is OmO's #8850 from the other side, and it is the same error the exit-code
protocol fixes in `verification.py` - **a check that could not run is not a check
that found nothing.** `_failures` now raises `MutationDidNotParse` for a run with
no summary, so it is reported as an error rather than as a survivor, and "error
during collection" is named separately from "pytest produced no summary".

The fourth was worse in a way only running it showed: the re-probe guard's witness
passed `pid=os.getpid()`, on the reasoning that the guard declines before any
signal - which is exactly what it does *while the guard is present*. Remove the
guard and the reaper SIGTERMs the pytest process, so the run dies with no output
and the mutation is unmeasurable. **A fixture that kills the runner it is being
measured by cannot measure anything.** It tracks a throwaway `sleep` now, and
asserts it is still alive afterwards, so the guard's absence is observable from
outside: alive means it worked, dead means it did not.


before editing, and follow the verification steps before calling any change
done.

  (`HARVEST-2/E-memory-mcp-special.md`'s "threshold gate") was already found
  false. Check a claim against the code before acting on it.

(2026-10-12), including a 286-line deep pass, so nothing here depended on having
read them. `harness-study/` is **not a git repository**, so a harvest nothing
points at exists on one disk until that disk is reused.

**Recorded against myself, in the same pass: `git commit --only <file>` is not
safe in this workspace, and the rule above did not say so.** The workspace's
`AGENTS.md` documents `git commit` with no paths sweeping another session's staged
work, and prescribes `--only`. It scopes **paths, not lines**. `git add AGENTS.md
&& git commit --only AGENTS.md` was run while a concurrent session had ~200 lines
of an uncommitted section in the same file, and **their work landed inside my
commit** (`c3ba7b5`, whose message is about the harvest). Nothing was lost and no
file was clobbered; the cost is that their work is now attributed to me and their
next commit will not contain it, because the file is clean. The fix is the one the
workspace already gives for the narrow case: **back up, write the note, and commit
only what you can show is yours** - here, by checking `git show --stat` named the
line count *before* pushing the commit. Rewriting the history is a person's
decision, not a mechanical one, and it is recorded rather than fixed.

| `HARVEST-LINUX-HELLO.md` | linux-hello | three transfers, all measured: a pure `plausible()` beside detection so the face decision is testable without OpenCV; a **15-line V4L2 capability probe** - `/dev/video1` here is a metadata node that cannot capture, while `QUERYCAP` answers for it anyway; and **infrared capture in both photo skills**, verified against a real `v4l2loopback` IR camera: 58,791 bytes of h264 holding 90 frames, 206 levels from a 127-level source, which is why both replies state what ffmpeg's conversion did. The anti-spoofing set, the IR liveness constants, `mmap` streaming, the warm daemon and the PAM profile are refused with reasons. Recorded as a defect in the upstream: **face templates written world-readable (dir 0755, file 0644)** |
| `HARVEST-BWRAP.md` | bubblewrap | the three sandbox protections that belong to the machine |
| `HARVEST-MAZE.md` | Maze-AI | nothing; a short negative result |
