## An "unwired" finding that was a 90-second snapshot of somebody wiring it (2026-10-12)

`grep -rn "code_hl" --include=*.py .` returned **nothing**, about a 400-line
module. Every check the repo prescribes was run and every one agreed: no
importer, no string-held reference, no `usr/bin/` launcher, no test, no registry
marker. The write-up was one sentence from being *"built and wired to nothing,
again."*

It is wired. `gui/blocks.py:54` imports it and `:417`/`:488` call
`code_hl.highlight(...)`, and `tests/test_code_highlighting.py` exists. The
mtimes say what happened:

    blocks.py   19:41:38   <- the import landed here
    test file   19:42:57
    code_hl.py  19:43:08
    my grep     before 19:41:38

**I measured a tree that was being edited underneath me, and the conclusion I
drew was true for ninety seconds.** The other session wrote the module, then
wrote the wiring, then wrote the test — and I looked in the middle of that.

### The rule, and it is not "re-check before recording"

The checks were all correct and all agreed; re-running the grep thirty seconds
later would have been enough. The real hazard is what the finding *looks like*:
**an unwired module is the single most common defect in this repository, so a
measurement that supports it is believed without a second look.** A plausible
finding about a well-known problem is the easiest one to ship unchecked, and
this is the fourth time this session a confident reading was contradicted by
re-measuring.

Two habits follow, and the second is the one that generalises:

- **Timestamp any claim about the tree.** A finding with no time on it cannot be
  told from a stale one, and "no reference anywhere" is meaningless without "as
  of when".
- **An untracked file being actively written is a tree in motion.** Its wiring
  is *the thing being written*, so an absence measured against it is measuring
  the author's progress, not the code. For a file whose mtime is minutes old,
  "unwired" is a claim about the session, not the repository.

## Code in a reply is coloured, and GtkSourceView was the wrong answer (2026-10-12)

Asked whether `gtksourceview` could be a dependency. Measured it on both target
distributions first, and **the answer changed twice** - so the measurement is the
entry.

### What Arch actually ships

`gtksourceview5`, `extra`, **5.22.0-1**, and cheap in a way the raw PKGBUILD does
not suggest: of its 13 declared dependencies **GTK4 already pulls 9**, so the
marginal cost is `hicolor-icon-theme`, `libxml2` and `pcre2`. I first told the
user "12 dependencies" from the raw list, which was **wrong as an argument** - the
cost was never the reason.

**And it cannot highlight.** Arch's PKGBUILD is a vanilla `meson install` with
nothing added for language specs, and `pkgname` is only `gtksourceview5` +
`-docs`. The shipped package contains:

    usr/share/gtksourceview-5/language-specs/language.dtd
    usr/share/gtksourceview-5/language-specs/language.rng
    usr/share/gtksourceview-5/language-specs/language2.rng

- the **schema** for writing a `.lang`, and **zero** language definitions. The
GTK3 line ships **173**. Identical on Ubuntu 5.18, so it is upstream and not a
packaging drop.

Meanwhile the two mechanical reasons to want the widget are **already there**:
`CodeBlock` is a selectable label inside a 260px scroller. And it is
**read-only** - an editor widget answers "I want to type here", which a
transcript does not.

`python-pygments` **2.21.0** is in Arch `extra` and would highlight today with no
authoring. Not taken: shipped code here uses the standard library, and `sox` is
already an optdepend rather than a hard one for the same reason.

### Why the palette is per-theme, and it is arithmetic

Not a preference. For **4.5:1** a colour's relative luminance must be
**<= 0.1833** against white and **>= 0.2544** against Adwaita's dark `#242424`.
**Those bounds are disjoint**, so **no single colour is legible on both themes** -
a one-palette highlighter is wrong on one of them, which is the
light-theme-hex-on-a-dark-desktop defect this file already records once in the
Diff panel. Ten candidate colours were measured before the palettes were chosen;
none cleared both, and that is what the arithmetic predicts.

`gui/code_hl.py` asks `Adw.StyleManager` which theme is in force, and
`TranscriptView` owns **one** `dark-changed` connection that re-renders. A block
connecting its own bound method to a process-wide singleton would keep itself
alive for the life of the app, and a long conversation is many blocks. The walk
is over the **subtree**, because a turn is a container holding its blocks - a
first-child-only walk finds nothing and reports success.

### One scanner, ten tables

A tokenizer per language is sixteen near-copies of the same loop, which is the
shape this file records biting twice (`wpctl` three times, the finite check four
times). The scanner is written once; a language is a table. Diff gets its own
seven-line loop because it is per-line rather than per-token, which is less
general than contorting `Spec` with three fields only it would read.

Token text is escaped **after** tokenising and **before** it enters a tag, so
model-supplied markup cannot escape into the label, and nothing a model writes is
ever inside an attribute - a test asserts every `<span>` carries exactly one
attribute and that it is a colour from our own table. An unrecognised language
returns escaped code **unchanged**: no half-right colouring.

### Three defects of my own, all found by running it

- **A plain-text branch that swallowed to end-of-line.** A four-line Python
  sample carrying a keyword, a comment, a string, a number and a call produced
  **1 span instead of 6** - an indented comment was inside a "plain" run and
  never seen. Fixed by emitting one character at a time.
- **An infinite loop on the first newline.** `code.find("\n", i)` returns `i`
  when `code[i]` *is* that newline, so the run was empty and `i` never advanced.
  **A highlighter that hangs is worse than one that does not colour.**
- **A double-`else`** that is a `SyntaxError`, and a `Spec` whose `keywords` had
  no default.

And an inverted assertion in the test: I asserted the two luminance bounds
*overlap* when the entire point is that they are disjoint. pyflakes found a
`Gtk.Label.get_markup()` that does not exist in the same run.

### The control this file's own lesson applies to

The contrast assertions only check each palette against **its own** background, so
**one palette copied twice passes all of them**. `test_the_two_palettes_are_
genuinely_two` asserts each palette **fails** on the other's - which is what makes
the theme switch load-bearing rather than decorative, and is the difference
between a contrast check and a proof of the switch.

The round-trip uses `Gtk.Label.get_text()`, not `get_label()`. `get_label()`
returns the markup source whether or not Pango parsed it, so an assertion against
it passes on a label the toolkit silently refused - the control this file already
had to learn when the Diff panel's fills were measured on words that were never
coloured. The block test uses **all three** read-backs (`get_use_markup`,
`get_label`, `get_text`) because each answers a different question.

**Mutations, five, all run and all caught**: one palette copied twice; token text
no longer escaped; the plain-text run restored; an unknown language silently
coloured as Python; and the theme walk narrowed to direct children.

### What this does not establish

**It is a lexer, not a parser.** A `#` inside a Python string is handled the way a
lexer handles it, not the way Python does; so is a `"""` opened inside a comment.
`.lang` specs get that right and a lexer will not, and the honest comparison
between the two is not "specs are more code" but "specs are a state machine".

**Nothing was rendered and looked at.** Every gate here is structural - a
round-trip, a contrast ratio, a tag shape. This repository records twice that a
widget can pass every check and still be unreadable: the organ strip passed its
width test while rendering as one run-on string, and the voice-style row was
inspected only after shipping.

## Five mutations, and the ninth witness that could not fail (2026-10-12)

The commit above recorded the syntax-highlighting gates as **not**
mutation-verified. They are now, and the verification produced two findings worth
more than the tally.

### A harness that hangs looks exactly like a harness that buffers

Four attempts produced **no output at all**, and I read that as buffering. It was
not: **mutation 3 restores the infinite loop**, so pytest never completes and
prints nothing. The harness was not slow or silent - it was stuck, and the
300-second timeout was the only thing that ever said so.

**That cost four turns and I blamed the wrong thing each time.** The symptom is
identical to a buffering pipe and to a slow cold tree, and the distinguishing
evidence is the one I did not look for: a run that *should* take 0.7s and takes
300s is not buffering, it is hung. This file already records the mirror - *"a
check that could not run is not a check that found nothing"* - and this is the
same sentence about a **test run** rather than a check.

### Five mutations, five caught - and one only after the witness was rewritten

| mutation | verdict |
|---|---|
| one palette copied twice | CAUGHT - 2 failed |
| token text no longer escaped | CAUGHT - 9 failed |
| plain text swallowed to end of line | CAUGHT **by hanging** - the mutant never finishes |
| unknown language coloured as Python | CAUGHT - 1 failed |
| theme walk narrowed to direct children | **SURVIVED**, then CAUGHT |

**The survivor was my test, and it is the ninth of its kind this session.** It
built a `CodeBlock`, buried it a level down, called `_on_dark_changed()`, and
asserted the text was unchanged and the markup held a span. Both hold - because
**the block is already coloured by its own constructor**. The assertions passed
for code that never re-rendered, which is the recorded *"a witness that cannot
fail"* in a file where it has now happened nine times.

The fix is to make the two states **differ**: build under one theme, switch
`_is_dark`, then assert the markup came back carrying the *other* palette's
colours. That can only happen if the walk reached the block. Re-run against the
mutation: **1 failed, 65 passed**.

**A test that renders at construction cannot detect a failure to re-render**,
and any assertion about a post-hoc refresh needs something that changes between
the two moments. That is the generalisable half, and it is the same lesson as
`Report.honest()`'s `near-miss` branch: a fixture that cannot reach the code it
claims to measure measures the fixture.

### The harness rewrote the shared tree, and a concurrent session read it

The first attempt applied each mutation **in place**, in a tree two sessions work
in. A second session's pytest (`XDG_STATE_HOME=/tmp/opencode/chl`, PID 530466)
started running my new test file **while mutation 3 was applied** - so it would
have read deliberately broken code and reported failures on correct code. That is
the exact incident `conftest.py`'s `_mutation_in_flight` documents and cannot
prevent from inside a suite, and **I caused it**.

Stopped by killing my own driver **by PID** (never by name - the workspace rule),
and both files restored byte-identical. The rerun copies the package to a temp
tree and mutates there, so the shared tree is never rewritten at all. **A
mutation harness in a shared tree should not touch the shared tree**, and the
lock in `tools/mutate.py` guards two mutation runs from each other rather than
guarding either from a plain `pytest`.

## Rendered and looked at: the colours paint (2026-10-12)

Every gate above is structural - a round-trip, a contrast ratio, a tag shape -
and this file's own history is that a widget can satisfy all three and still be
unreadable. The organ strip passed its width test while drawing eight labels as
one run-on string; the voice-style row was inspected only after shipping. So the
markup was rendered and **the picture read**.

    # a comment          <- grey      1314 px
    def                  <- pink       347 px   (#b02a8b, light) / 345 (#ff7b72, dark)
    f(x):                <- f orange    42 px   (the `name` colour, distinct from keyword)
    # an indented comment<- grey      ~650 px
    return               <- pink
    "a string"           <- green      327 px
    42                   <- blue        86 px

Dark re-renders with the dark palette and the same counts to within
antialiasing (comment 1226, keyword 345, string 325, number 89, name 38), so
**both palettes reach the screen** - which is the thing the disjoint-luminance
argument only ever claimed should be possible.

`preproc` and `error` measure **0 px, and that is correct**: the sample is
Python, which has no preprocessor, and it is not a diff, so it has no removed
line. A zero with no reason is a defect; a zero with a reason is a measurement.

### The recipe, after five attempts that each failed for a recorded reason

**No window at all.** Draw into a `Gtk.Snapshot` directly, exactly as
`automation_overlay`'s cue layer does:

    layout = Gtk.Label().create_pango_layout("x")      # for its Pango context
    ok, attrs, plain, _len = Pango.parse_markup(markup, -1, "\x00")
    layout.set_text(plain); layout.set_attributes(attrs)
    snapshot.append_layout(layout, Gdk.RGBA())        # (layout, COLOUR), not a position
    node = snapshot.to_node()
    Gsk.CairoRenderer.new() -> realize(None) -> render_texture(node, viewport)

What each earlier attempt cost:

| attempt | why it failed |
|---|---|
| window + `present()` + timer | a timer added inside `activate` never fires on broadway - four runs produced no output and I read it as buffering twice |
| `Gtk.Widget.snapshot()` | not exposed by this PyGObject; it suggests `do_snapshot` |
| `Gtk.WidgetPaintable` | NO NODE - an unmapped widget has no surface, this file's own recorded trap |
| `Gdk.Texture.download()` | takes 3 arguments here, not 4 - which is why `test_automation_overlay.py` decodes the PNG by hand, and its decoder was lifted rather than rewritten |
| `create_pango_layout(markup)` | **does not parse markup in GTK 4** |

**And that last one is the one worth keeping.** It did not fail - it produced a
perfectly good image of the *tags as literal text*, with every token colour at
**0 px**. `create_pango_layout` treats its argument as plain text, so the
renderer faithfully drew `<span foreground="#6a737d">` as characters.

### The instrument had no positive control, and said so by passing wrongly

The first version reported **all seven token colours at 0 px and all four
negative controls at 0 px**, and printed *"the counting method is trustworthy"*.
Every number was vacuous: a blank image matches no colour at all, so a negative
control **cannot distinguish "this colour is absent" from "nothing was
rendered"**.

**The positive control is what caught it** - non-black pixels and distinct
colours in the image - and it is now in the probe:

    POSITIVE CONTROL: 2299 non-black px, 269 distinct colours of 19780
    OK - the image is NOT blank, so a 0 below means 0

**A control that only ever proves a thing is missing proves nothing about a
thing that is present**, and a colour-counting probe needs both directions. This
is the same sentence as the Diff panel's fills being measured on words that were
never coloured, arrived at from the measuring instrument rather than the product.

The negative control still reports **5 magenta and 1 blue pixel** at tolerance 3
- subpixel antialiasing fringes, not a palette entry. So the probe prints
*"do not trust any number above"*, which is the correct thing for it to say: the
fringe pixels are indistinguishable from a real colour by this method. The
counts are still meaningful at a 260:1 ratio, and **the picture is the evidence**,
not the histogram.

### What is still not done

**The probe lives in `/tmp/opencode/` and this session ends.** That is exactly
what this file's own rule forbids - a check written by hand into a scratch dir is
lost - and the fix is a `slot-test` in `shani-testbed`, where a real display and
the image's own Python exist. Not built here. What is durable is the recipe
above and the measurement, and a future pass should re-run it rather than trust
the numbers.

## The reachability scan counted prose, and its control named its own subject (2026-10-12)

Follow-up to the entry above. The word-mention scan landed this session had the
**mirror-image** mistake of the one it was built to fix, and measuring it found
both halves at once.

**The false positive.** `TranscriptView.set_suggestion_handler` is dead -
`tools/deadcode.py` reports it, and it has no caller of any kind, not even a test
- and it is named exactly once outside its own definition: a `window.py`
docstring explaining the pattern `None` follows. A raw-text scan counts that
word and calls the method live. So the extractor tokenises now and drops
comments and docstrings.

**Why strings are still kept, because dropping them is the other error.**
Dropping *all* string literals - deadcode.py's deliberate rule - calls **four
live methods dead**:

| name | how it is reached |
|---|---|
| `show_devices` | a `getattr` string tuple at `phone_link.py:370` |
| `speaking_row` | `voice.py`'s `_FORWARDED` `setattr(page, name, getattr(...))` |
| `webkit_version` | called inside a subprocess harness held as a string, `tests/test_browser_window_probe.py` |
| `activity_text` | the same, `tests/test_browse_in_app.py` |

None of the four appears as a code token anywhere. So the rule is **prose goes,
dispatch strings stay**, and both directions are asserted against real names,
because either alone is satisfiable by a scanner that is simply broken.

**And the control for this named its own subject, twice.** Spelling the dead
method in the test puts it in the test's source, which `_all_files` reads and
counts - so the control manufactured the very caller it asserts is absent.
Measured: the first version named it four times and failed `assert 3 == 0`, every
count from its own docstring. Moving the name out of the test body failed again
at 3, because the module-level `_index` docstring still spelled it. The name is
composed at runtime now with a guard asserting it is absent from the file's own
text. **A control that names its subject is a control that cannot fail** - the
same trap as the enum scan that found its own literals, the grep that matched
its own comment, and `price`/`collapse` matching English words.

Three mutations, all caught, both files restored byte-identical afterwards:
prose counted again (1), all strings dropped (2), a true orphan on the real tree
via `_record_row`'s call site (1).

### Recorded, not fixed: the sibling that is wired and the one that is not

`TranscriptView` carries **two** near-identical methods.
`set_regenerate_handler` is wired, and the chain is three links so a reader can
check it: `app/conversation.py:180` calls `self.window.set_regenerate_handler(...)`,

and that is `widgets.py`'s method. This file already records the false claim that

`set_suggestion_handler` is wired to **nothing at all**: no caller in `usr/`,

outside its own definition, and its sibling still 2.

Not wired here, because what a *suggestion* handler should do is a product

## A skill is a subprocess, so its answer string is the only channel it has (2026-10-12)

### The design that could not work, and the first run that proved it

Artifacts (files a skill made, rendered as a thumbnail in the transcript) were
declared with a thread-local ledger: the skill recorded its output paths while
it still held them, and `tools` drained the ledger immediately after the handler
returned, on the same thread, with nothing awaited in between. That reasoning
was sound and the implementation was correct. Every dispatch still came back
empty.

**A skill does not run in this process.** `tools` interpolates the arguments
into a `python3 -c` program and runs it, so the skill body executes in a
different process and its in-process state cannot cross back except through its
answer string. Measured by printing `os.getpid()` on both sides of a real
`create_document` dispatch - the traced `produced()` never fired in the caller's
process. The ledger was deleted; there was nothing to fix, because the state
simply does not travel.

So `DECLARES_ARTIFACTS` reads the path back out of the sentence the skill wrote
about itself, and that is now a property of the architecture rather than a
preference. `edit_image` is the case that proves why it has to be the skill's own
wording and not a heuristic: it answers *"Saved cat.jpg (resized): 40 KB"* - a
bare file name with no directory - so no amount of pattern-matching recovers a
path from it.

### Three fields, two of them dead, and the plumbing looked complete

Adding `artifacts` is a five-hop change, and the hops were all wired. It still
delivered nothing, twice:

1. **`ToolOutcome` had no `artifacts` field.** The assistant reads
   `result.artifacts` off whatever `_run_tool` returned, and that is a
   `ToolOutcome`. `getattr(result, "artifacts", ())` answered `()` - quietly, at
   runtime, with no error at any hop.
2. **The subprocessed dispatch dropped it.** The in-process return passed
   `artifacts=`; the post-condition return built `DispatchResult` with
   *positional* arguments, so the field took its `()` default. Found by spying
   on every `DispatchResult` the dispatcher builds, which printed
   `artifacts=()` with `artifacts_for` never having been called.

The second is this repository's own dead-code class reached through a field
instead of a module, and the only reason it was caught is that a real dispatch
was run and its output printed. Nothing about reading the diff would have shown
either one.

### The negative control had to be able to fail

`files.paths_in` is the shared extractor, so each skill declares with one line
rather than a near-copy. Its test asserts that a loose pattern would be
dangerous - and it is:

| pattern | `I could not write anything.` | `Saved /tmp/a.md (not a number).` | `A page said: Saved /tmp/from-the-web.md (12 bytes).` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `^Saved (.+?) \(\d+ bytes\)\.$` | `()` | `()` | `()` |
| `Saved (.+?) \(\d+ bytes\)` | `()` | `()` | **`('/tmp/from-the-web.md',)`** |

The loose one pulls a path out of a sentence that *quotes a web page* - which is
the whole reason a file is rendered from a declaration rather than scraped from
the model's prose. The `^` anchor is load-bearing, not decoration.

### State of this feature

- Six skills declare: `generate_image`, `create_document`, `convert_document`,
  `take_photo`, `analyze_table`, `recording`. One shared extractor, six lines.
- `edit_image` and `office_document` still declare nothing, for the reason above:
  one names a bare file name, the other names a *directory*. Neither can be
  converted by pattern, and inventing a path for them would be fabricating it.
- Mutation-checked: reverting the post-condition fix fails
  `test_a_dispatched_skill_that_makes_a_file_declares_it`. 22 tests in
  `tests/test_a_made_file_is_shown.py`.
- Pre-existing and unrelated, recorded so it is not re-investigated:
  `test_reply_blocks.py::TestWidgetsFor::test_math_falls_back_to_the_source_when_matplotlib_is_absent`
  fails with `AttributeError: 'MathBlock' object has no attribute 'language'`.
  Verified by swapping in the pre-`ArtifactBlock` `blocks.py` and getting an
  identical failure - it is not a regression from this work.

## The lock fix never landed, and the entry that proved it read as though it had (2026-10-12)

The two entries above diagnose the trigger tests' shared-OS-lock failure and then
*prove* the remedy: *"isolating `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` takes the trigger tests from 6
failures to 137 passed ... The fix is one line and it is in the test, not the
product."* **Nothing was committed.** `grep -n XDG_RUNTIME_DIR tests/conftest.py`
returned nothing, today, after both entries.

So the suite was **conditionally green**: it passed only because no Chronoa
process happened to hold the lock at that moment. Re-measured the same way the
entry above measured it - hold the flock in another process, run the file:

| state | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| lock held by another process | **6 failed, 131 passed** | **137 passed** |
| lock free | 137 passed | 137 passed |

**And "proved" is not "applied".** The proof ran the file with
`XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` pointed at an empty directory *on the command line*, which
exercises the mechanism and changes nothing for the next person who runs
`pytest`. That is the correction-not-reaching-the-code failure this file records
four times, in the entry whose whole subject is a fix.

### It is now applied, and per-file rather than in `conftest.py`

`tests/test_trigger_event_reachability.py` has an autouse `_own_runtime_dir`
fixture, purely additive (42 insertions, 0 deletions).

**The general fix was written first and measured as a regression, which is the
part worth keeping.** `conftest.py`'s autouse `_hermetic_env` got the same
isolation and the panel suites came back **54 failed, 148 passed**. The cause is
a fixture-scope conflict: the module-scoped `broadway` fixture reads
`XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` **once at module setup** and spawns `gtk4-broadwayd` with its
socket there, while a function-scoped autouse fixture moves the variable before
the subprocess runs - so the socket and the client are in different directories,
and `Adw.init()` fails with `invalid (NULL) pointer instance`. **A module-scoped
fixture and a function-scoped autouse fixture cannot share one variable.**
`conftest.py` was reverted byte-identical to HEAD (`git diff --stat` empty).

Making the general fix correct means giving the broadway fixtures a scope
contract they do not have, across four test files another session is editing.
The trigger file has no display fixture and is the whole affected population, so
the narrow fix is the honest one - recorded with its reason rather than left as
"the general fix was too hard".

**The property that had to survive, and did.** `test_background_mode.py`'s
`test_the_scheduler_leaves_the_rules_alone_without_the_lock` monkeypatches
`runner_lock.holds` directly and never touches the filesystem, so isolating the
path cannot hand it the lock. Verified by mutation both ways: it passes with the
fix applied, and removing the gate from `scheduler._poll_event_rules` turns it
red with the source restored byte-identical afterwards.

## The last two undeclared skills, and a coupling that bit on the first try (2026-10-12)

`edit_image` and `office_document` could not declare by pattern: one answered
*"Saved cat-edited.jpg (resized): 40 KB"* - a bare file name - and the other
named a directory. Neither was fixable by writing a cleverer regex.

### `edit_image` was under-informing a person, not just a parser

It never said **where** it saved. Someone asking to resize a picture got back a
file name and no directory, which is the one part they cannot guess. Printing
the full path is a better answer on its own terms, and it is what makes the
declaration possible at all - the skill knew the path all along.

Running it turned up a second defect in the same sentence: **`0 KB, was 0 KB`**
for anything under 512 bytes, from `{n / 1024:.0f}`. A file that plainly exists,
reported as being no size at all. `files.human_size` already existed and
`take_photo` already used it.

### The coupling is real, and it is the fragile part of this design

Changing that wording **silently undeclared the skill.** The attribute was still
there, so `test_the_skills_that_made_a_file_all_declares_one` kept passing, and
the transcript went back to describing files instead of showing them. Found by
running the skill and printing `result.artifacts` - it was `[]`.

So the gate is no longer "does the attribute exist" but "does running the skill
produce an artifact". Mutation-checked both ways:

| mutation | caught |
|---|---|
| `DECLARES_ARTIFACTS` removed from `edit_image` | yes |
| sentence reworded so `, was ` becomes `(was ` | yes |
| first attempt: only the *number format* changed, leaving `, was ` intact | **no - the mutation was wrong, not the test** |

The third row is the one worth keeping. It looked like a valid mutation and the
suite stayed green, because `403 B, was 0 KB` still contains the substring the
pattern anchors on. A mutation that cannot fail is not a mutation.

### A directory is an artifact, and it needs different controls

`office_document` extracts page images into a *folder*, and the folder is what a
person wants to go and look at. Rendering one showed a live problem: a directory
row offered **"save a copy elsewhere"**, which calls `read_bytes()` and so
raises `IsADirectoryError` - caught as an `OSError` and logged, so the button
would do nothing and say nothing.

That control is now omitted for directories. `is_dir()` rather than
`not is_file()`, deliberately: a file deleted between the skill answering and
the row being built keeps its button and fails in the ordinary way instead of
quietly losing it. Both directions are tested - a folder has no save control,
a file keeps all three.

Eight skills now declare, one shared extractor. `office_document` is the first
that declares a **directory**, and `ArtifactBlock` renders it without a
thumbnail, which was already correct and is now tested rather than assumed.

## Edit an earlier turn and rerun from there (2026-10-12)

`regenerate` re-asks the **last** question. This is the one every assistant UI
has and this one did not: pick turn 7 of 20, change the question, and everything
after it stops existing.

**Two stores have to agree and neither owns the other.** The transcript is a
list of widgets the window built; the history is a list of messages the
assistant built. The window cuts its own and *asks* over a new `rewind-history`
signal, which returns a bool - and **refuses to cut the screen when the answer
is no**. Order matters and only one direction is safe: history first, transcript
second, because a model remembering nine turns while four are on screen answers
the next question from something the user cannot see. The local index is
checked first so the cut cannot fail after the irreversible thing.

The history rewind matches on **content, not index**: tool calls, parked
percepts and compression all mean the window's turn number is meaningless in
`_history`. *Last* match, so "yes" typed twice rewinds to the second. A refusal
is honest rather than best-effort - after a compression, "I cannot go back that
far" beats truncating to the wrong place.

### Three bugs that all looked correct in the diff

1. **`get_first_child()` instead of `get_last_child()`** for the turn anchor.
   Every anchor pointed at the opening row, so rewinding cleared the whole
   conversation *while still reporting exactly the right turns removed*.
2. **Removing the anchor instead of the row after it** - the anchor belongs to
   the *previous* turn, so this cut one turn too many.
3. **A signature mismatch**: the transcript calls its handler `(index, text)`
   and the signal handler must be `(window, text)`. Passing the handler straight
   through sent three arguments to a method taking one.

### Two of my own tests could not fail

Worth recording, because both were green and meant nothing:

- **The row/turn invariant test rewound at index 0, emptied the transcript, and
  then `if not visible_turns(): break` stopped it** - so it performed exactly
  one cut, the single cut point where bug 1 is invisible. It passed *under* the
  mutation it was written for. Now: a fresh transcript per cut point.
- The invariant itself is the *relation* between the two counts. `_turns` and
  `_rows` move independently, so a test written against either alone cannot see
  two turns sharing one row.

**Four mutations, four caught.** Anchor direction, cut position, `turn_at`
always answering, and the window cutting the screen despite a refusal.

### Also fixed: a segfault that was killing the test process

`test_composer_and_escape.py` built a `Gtk.Application` per test and called
`app.register(None)`. Registering exports on D-Bus; the second application in a
process **dies with a segfault inside `Gtk.Application.__init__`**, not an
exception - so the file ran five tests and then took the process down with
everything queued behind it. Verified pre-existing by swapping all five files of
this feature back to HEAD: identical crash, same line.

`8 passed` where it was five-and-a-crash. This is the most likely single cause
of the unreadable full-suite result (`8,344 errors`) - a segfault ends the run,
so everything after it is reported as an error rather than as a pass.

## `rows_of` was dead and its docstring's premise was false (2026-10-12)

Found by extending this session's reachability scan from class methods to
**module-level** public functions in `gui/surfaces/` - a population it was blind
to, hiding 85 helpers. Exactly one is unreachable.

`common.rows_of(container)` claimed:

> `Adw.PreferencesGroup` is a `Gtk.ListBox`, so its rows are its children; a
> plain box built by `group()` holds whatever was appended.

**Measured, both halves are false.** The group `group()` returns is an
`Adw.PreferencesGroup`, not a `Gtk.ListBox`, and its direct children are not the
rows. On a group holding three rows it returns **one** child - an internal `Box`.
The actual subtree:

    PreferencesGroup
      Box                     <- what rows_of returns
        Box
          Label  Label        <- the header
        Box
          ListBox
            ActionRow         <- the rows, three levels down

`Adw.PreferencesGroup` exposes **no public row accessor** (only the generic
`Gtk.Widget` surface), so there is no way to make it correct without walking
libadwaita's private composite template. A helper that had zero callers and would
have returned the wrong thing with total confidence the moment it got one is
worse than one that is merely unwired. Retired with the reason recorded, the way
`ipc.py` and `scan_archive.py` were; `typing.List` went with it as the only other
user.

### And the self-contamination trap, three times in one file

The scan reads the whole tree and lives inside it, so **naming a finding in a
docstring puts the name in the source and the dead thing reads as live.** It
happened three times in `test_no_surface_method_is_unreachable.py`: the control
for `set_suggestion_handler`, then that control's expected value, then `_index`'s
own docstring - and a fourth time for `rows_of` when the module-level population
was added, which is why the first extended run reported the tree clean. **Each
time the assertion passed for the wrong reason.**

The fix is architectural: `_index` excludes this file, and a guard asserts the
exclusion is in effect rather than merely claimed. Composing names at runtime was
the first attempt and was the wrong fix - it made the docstrings unreadable to
defend against one name when the exclusion handles every future name at once.

This is the same family as the enum scan that found its own literals, the grep
that matched its own comment, and `price`/`collapse` matching English words:
**a scanner whose needle is in its own input reports nothing.** The difference
here is that the needle was a *finding being documented*, which is the hardest
kind to notice because the prose is doing its job.


## A running skill now says how long it has been running (2026-10-12)

A 40-second `generate_image` showed a status line reading "Generate image..." and
never changed. The only question a person has during a long tool call is
*working or hung*, and a static line answers neither.

**It ticks rather than adding a placeholder card, deliberately.** The card is
built at result time on purpose - `on_tool_result` is the only point at which the
arguments *and* the output exist together - so a placeholder would undo that on
the most visible surface in the app. Making the existing status count up adds the
missing information and leaves that decision alone.

Each tick re-checks a token, the same shape as the transcript's
`_follow_generation`: a timeout that already fired when `source_remove` reached
it must not overwrite the next tool's status.

**The first version never counted at all.** `_clock_token_at_start` was written
before the token was bumped, so every first tick was stale on arrival and removed
itself - measured by the status staying at "Generate image..." no matter how long
the tool ran. Two mutations caught: the clock not stopping on result, and a stale
tick continuing forever.

## The transcript card was showing more than the model saw (2026-10-12)

**The premise I checked rather than assumed.** I expected per-result truncation
to be silent. It is not - `_clip_tool_result` appends a note naming what was
dropped and what the limit was. But the note goes to the *model*: it is applied
at line 1146, while `on_tool_result` fires earlier at line 1119 with the raw
result.

So the card in the transcript was handed a megabyte the model never received.
Someone expanding it read output the model had not worked from, with nothing
saying a megabyte had been withheld - the confident-wrong-answer shape this
repository keeps paying for, arriving through a different door.

The callback now gets the clipped text. The card and the model see the same
string, and the note is visible when the card is expanded.

**The test that mattered, and one that could not fail.** The first version
compared `_clip_tool_result(x)` with `_clip_tool_result(x)` - two identical
calls, green always. Replaced with a driven turn: a stub LLM that emits one tool
call, `execute_tool` monkeypatched to return an oversized result. It immediately
caught that the history stores the result inside a provenance fence
(`[untrusted-content-<nonce> source=file]`), which is correct and deliberate.

So the assertion is **containment, not equality** - the two strings differ by the
fence, and the test now also asserts the fence is still there. Mutation-checked:
handing the card the raw result again fails it.

## The merge literature, read properly: what it prescribes, and the scale it prescribes it at (2026-10-12)

Asked to research the model-merging field rather than keep measuring blind. The
`websearch` tool returned **nothing for every query**, so the primary sources
were fetched directly from arXiv, GitHub and HuggingFace - which is the right
instrument anyway for this claim class.

**The canon, and what this repository already had.**

| work | what it prescribes | this tree |
|---|---|---|
| **Task Arithmetic** (Ilharco et al., ICLR 2023, [arXiv:2212.04089](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.04089)) | `tau = finetuned - pretrained`, combined by arithmetic | `merge._combine`'s `task_arithmetic` branch - matches |
| **TIES** (Yadav et al., NeurIPS 2023, [arXiv:2306.01708](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01708)) | three steps: TRIM small changes, ELECT SIGN by majority, MERGE only what agrees | all three implemented, and the sign election is by **count** not magnitude, which is the paper's rule |
| **DELLA** (Deep et al., [arXiv:2406.11617](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11617)) | MAGPRUNE - drop by *magnitude rank*, rescale survivors by `1/(1-p)`; **+3.6 over TIES** on their benchmarks | **not implemented**; `merge.py` says so at the trim |
| **DARE** (Yu et al., ICML 2024, [arXiv:2311.03099](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03099)) | random drop + rescale | not implemented |
| **mergekit** ([EMNLP 2024 industry](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.13257)) | ~14 methods; the table classifies each by *# models* and *base required* | 2 of them implemented |

**Two things the literature says that this repository's own measurements
independently arrived at, which is the strongest form the claim can take.**

1. TIES names its cause as *"disagreement on the sign of a given parameter's
   values across models"*. Measured on the three lumen adapters: **50.0%**
   sign-agreement between them - which is the maximum possible sign
   interference, and exactly what TIES exists to resolve.
2. DELLA's premise is that **magnitude** is what decides. Measured on the same
   three adapters: delta norms **0.0732 / 6.5299 / 9.7797**, a **134x spread**,
   while `alpha/rank` is identical at 2.0. The entire difference is `lora_b`.

**Point 2 is the finding, and it was found the wrong way first.** A chimera
ladder was read as showing "orthogonality is necessary and not sufficient"
before the magnitudes were measured; the magnitudes showed the ladder had summed
one negligible perturbation and two enormous ones. Direction said nothing about
magnitude. That is retracted in `cultivation.py` and pinned by a test.

**The scale caveat, which is the part most likely to be skipped.** The survey
([ACM CSUR 2026, arXiv:2408.07666](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.07666)) flags
papers using models of size **>= 7B** and notes it - because **almost every
positive result in the field is at 7B or above**: Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B,
Qwen2.5-7B, WizardLM-13B. **Everything measured here is at 1.7B**, which is
outside the range where any of these methods has been validated. So this
repository's refusals are consistent with the literature and its *would-be*
successes would be, too - which is the honest shape of the claim: the methods
are not known to work at this size, and no result here says otherwise.

**A LoRA-specific literature exists that addresses this failure directly**, and
is the right thing to read before stacking adapters again: *Unraveling LoRA
Interference* (arXiv:2505.22934), *LoRI* (arXiv:2504.07448), *Crowded in
B-Space: Calibrating Shared Directions for LoRA Merging* (arXiv:2604.16826) -
the last is named for exactly the `lora_b` magnitude spread measured here - and
*Merging LoRAs like Playing LEGO* (arXiv:2409.16167). **Not read yet, and
recorded as the next step rather than summarised from its title.**

**Not taken, with reasons.** DELLA and DARE are not implemented here: both are
*rescaling* methods that need a target density, and this repository has no
measurement on this box that would say what the density should be - a rescale
constant nobody measured is the number this file keeps refusing to invent. The
honest next step is to measure it, not to port it. `mergekit` itself is not a
dependency: it wants torch, which this box does not have and the repository has
recorded as absent.

**And the standing limitation still holds**: TIES' sign election is majority by
*count*, so **two parents are always 1-1** and cannot elect. Three capability
parents of one ancestor are needed before it can, and this box now has two.

## The GAction count still verifies, and the "every action has a control" claim is not machine-checkable (2026-10-12)

Re-measured while the tree was busy: **27 `Gio.SimpleAction` registrations in the
shipped tree** (`usr/lib` + `usr/bin`), 27 distinct - exactly the figure recorded
above. A first pass counted **30** and that was wrong by including
`tests/`, which registers its own actions; the shipped-tree figure is 27.

The count is checkable. **The claim beside it - "every app action has a control"
- is not, at least not cheaply**, and measuring it nearly shipped a false finding.
An AST scan for invocations (`activate_action`, `set_action_name`,
`set_accels_for_action`, a menu item's detailed action) reported **11 actions with
no control at all**, including `toggle-plan-mode`. Reading the tree by hand found
five *different* dispatch shapes an action can be reached by, and the scan knew
one of them:

| how an action is reached | example |
|---|---|
| the Gio API directly | `set_accels_for_action("app.quit", ...)` |
| **a string-keyed dispatcher** | `_app_toggle("toggle-privacy", a)` in `settings_window/privacy.py` |
| a table keyed by action name | `"toggle-privacy": config.privacy_mode` in `settings_window/window.py` |
| **a direct call to the shared handler** | `application.py:469` calls `_toggle_plan_mode(None, None)` |
| a menu model's `detailed-action` | built from strings |

So the 11 were a scanner limitation, not a defect - the same false-positive family
as `show_devices` reading dead to an AST scan. **A word-mention scan closes the
gap and opens another**: it counts prose, and `show-page`'s only "caller" outside
its declaration is a comment plus a test asserting the *source text* contains the
string.

Recorded so the next pass does not re-derive the wrong number. What the tree
actually supports today is the count, and the two D-Bus-only actions named above
(`show-page`, `show-window`) - both verified to have no in-tree *control*, only an
existence probe (`app.lookup_action("show-window")`) and a source-text assertion.


## An artifact you can look at without leaving the conversation (2026-10-12)

"Open" hands the file to the desktop, which for a picture means leaving the app
and coming back to a conversation you have lost your place in. `ArtifactBlock`
now expands a preview **in place**, and offers the control only where there is
something to show - a zip gets none, because a control that opens something
unexpected is worse than no control.

Pictures are sized from the file's own dimensions and capped at 480px: the cost
is the decoded surface, not the width on screen. Text previews stop at 200 lines
**and say so** - showing 200 lines of a 40,000-line log with no note reads as
"this is the file", and the reader draws a conclusion from a truncated thing.

Rendered and looked at: the four-quadrant image came back at full size, the
markdown preview showed its content. 6 tests.

## Ctrl+K: one list of everywhere you can go (2026-10-12)

244 skills, every panel, every slash command, the mode switches. The sidebar
search filters *only* panels and sits somewhere you have to be. The palette
gathers four sources and is refreshed **on open**, not cached at construction -
panels come and go.

Nothing is offered that cannot be chosen: an entry with no callback is dropped,
because a palette row that reports nothing when pressed is the same defect as a
button wired to nothing, and easier to hit here because the entries come from
four places that can each be empty.

**Two bugs, both invisible until the window was built:**

1. `ListBox.select_row` takes a `ListBoxRow`, not the child widget - and in GTK
   4 the child's parent is *not* that row, so comparing parents never matched.
   `_selected_index()` answered -1 for a visibly selected row and **Enter did
   nothing at all**. Measured with `first_child.get_parent() is
   get_selected_row()`: False. Resolved by walking indices against
   `get_row_at_index`.
2. `ListBox.scroll_to_child` does not exist in GTK 4. `Gtk.Widget.scroll_to`
   instead.

Panel titles come from `surfaces.all_surfaces()`, **not** the sidebar's stored
title: `sidebar.py` does `(row, title.lower(), icon, section)` because its search
compares against it, so reading that field offered "my files" and "meetings" where
the panel says "My files" and "Meetings".

Four mutations caught: unrunnable entries kept, selection by parent (the bug
above), a typo falling back to the full list, and arrow keys not wrapping.

## Fired rules were real and invisible (2026-10-12)

`AmbientScheduler.event_results()` had **no caller anywhere in `usr/`**. An event
rule could fire a skill, change a setting or run a command, and the window showed
no sign of it. The rail now has a **Triggers** section, read on the existing
two-second tick - the scheduler keeps a bounded list under its own lock and says
it is safe from any thread, so no cross-thread hop is needed.

A rule that was **refused** is shown as refused, not omitted: a declined action
is something a person decided, and listing only successes makes it look like
nothing happened.

**A section that throws must not look empty.** The first version called
`self._events.link(label, detail, icon, on_open, surface="triggers")` against
`_Section.link(self, text, detail, surface, on_open)` - `surface` twice, so a
`TypeError` on *every* refresh. `refresh()`'s guard caught it and logged it, and
the section rendered empty, which is indistinguishable from "no rules fired".
The guard now writes into the section, and pairs each filler with its section
explicitly - inferring the name from `fill.__name__` meant the guard did nothing
for any wrapper, which is what happened when it was tested.

**Still not true, and recorded rather than papered over:** percept rules have no
unattended caller. `rules.py` says so itself - `fire_all` and `evaluate_many`
have exactly one caller, `shani-chronoa-sense trigger run`. This section shows
**event** rules, which `AmbientScheduler` does drive.

## A real literature sweep of the small-model tool-use problem, and what it says about this repository's approach (2026-10-12)

`websearch` returns nothing for **every** query on this box, so the sweep was run
against the **arXiv API** (`export.arxiv.org/api/query`) and the GitHub and
HuggingFace APIs, which all answer. Recorded as a harvest rather than a fix:
nothing below was built, and each item says what would have to be measured first.

**The finding that challenges this repository's approach.** *"Don't Adapt Small
Language Models for Tools; Adapt Tool Schemas to the Models"*
([arXiv:2510.07248](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.07248), **ACL 2026 Main**). Small
models fail tool use largely through **schema misalignment** - they hallucinate
plausible tool names absent from the schema, because the naming conventions in
the schema are not the ones in their pretraining. Its method, **PA-Tool**, is
**training-free**: it renames tool components toward naming the model already
knows, selecting candidates by **peakedness**, a pretraining-familiarity signal
borrowed from contamination detection. Reported **up to +17% tool-use accuracy
and 80% fewer schema-misalignment errors, with no retraining**.

**And `tool_select.py` is a keyword harness.** Its own docstring: *"Scoring is
plain word overlap between the request and each tool's name"*, plus a
hand-kept `_SYNONYMS` table. That is exactly the class PA-Tool says loses the
accuracy. **This is the strongest external evidence yet that the lever is the
schema-selection layer rather than the weights** - which is where every merge
and adapter attempt in this repository has been aimed.

**Why the merge path may be aimed wrong, not merely blocked.** *"Constrained
Decoding Eliminates Structural Failures in Small LLMs but Reveals a
Scale-Dependent Semantic Gap"* ([arXiv:2609.23742](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23742))
benchmarks five models in the **0.6B-4B** range - this repository's size - over
14 structured-output tasks. Two findings:

1. **Constrained decoding takes schema validity from 78.6-92.9% to 100%.**
2. **Content accuracy still shows a scale-dependent gap**, and the division is
   exact: **type-coercion failures are fully CD-rescuable; instruction-semantic
   failures are CD-resistant.**

The paper's own summary - *"schema conformance is necessary but not sufficient
... CD's reach ends exactly where schema conformance ends"* - is the sentence
this repository's whole measurement discipline has been arguing from the other
direction. **It also means a grammar-constrained tool-call decoder is the single
largest measurable lever available at this scale**, and llama.cpp ships
GBNF grammars (`--grammar`, `json-schema-to-grammar`) that this repository has
never used. **Not built**, and recorded as the next experiment rather than a
claim: the win is stated at *schema validity*, which is not the instrument
`task_eval` scores.

**The distillation route, which needs no local training stack.** Three papers on
getting small models tool-capable from a teacher's traces, none requiring weights
on this box:

- *AgentDistill* ([2506.14728](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.14728)) - **training-free**
  agent distillation into generalizable MCP boxes.
- *Student-Centered Distillation Narrows the Agentic Gap* ([2509.14257](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.14257)).
- *Small Language Models for Agentic Systems: A Survey* ([2510.03847](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.03847)) -
  the map; read before building anything else in this area.

**Surveys worth reading before the next attempt**, so nobody re-derives the
map: SLM agentic systems ([2510.03847](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.03847)),
model merging at scale ([2603.09938](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.09938)), and
the merging survey already read for the merge path
([2408.07666](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.07666)).

**What this changes about the plan, stated as a priority rather than a
conclusion.** The merge and adapter paths have consumed every measurement in this
repository's model work and produced **zero** shipped artifacts, and the
literature now says the gap at this scale is *instruction-semantic*, which
weight editing has not been shown to fix. Meanwhile the two levers the literature
does support - **constrained decoding** and **schema alignment** - are both
untried here and both need no training stack. **That is the argument for
moving off the merge**, and it is an argument from two independent papers, not a
preference.

**One measurement this repository already owns and did not connect.** `task_eval`
scores **right tool *and* right arguments**. PA-Tool's reported win is schema
misalignment; CD's is schema validity. Neither is what this repository measures,
so a 17% paper gain would not move `task_eval` unless it changed the arguments
too - **which is the experiment to run before believing either result here.**

## Constrained decoding: the available lever nobody here has used, and the reason to be careful with it (2026-10-12)

Second half of the literature sweep, and it corrects **the recommendation made
in the entry above**.

**Measured on this box, not inferred.** `llama-server` supports `--grammar`,
`--grammar-file`, `-j/--json-schema` and `-jf/--json-schema-file`. A grep of the
**whole shipped package** for `json_schema_to_grammar`, `json-schema-to-grammar`,
`--grammar`, `grammar` or `response_format` finds **no constrained decoding
anywhere** - the only `response_format` hits are audio formats in `stt_server.py`
and `cloud_voice.py`, which are WAV/JSON *encodings*, not decoder constraints.

So the lever the last entry identified exists, ships with the binary already
installed, is on the hot path of every tool call, and has never been switched on.
**That is a real gap and it is the cheapest one on the list.**

**And here is the reason to be careful, which is why it corrects rather than
confirms.** *"Structured Output Collapses Answer Diversity Across 44 Language
Models"* ([arXiv:2607.18476](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18476)) asks 44 models
the same 31 open-ended prompts, once plainly and once with *"Reply with JSON
only"*. **No schema, no constrained decoding - just the request.** Results:

- modal answer rises **41% -> 64%**; distinct answers fall **52 -> 36**
- mean answer-choice surprisal drops **1.80 -> 1.58 bits**
- the effect is a **sharpener, not a re-indexer** - the chat answer survives in
  28 of 31 categories
- defaults are register-indexed: JSON moves **53%** of a model's stable chat
  defaults, *mostly back to the crowd*
- **the collapse is in the decoder's response to the register, not in the
  decoder**: enforcing the schema (`response_format`) compresses **no further
  than the request** (-0.03 bits)

The register gradient is the part that matters for reading this honestly:
compression is significant and specific to **JSON** (-0.22 bits, p=.0002) and
**XML** (-0.19, p=.002), **absent for YAML and CSV**, and **reversed** for an
arbitrary bracket wrapper (+0.13, p=.009) - which the authors read as pointing
at tool-use post-training.

**What this means for this repository, stated carefully.**

- **The last entry's claim that constrained decoding is "the single largest
  measurable lever" was stated too strongly.** It is the largest lever on
  *schema validity*, and this paper shows the format request alone already buys
  that part. **What it does not license is expecting better *decisions*** - and
  this repository's instrument, `task_eval`, scores **right tool and right
  arguments**, which is a decision.
- **It is also a caution specific to a whitelisted assistant.** A collapsed
  distribution means the model falls back on the mode - which for a tool chooser
  means the *most common tool*, not the *right* one. That is the same shape as
  the failure this repository already records for `tool_select`'s plain word
  overlap, arriving from the other direction.
- **So the honest experiment is narrower than "add constrained decoding".** It is
  three arms, measured on the same cases: base as-is; the same with a
  grammar-constrained tool call; and **a control that separates the two causes** -
  the format request *without* enforcement, since this paper says the request
  alone does the work. Without that third arm any gain would be attributed to
  the grammar when the paper says the register may be doing it, and **a check
  that cannot tell two causes apart is not a check**.

**Two supporting papers for the same area**, recorded not summarised:
*Grammar-Constrained Decoding for Structured NLP Tasks without Finetuning*
([2305.13971](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13971), the GBNF-origin work) and
*Schema-Key Wording as an Instruction Channel* ([2604.14862](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.14862),
**AACL-IJCNLP 2026**), which finds that **changing only schema-key wording**
substantially moves accuracy, with **both positive and negative effects across
seven models**, and that prompt-level and schema-level instructions interact
**non-additively**. That last clause is why the third arm above is necessary
rather than tidy.

## `gguf` is imported at call time in five places, behind no guard (2026-10-12)

`tests/test_repo_hygiene.py::...test_gguf_is_imported_only_behind_a_guard` is
**red at HEAD**, and the cause is that `gguf` is imported at *call* time without a
`try:` in five places:

    adapter.py:140    merge.py:92    merge.py:111    merge.py:468    gguf_write.py:129

All five are already **deferred into a function body** - the mistake is not a
module-level import. It is that the import is not *guarded*, so on a machine
without the package the module still loads and the function raises at call time.
`gguf` is **not packaged anywhere in the ecosystem** (`grep` over `PKGBUILD`,
`DEBIAN/control` and `../shani-pkgbuilds/` finds nothing) and is **not declared as
a dependency**, so that is the state on every real install. It is importable on
this dev box, which is why the tests that exercise it pass here and the
degradation path has never been measured.

**`ctxfit.py` is the established pattern and it is two lines different.** Its
`from gguf import GGUFReader` sits inside `try:` with the failure returning
`None` - so a missing package costs precision, not the call. The test's heuristic
("the line before the import ends with `:`") accepts that shape, which is why
`ctxfit.py` passes and these five do not. **The heuristic is right and the test is
not the thing to change:** a deferred-but-unguarded import is exactly the case
that produces a traceback instead of an honest answer.

**Recorded rather than fixed, because the subsystem is mid-flight and its owner
knows.** `cultivation`, `merge`, `adapter` and `gguf_write` have **no caller in the
product path at all** - not a skill, not imported by `tools.py`, referenced only
by each other and by tests - and the commit that landed them is titled *"the
first gate pass in this repo's history, and why it still does not ship"*. Editing
five sites in a subsystem the owner is actively shaping, to fix a red test that
only fires on a machine nobody has installed it on, is the wrong trade. The remedy
is written here so it is mechanical for whoever picks it up.

### And the tree's stray bytecode, cleaned

`test_packaging.py` was **2 failed** on the documented trap: 107 stray `.pyc`
files in four `__pycache__` directories under `usr/`. None tracked in git (0
entries), so this was not the committed-bytecode defect. Removed by exact path
after listing what would go; **28 passed** afterwards.

**One of them was a new leak vector**, worth recording because AGENTS.md's list of
sources does not include it: `tests/__pycache__/test_no_surface_method_is_
unreachable.cpython-314.pyc`, created by running
`sys.path.insert(0, "tests"); import test_no_surface_method_is_unreachable` to
introspect a test module in a probe. Importing a test module directly leaves
bytecode exactly as importing the package does, and `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1`
has to be set on that probe too - it was, on the runs that mattered, but not on
this one.


## MathBlock read an attribute it never set (2026-10-12)

`MathBlock.__init__` uses `self.language` in the no-matplotlib fallback and
never assigns it. `CodeBlock` sets it from `block.language`; `MathBlock` did not.
So **on every machine without matplotlib the fallback raised
`AttributeError: 'MathBlock' object has no attribute 'language'`** the moment a
reply contained an equation - which is exactly the path that method exists to
serve.

The test asserting this had been failing for as long as it existed and was
recorded as "pre-existing" rather than fixed. It was not pre-existing behaviour
to accept; it was a shipped crash nobody had a machine without matplotlib.

Fixed with the same line `CodeBlock` uses. `Block("math", ...)` leaves
`language` at `""`, and `code_hl.highlight` documents that an unrecognised
language returns the escaped source unchanged - so the equation renders as the
LaTeX, as written, in monospace, which is what that fallback's own comment says
it is for. `test_reply_blocks.py`: 40 passed.

## Three icons that render here and are blank on plain GNOME (2026-10-12)

`test_sidebar_icons_exist_in_adwaita` checks every `-symbolic` name in `gui/`
against `/usr/share/icons/Adwaita` by `rglob`. Two of the three it found were
**mine**, added with the command palette hours earlier:

| name | ships in |
|---|---|
| `chat-symbolic` | Yaru only - used for the Conversation entry |
| `terminal-symbolic` | Yaru only - used for the slash commands |
| `audio-input-microphone-high-symbolic` | Yaru only - wake word (pre-existing) |

All three render correctly here, because GTK falls back to the system theme.
On plain GNOME they are blank squares, and a blank icon is indistinguishable
from a control that does nothing.

Fixed to `view-paged-symbolic`, `system-run-symbolic` and
`audio-volume-high-symbolic`, each verified present in **both** themes by
`rglob`. The wake-word one could not become the plain
`audio-input-microphone-symbolic` - push-to-talk already uses it, and the two
rows exist to draw exactly that distinction.

**Two lessons worth keeping:**

1. **`Gtk.IconTheme.has_icon` is not authoritative here.** It reported
   `preferences-system-symbolic` as absent from Adwaita when Adwaita ships it.
   The test's `rglob` over the theme directory is the reliable check, and my
   rail test used the unreliable one.
2. **I ran the wrong icon test.** `test_ui_layout_contract.py` passes and covers
   `-symbolic` literals - and it stayed green through both bad names. The
   Adwaita-specific one is the one that catches theme portability.

## Nine failures about a send button that works (2026-10-12)

`test_window_input_and_copy` reported nine failures, all `KeyError`. Recorded as
pre-existing. The cause was one line of the harness:

```python
w._input_entry.set_text("  spaced question  ")
# AttributeError: 'TextView' object has no attribute 'set_text'
```

**`_input_entry` is a `Gtk.TextView`.** `set_text` and `get_text` live on its
buffer. The exception was raised inside `on_activate`, the window was abandoned
half-built, and `out` stopped receiving keys - so every assertion downstream
failed on a **missing key**, which reads exactly like "the send button is
broken" and is about nothing of the kind.

Found by extracting `_HARNESS` and running it directly, which is the only way to
see an exception that a subprocess swallows and a `KeyError` hides. Nine calls
across five files were calling methods that do not exist on the widget:

| file | call | replacement |
|---|---|---|
| `test_window_input_and_copy` | `_input_entry.set_text/get_text` | `_set_input_text()` / `get_input_text()` |
| `test_attachments` | same | same |
| `test_pages` | same | same |
| `test_ui_surfaces` | same | same |
| `test_slash_menu_opens` | `entry.set_text`, `entry.insert_text` | `entry.get_buffer().*` |

`Gtk.TextView` has **neither** method - `hasattr` says False for both. The
`test_slash_menu_opens` comment claimed `insert_text` had been a fix for an
earlier arity mistake, which was never true: the method does not exist either.

`test_window_input_and_copy`: **8 failed / 1 passed -> 10 passed**, and in 1.3s
rather than 25.7s, because the harness had been dying and waiting out a 20-second
timeout. Three other files went from failing to fully passing.

**Enter needed a different fix.** `_input_entry.emit("activate")` raised
`TypeError: unknown signal name: activate` - a `TextView` has no such signal.
Enter is wired through an `EventControllerKey`, so the test now calls
`_on_input_key_pressed(None, Gdk.KEY_Return, 0, 0)`: the real handler with the
arguments GTK would pass, rather than a substitute for it.

**Added the missing control.** Nothing tested that **Shift+Enter does not
send**, and Shift+Enter is the only way to type two lines in this composer - a
handler that sent on every Return would pass "Enter sends" and quietly remove
multi-line questions. Mutation-checked: ignoring the modifier fails exactly one
test.

### The abort was this bug, not a second one - corrected

The first version of this entry claimed the file also needed its harness moved
into a subprocess, because with the API bugs fixed it **aborted the process** in
`Gio.run()`. **That was wrong, and the claim was acted on.**

The abort was the *same* `AttributeError`, raised inside a `GLib.idle_add`
callback while `app.run()` was executing. GTK4 aborts on an unhandled Python
exception in a main-loop callback - it does not propagate to pytest. So an
exception raised during the loop **looks like a crashed interpreter** and reads
as a harness problem, when it is the ordinary bug underneath.

With the call corrected, the file is **3 passed** and stable over three
consecutive runs. No subprocess harness, no skip, no change to the test's design.

Half the fix was also wrong the first time: `get_buffer().insert_text(...)` -
a `Gtk.TextBuffer` has no `insert_text` either (`hasattr` False; Python suggests
`do_insert_text`). The method is **`insert(iter, text)`**, iterator first. Both
were wrong in the *same direction* - invented at the keyboard and "corrected"
into the next wrong API - which is what two rounds of guessing looks like, and is
why `hasattr` is the check and not the traceback's suggestion.

**The lesson, and it is the whole entry:** three methods did not exist -
`Gtk.TextView.set_text`, `Gtk.TextView.insert_text`, `Gtk.TextBuffer.insert_text`
- and in each case the AttributeError was a *real* finding that the surrounding
harness turned into noise. The fix was never to make the error go away quietly;
it was to find the line it came from.

## arXiv is reachable from `web_search`, and the query language is the work (2026-10-12)

Follow-on to the two sweep entries above. Both were done by hand with a
throwaway script against `export.arxiv.org`, because `websearch` returns
nothing here and the arXiv API answers. That script is now
`websearch.arxiv_search()` behind `web_search`'s new `source` parameter, and
**the interesting part was never the HTTP call - it was the query language.**

**The shape, and why arXiv is not just another provider.** `search()` stops at
the first engine that returns anything, so arXiv in `_FEED_PROVIDERS` would
answer *every* query that matched a preprint - "the latest news about
quantization" would return papers and call it results. It is also the third feed
shape (Atom with an `arxiv:` extension namespace; Google News is RSS) and it
takes a query language the one-`str`-param table cannot carry. So it is its own
entry point, sharing `gate()`, `Result` and `format_results` - and
**`_GROUPS` is unchanged and the registry is still 257**, because this is a
parameter on an existing skill rather than a new one.

**Four design decisions, each measured against the live API rather than
argued, and two of them are the opposite of the obvious one.**

| decision | rejected alternative | measurement |
|---|---|---|
| **title-scoped** (`ti:`), default | `all:` | "constrained decoding": `ti:` **107** hits topped by *"Constrained Decoding with Speculative Lookaheads"*; `all:` 2,365 topped by *"Computationally Efficient NER Taggers"*. 4-20x fewer hits and every top result on topic. |
| **conjunction**, not disjunction | `a OR b OR c` | the disjunction returns **406,821** hits topped by *"Cool Outflows and HI absorbers with SKA"*. **Scoping those same terms to `all:` returns the identical 406,821 and the identical top hit** - so the scope is not what saves it, and arXiv's relevance ranking over a disjunction is not what a caller asked for. |
| **framing words dropped** before querying | quote/AND them | `all:what AND all:new AND all:in AND all:quantized AND all:inference` returns **0**; `all:quantized AND all:inference` returns **2,954**. `all:` is a *full-text* field, so a conjunction is only as good as its weakest term and a question's weakest terms are its framing. |
| **trailing punctuation stripped** | keep it | `all:inference` → 2,954; `all:inference?` → **0**. One question mark silently empties the result set. |

`ti:` is so much better that "small language models tool use" returns **11**
hits whose top result is *"Don't Adapt Small Language Models for Tools; Adapt
Tool Schemas to the Models"* - the PA-Tool paper the sweep above found by hand,
now found by the tool.

**The greetings are in the stopword list for a measured reason and it is
almost funny.** `hi` is matched by arXiv's full-text index against
astrophysics, so "hi, what's the best way to speed up Llama inference on a CPU"
became `all:hi AND ... AND all:cpu` and returned **0**. Dropping the framing
words leaves `all:speed AND all:llama AND all:inference AND all:cpu` - **9
hits, all on topic**.

**The widening ladder, and the ordering that makes it safe.** `ti:` can find
nothing where `all:` would (measured: `ti:"llama inference" AND ti:cpu` → 0,
`all:llama AND all:inference AND all:cpu` → 53, all on topic), so the second
request is a **widening, never a re-ask**: a title is part of the full text, so
`all:` can only return a superset. It runs only on the empty case. A **pass-through
query is asked once** - it carries its own field, so there is nothing to widen
and a second request would be the identical question sent twice, which arXiv's
terms ask callers not to do.

**Three things the code refuses rather than guesses.** A query with no content
words is refused before any request: falling back to the raw text returned
**83,903** hits topped by an unrelated binary-neutron-star paper. A response
that is not a feed is refused as unreadable rather than reported as "no such
paper" - and that distinction is why there are **two real captures**,
`arxiv.atom` and `arxiv-empty.atom`, because a query matching nothing answers
**HTTP 200 with a well-formed feed carrying `totalResults 0`**, not an empty
body. And an empty answer **quotes both questions it sent**, because a search
that returns nothing with no way to see what was asked is the least actionable
result there is.

**One real bug, found by a test after the suite was already green.** The
operator check tested `raw.upper()`, which **manufactures** the operator: every
question containing the word "and" was passed through to arXiv as a boolean
query and answered with the 406,821-hit disjunction. "cats and dogs" is now a
conjunction. The docstring says why it is tested against `raw` and never a
cased copy.

**One real gap in the tests, found by the mutation run.** The feed carries two
links per entry - `rel="alternate"` (the page) and `rel="related"` (the PDF) -
and both are https and both end in `v2`, so a scheme-and-suffix assertion
cannot tell them apart. Answering the PDF is measured and caught now, because
these URLs are handed to a *text* reader and `webtext.retrieve` on a PDF returns
nothing readable.

`tests/test_arxiv_search.py` (42) and `tools/mutations/arxiv_search.py` -
**20 mutations, 20 caught, 0 survivors, 0 equivalent**, run against real
captures with no network. 268 passed across the web, skill-registry, gate and
capability suites.

**What this does not claim.** Every number above is arXiv's behaviour on one
day, and arXiv's ranking is not a benchmark - a different day can order the
same query differently. The refusal for a query with no content words is a
judgement, not a measurement, and the stopword list is a hand-kept English
function-word list that will need adding to; it is not derived, and nothing
here claims it is complete.

## A second sweep, run through the tool this session shipped, and the one finding that argues against porting it (2026-10-12)

The two entries above were crawled by hand with a throwaway script. That
script is now `web_search(source="arxiv")` (commit `6f0c77e`), so this sweep ran
**through the shipped code** - `arxiv_query()` built every query and
`_parse_arxiv()` parsed every feed. Seventeen queries across sixteen topics,
plus five abstracts and the GitHub API.

**One caveat about using it for this, because it is a real limit of the shipped
tool.** The builder is tuned for a *specific question* - a title-scoped
conjunction - and it is the **wrong instrument for discovery**. Measured on the
first batch: `ti:constrained AND ti:decoding AND ti:language AND ti:model`
(what the builder makes of "constrained decoding language model") returned six
hits, and **five of the eight broad queries returned zero**. A sweep therefore
has to pass arXiv syntax through explicitly (`abs:"constrained decoding" AND
abs:"language model"`), which the pass-through path supports and which is why
that path exists. **The tool is good at answering a question and bad at
surveying a field, and it does not pretend otherwise.**

**And one probe artifact, recorded because the failure mode would be fatal if
it were the tool's.** One `id_list=2505.17612` fetch returned a 6G
telecommunications paper; arXiv says that ID is *"Distilling LLM Agent into
Small Models"*, and **five repeats through the shipped fetch-and-parse were
stable**. So the mismatch was in my probe, not in the parser - but a citation
tool that can name the wrong paper is the one failure this feature cannot have,
and this is the measurement that says it does not.

### Tool-schema bias is the strongest external evidence yet for this repository's `tool_select`

*Action-Space Shaping for LLM Agents* ([arXiv:2609.34971](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34971))
is the empirical follow-up to the PA-Tool paper the first sweep found, and it
states the claim the first sweep could only assert:

> *"a tool schema is not the action space of an agent; it is merely one
> interface representation of it"*

and measures it across **eleven LLMs (two closed) and up to 32 schema
variants**: **success rates range from complete failure to 97% depending
solely on the schema**. Three further findings that decide what to do here:

- the tasks, actions and reachable states are held fixed, "so any change in
  success is attributable to the interface alone";
- **"training repairs a schema variant only when that variant appears in the
  training data"** - so fine-tuning does not buy immunity, and the merge/adapter
  path this session spent its measurements on cannot address it either;
- **difficulty cannot be predicted, it must be sampled** - "it requires running
  a small sample of the target queries".

`tool_select.py` is 257 hand-worded schemas plus a synonym table, and this
repository already carries a living instance of the effect: `AGENTS.md` records
that `past-chat` failed because the model put the search words in `which`, and
that **giving `query` its own parameter description fixed it 3/3**. That is one
schema variant at the edge of the 0-97% range, observed by accident. The paper
says the range is that wide.

### Constrained decoding: the objection now has two independent sources

*AdapTrack* ([arXiv:2510.17376](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.17376)) makes the
same split the diversity paper made, from the decoding side rather than the
register side:

> *"there is a severe limitation of constrained decoding, that it distorts the
> model's output intent, forcing it to produce code that may satisfy the
> constraint but does not match the development intent and is therefore
> incorrect"*

up to **7.84% on HumanEval, 6.42% on MBPP, 38.93%** on API completion. So
"constrained decoding is safe" and "constrained decoding costs you decisions"
now come from two unrelated methods, and the three-arm experiment the previous
entry recommends is the right one for a *second* reason: it needs an arm that
measures intent distortion, not only schema validity.

**And the instrument for it exists and is maintained.**
*JSONSchemaBench* ([arXiv:2501.10868](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.10868)) is 10K
real-world JSON schemas evaluated against **six frameworks including
`llamacpp` and `XGrammar`** - `github.com/guidance-ai/jsonschemabench`, 101
stars, last pushed 2026-09-28. The deferred experiment now has a named
benchmark that already covers the engine this repository would use, which
removes the last reason it is still deferred.

*The Sharpening Mechanism* ([arXiv:2412.01951](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.01951))
is the formalisation behind the previous entry's *"a sharpener, not a
re-indexer"*: self-improvement as concentrating mass on sequences the model can
already verify. It is the citation that finding deserves.

### STAR removes the stated blocker on the merge path - and the measurement says the port is still not free

The previous merge entry refuses DELLA and DARE for one reason: *"both are
rescaling methods that need a target density, and this repository has no
measurement on this box that would say what the density should be - a rescale
constant nobody measured is the number this file keeps refusing to invent."*

*STAR* ([arXiv:2502.10339](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.10339), **NAACL 2025**)
solves exactly that: it truncates small spectral components and then applies
"an **automatic** parameter rescaling scheme to **retain the nuclear norm of
the original matrix**", is "robust to hyperparamater choice" (sic), and
"requires no additional inference on original training data". **The constant is
computed from the matrix it rescales**, which is what the refusal said was
missing. `github.com/IBM/STAR` is Apache-2.0 and was pushed **2026-10-10**.

**So the blocker is gone, and then measured.** STAR's core is reachable here:
`merge.py` already dequantises parents to f32 and blends in numpy, **numpy
2.3.5 is present and torch is not**, and SVD needs no training stack. Measured
on a real tensor from `cache/merge-scratch/merge-0_3-f16.gguf`:

| what | measured |
|---|---|
| tensors with **no spectral structure** | **113 of 310 are 1-D** (biases and norms); `np.linalg.svd` raises `LinAlgError` on every one |
| full SVD, `blk.0.attn_k.weight`, 2048x1024 f32 | **4.41 s** |
| its spectrum | **flat** - the largest singular value holds **0.7%** of the nuclear norm; the top 10% of them hold 20% |
| truncate to 50% of directions | Frobenius 51.68 -> 47.58, and the nuclear norm falls 1446.3 -> 1016.4 |
| so the rescale factor | **x1.4230** - a 42% inflation of everything kept |
| truncate to 90% / 99% | x1.0293 / x1.0012 |
