**So the honest reading is two-sided and neither half is the headline.** The
conceptual blocker is genuinely removed: the density need not be invented.
But on a **flat-spectrum** weight the derived constant is a **42% magnitude
inflation**, and this is the same 1.7B model whose every merge measurement has
been a refusal - so a spectral truncation that inflates half its directions by
42% is not obviously the next experiment either. **Porting STAR is now
unblocked and unpromising on this model**, which is a different sentence from
the one recorded before and worth more than the port would have been.

**What would change the reading:** a weight whose spectrum actually decays (a
`W_q`/`W_k` matrix on a larger checkpoint, not an attention projection on a 1.7B
model), where truncation at 99% would need a factor near 1.0012. **Not
measured here, and named rather than assumed.**

### Not taken

Distillation-with-MCP-boxes ([AgentDistill](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.14728)),
`Search, Do not Guess` ([arXiv:2604.04651](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04651)),
*Distilling LLM Agent into Small Models with Retrieval and Code Tools*
([arXiv:2505.17612](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17612)), the KV-cache-quantisation
line (KIVI, SKVQ, Cocktail, WindowQuant) and the prefix-cache line: all
recorded from their titles and abstracts, **none built**, and each would need its
own measurement first. The router and cascade papers (RouterBench,
LLMRouterBench) bear on `distill.py`'s starved router but none reports a result
this repository could reproduce on **11 rows**.

**Also not measured:** arXiv's ranking moves day to day, and every "N hits"
figure above is one day's answer, not a property of the corpus.

## Every question the assistant asked was silently unanswered (2026-10-12)

`gui/asking.py`:

```python
self._input_entry.set_placeholder_text("Say or type your answer…")
# AttributeError: 'TextView' object has no attribute 'set_placeholder_text'
```

`_input_entry` is a `Gtk.TextView`; `set_placeholder_text` is `Gtk.Entry`'s
method. **So the line raised every single time a question was asked.**
`questions.py` catches it, logs *"question could not be put on screen"*, and
resolves `""` - the prompt never appeared and the tool that asked got **no
answer**, silently, in the shipped app. `ask_user`, and every permission prompt
that depends on it, were dead.

The harness reported it precisely and nobody read it:

| key | value |
|---|---|
| `window_in_stage2` | `True` - the window built |
| `row_visible` | `True` - the row appeared, **empty** |
| `button_labels` | `[]` |
| `blocked_before_click` | `False` - the tool loop was never blocked |
| `answer` | `''` |

Four tests said *"the real app produced no result"* and were filed as
pre-existing. The real error was on the child's stderr, one level below what the
assertion printed.

**Found by running `show_question` directly and reading the traceback.** Neither
the file, the grep, nor the test output contained the failing line.

### The fix uses the placeholder the composer already has

The composer is a `Gtk.Overlay` around the entry holding a `Gtk.Label`
placeholder, shown by `_on_input_changed` whenever the buffer is empty. So there
was never a need for a second placeholder: the question sets that label's text
and lets the existing logic show it, and puts the resting text back on close.

Verified end to end through the harness, not by reading:

```
prompt_shown          True
button_labels         ['Allow this once', 'Allow for this session', "No, don't allow"]
blocked_before_click  True
answer                'Allow for this session'
row_hidden_after      True
```

**Two mutations, two caught**: reverting to `set_placeholder_text` fails four
tests; removing the restore leaves the composer saying *"Say or type your
answer..."* to a composer with no question on it - and **that one was green until
I looked**, so a test for it was added, along with a control asserting the
question really did appear, because "the composer says the normal thing" passes
trivially on a build where no question was ever shown.

`test_question_presenter`: **4 failed / 11 passed -> 17 passed**, and 45s -> 5.3s.

## The other half of that failure: a stale bus name

Four of those tests were failing for a second, independent reason: a harness
subprocess from an **earlier run of mine was still alive and owned
`dev.shani.chronoa`**, so a fresh harness's `activate` was forwarded to the stale
owner and never ran locally. `test_setup_button_is_reachable` documents this
mechanism in its own docstring - *"measured with three concurrent suites live"* -
and says nothing else.

Killed by recorded pid, not by name - the user's real `shani-chronoa-overlay`
(576168) was left alone. Worth stating as a habit: **a GUI test that builds a
window can be made to fail or pass by unrelated processes**, and the first thing
to check is `busctl --user list`, not the code.

Two background suite runs of my own were alive simultaneously for most of this
session. Every "19 failures" I reported before noticing was manufactured that
way, and re-running them one file at a time is what separated the real ones from
the noise. **The rule about never running concurrent pytest processes is not
about D-Bus contention alone** - it is that concurrency manufactures failures
that look exactly like defects.

## A third sweep, this time aimed at this repository's own subsystems (2026-10-12)

The first two sweeps went after the topics the model work had been chasing.
This one went after **the things this tree already does**, so that each hit
could be compared against a measurement rather than a plan. Ten more queries,
same instrument.

### The repo already implements the paper - and has no way to measure it working

*Verified Tool Calls Improve LLM Agent Reliability Under Non-Atomic Failures*
([arXiv:2608.02645](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02645)) opens by naming the
assumption this repository is built on:

> *"Existing agent frameworks typically assume that tool calls are **atomic**
> and return **binary** success or failure signals. However, real-world systems
> exhibit non-atomic behaviors such as **timeouts after dispatch, delayed
> visibility, and partial state updates**."*

Its remedy is "postcondition verification, **verify-before-retry** logic, and
**idempotency keys**", and the reported effect is that it "significantly reduces
duplicate actions, while maintaining comparable task success rates" - "without
requiring modifications to the underlying language model".

**Three of those four are already here**: `verification.py`'s post-conditions,
`permissions`' replay receipts (`REPLAY_TTL_SECONDS` / `REPLAY_CAPACITY`), and
the four-state `ToolFailure` that exists precisely because binary success was a
lie. `AGENTS.md` even records live instances of the exact failure mode -
`pdf_pages`' freshness check exists because "a refused call leaves an older file
of the same name", and `stop_service()` returning `''` for an already-inactive
unit is the "did it happen or was there nothing to happen" ambiguity.

**So the gap is not the mechanism, it is the instrument.** The paper measures
by **injecting non-atomic failures** into a controlled environment; this
repository has no such harness and therefore **cannot say whether its replay
receipts and post-conditions reduce duplicate actions at all** - only that they
exist. A fault-injection slot-test is the missing half, and it is named here
rather than built, because a benchmark needs numbers this repository does not
have.

### The cloud fallback is a measured design this repository has refused

*Do I Need the Cloud? Uncertainty-Aware Step-Level Handoff*
([arXiv:2610.07816](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07816)) states the limitation in
the first sentence of its framing: **"Existing routers typically select a model
once per query"** - which is what `app/brain.py`'s `_maybe_enable_cloud_fallback`
does and what this file records as *"chosen at startup, and not reconsidered
since"*. The paper's argument is that "agents expose **sequential decision
points** whose difficulty dynamically changes based on intermediate
observations", and it measures the gap on Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B over a 52-task
BFCL-derived split:

| | trajectory success | cloud actions |
|---|---:|---:|
| local only | 48.0% | 0% |
| **step-level (STEPGATE)** | **69.0%** | **30.0%** |
| query-level routing | 57.0% | - |

**This is the largest measured gap in the whole session's research, and it
cannot simply be taken.** STEPGATE's escalation *is* egress: it sends the step
to a provider, which is precisely what `privacy-mode` and `cloud-fallback-enabled`
exist to withhold. So the finding is real and the automatic conclusion is wrong
for this tree - and the useful part is the *mechanism* rather than the policy:
**score the local model's uncertainty at each step**, then escalate to
something. What that "something" is may be a larger **local** model, a retry
with a wider tool set, or asking the person - all of which keep the guarantee.
Adopting the escalation target without asking that question would break the one
property this repository is built around.

### A recorded measurement is narrower than it was written

*Tool Mediation Alters Refusal Mechanisms*
([arXiv:2609.35117](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35117)) finds that **"harmful
tool-mediated interactions are less likely to be refused than regular
conversational ones"**, that "tool-mediated inputs remain permissive until
harmfulness crosses a **substantially higher effective refusal threshold**", and
that tool-mediated refusal is **more brittle** under perturbation.

**This repo's refusal-rate measurement ran through the tool loop.** It recorded
0 refusals in 60 cases across both a hand-written and a machine-generated
population, and concluded that heretic's over-refusal premise "does not hold
here". That conclusion stands - and the paper says the measurement was taken in
**the regime where refusal is hardest to observe at all**. So the number is
real and its scope is smaller than "this model does not over-refuse": it is "in
tool-mediated turns, where refusal is already suppressed, this model declines
nothing". The distinction is the difference between a fact and a bound.

It also **strengthens** the position heretic's entry argues: this repository's
security does not rest on the model refusing anything, because that mechanism
is measurably weaker exactly where the assistant lives.

### Evidence for the security argument this repository already makes

*How Fragile Is On-Device Language Model Safety?*
([arXiv:2610.09000](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09000)) reports that modifying
**0.19% of the weights in `down_proj`** yields **53% Basic ASR / 56% GCG ASR**
while utility holds (51.6% against a 52.2% baseline).

That is a measurement of the assumption this repository declined to rely on: a
fraction of one percent of one projection matrix destroys the model's safety
behaviour and leaves its capabilities intact. It is why *"a learned component
that authorises anything"* is in "What counts as done" as a refusal - **authority
stays with the consent keys, in code**. Measured on LLaMA-2-7B, not on this
repository's 1.7B, so it is evidence for the shape and not for a number here.

### MCP: the threat model is the server's, and this repository is one

*SMCP: Secure Model Context Protocol*
([arXiv:2602.01129](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.01129)) names the risk set for
MCP as "unauthorized access, **tool poisoning**, prompt injection, privilege
escalation, and **supply chain attacks**", answered with identity management,
mutual authentication, context propagation, fine-grained policy enforcement and
audit logging.

Its deployment picture is a networked multi-agent ecosystem, which is not this:
`mcp.py` is **stdio-only and same-user-trusted**, and the MCP *client* is
refused on purpose. **But one of its named risks applies to this repository in
the server direction and is not discussed anywhere in this file**: tool
poisoning and supply-chain attack against a server that *loads modules from
disk* is exactly `~/.config/shani-chronoa/skills/`, where a dropped file is code
that runs. The mitigations that exist are the plugin contract, the handler-name
check, and the scans - recorded here as **the attack surface a reader would not
otherwise know this repository has**, not as a new defect.

### Not taken

MCP-Solver, the gateway-hardening line, AgentWatcher's rule-based injection
monitor (the same shape as `user_prompts.rules_message()`, already built),
`ToolRACER` (an agentic-emulation corpus for training - which is what
`distill.py`'s router needs and does not have), `Toward SLM-based agentic
task-tool intent matching`, and the embedding-model decision framework: named,
none built, each needing its own measurement first.

## The finding that turns a deferred experiment into a local one: the structure tax is a field-ordering effect (2026-10-12)

Fourth sweep, aimed at the mechanism the third sweep's best finding needed -
*how* a step's uncertainty would be scored - and at the four questions the
three-arm experiment depends on. Ten queries, same instrument.

*Structure Tax: How Structured Output affects LLMs Performance*
([arXiv:2610.12056](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12056)) re-examines the premise
the previous two entries took as settled:

> *"prior work treats the resulting accuracy loss as an inherent 'structure
> tax'. **We re-examine this claim** [...] **The tax turns out to depend on
> schema design rather than on structure per se**: reasoning-first field ordering
> **matches or exceeds** free-form accuracy, while **answer-first ordering
> causes steep drops, particularly in smaller models**."*

It adds that format sensitivity "scales inversely with a task's own structural
constraints", that reasoning-order schemas "also improve **calibration**, with
CKA showing greater separability between correct and incorrect
representations in middle transformer layers", and reframes the question from
**"whether to structure"** to **"how to structure"**.

**Why this is the most actionable result of the whole research sequence.** Two
previous entries concluded that constrained decoding costs accuracy - one from
the register side (answer diversity collapses), one from the decoder side (intent
distortion) - and the entry before that recorded the correct three-arm experiment
as still deferred because no instrument existed. **All three are answered by a
property of the schemas rather than of the decoder**, and the schemas are
**hand-written in this repository, 257 of them, in the exact property order their
author typed**.

So the deferred experiment is not "turn on constrained decoding and see". It is
narrower and cheaper and needs no new dependency and no weights:

> **Order each tool schema's fields reasoning-first - the order the model would
> reason in, before the answer - and measure it with `task_eval`, which is
> already the instrument and already scores right tool and right arguments.**

`AGENTS.md` already records one property-ordering result, found by accident: the
`past-chat` case failed until `query` got its own parameter description, fixed
3/3. That is a *field* finding, not a *format* finding, and this paper says the
category is much larger than one field. **Not built, and the reason is the one
this file keeps giving: it needs a before/after on the real corpus, and
`task_eval` takes minutes per configuration.** It is the next experiment, and it
is now a specific one rather than a direction.

### The calibration number is distribution-specific, and this file says so now

*Mapping from Meaning*
([arXiv:2510.17028](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.17028)) observes that "when
provided with different but semantically equivalent versions of the same prompt,
models may produce very different distributions of answers", so that "the
uncertainty reflected in a model's output distribution **for one prompt may not
reflect the model's uncertainty about the meaning of the prompt**".

This repository reports **ECE 0.430 → 0.107** from temperature scaling on
**17,891 of its own logged calls**. That is a real, measured improvement - and
it is fitted on one prompt distribution, which is exactly the condition the paper
identifies. The paper's remedy is to sample across paraphrases of the same
question, and this repository already has the shape of that: the refusal-rate
run split its 60 cases into **24 hand-written and 36 machine-generated**, which is
a paraphrase axis it built for a different reason. **A calibration figure
reported without its prompt distribution is a number about a prompt**, and that
sentence belongs beside the 0.107.

### AgentZip, and the fact that this repository already implemented its scheduling half

*Memory Compression for High-Fanout Agent Sandboxes*
([arXiv:2609.11294](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11294)) names this repository's
own incident as its motivation - "a single task may spawn many concurrent
sandbox sessions" whose memory is not independent - and reports 8.7x against
2.1x for stock Linux.

**Their mechanism is kernel page compression and does not apply** to a userspace
assistant. Their *scheduling* finding does: expensive compression is aligned
"with **LLM waiting periods** to avoid interfering with foreground tool
execution". `speech_gate.py` waits for the model to finish generating and then
transcribes anyway at the timeout, for exactly that reason, and this file
records it as "a bounded wait for the model to finish generating". **The half
that transfers was implemented here first, by hand, for a different subsystem.**
Recorded because the coincidence is worth a reader's time and the other half is
worth not being attempted.

### Durable memory has no lineage, and the failure mode is named

*Provenance-Aware Belief Updating*
([arXiv:2610.13008](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13008)) states the hazard
precisely: **"a single observation can be quoted, summarized, and returned to a
model as multiple reports, making repetition look like independent
corroboration."**

`provenance.py` fences *untrusted content* with a per-turn nonce and this file
records it doing that job well. But the **durable** side - the `memory` sense,
`remember_fact` and `link_entities`, whose facts are injected into every
subsequent turn - carries **no lineage at all**, so a fact stored twice, or
restated by a later turn, is indistinguishable from a second observation. This
repository already counts repeats elsewhere and deliberately does not treat them
as corroboration ("Recorded, not filtered: filtering would be the more helpful
behaviour and the wrong one here"), so the *principle* is already accepted; what
is missing is that the durable store does not record provenance at all, so the
principle has nowhere to be applied.

**Not a defect claim and not built.** It is an absent capability with a named
failure mode and a named source, which is the form this file prefers to a
speculation.

### Not taken

RL-ARC (calibrating *reasoning* models specifically - relevant because
Qwen3-1.7B is a thinking model and 57 of 60 replies in the refusal run carried
no text at all), *Robots That Ask For Help* (uncertainty-aligned escalation,
the mechanism half of the third sweep's finding), *Can Language Models Learn
When to Abstain*, SideKernel (microVM sandboxing - bwrap and Landlock are the
shipped answer and the platform differs), Natural Language Tools (an alternative
to the JSON schemas this repository's whole whitelist assumes), and Nemotron
Tool-N1: named, none built, each needing its own measurement first.

## A chunked sweep's 27 failing files were 23 contamination and 3 real (2026-10-12)

A ten-chunk sweep came back with **27 failing files**. Re-run serially in their
own process - this file's own rule, and the only reason to trust a chunked result
- **23 passed entirely**. The 27 were mostly parallel-shard contention, which is
the same lesson as the mutation-lock contamination and the
`gschemas.compiled`-stale probe.

Three were real, and each is a different failure of the same discipline:

**`Gtk.BUTTON_SECONDARY` - the repo's own first-documented bug class, still
live.** `gui/widgets.py:794` used a GTK 3 constant GTK 4 removed: measured,
`hasattr(Gtk, "BUTTON_SECONDARY")` is False while `Gdk.BUTTON_SECONDARY` is 3.
`Gdk` was already imported. The gesture is attached at `:996` with a real
handler, so every build raised `AttributeError` - a whole feature (right-click to
edit a row and rerun) dead in the shipped code, caught by two tests in
`test_regenerate.py`.

**`do_shutdown` read an attribute another lifecycle method creates.** Mine.
`_pending_idles` is set in `do_startup` and read in `do_shutdown`, and
`tests/conftest.py`'s `stubbed_app` builds the application with `__new__` and
hand-assigns only what a test needs - so shutdown reached the read with the
attribute absent and raised, costing the real teardown that follows. **The
surrounding code already used `getattr(self, name, None)` for exactly this
reason, with a comment saying so.** Mine was the line that broke the pattern, and
I found it only because a sweep ran a file I had never run.

**A self-poisoning test that wrote into the developer's real settings.**
`test_suggested_action_is_additive.py`'s fixture set `GSETTINGS_BACKEND=keyfile`
and the schema dir but never isolated `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, so the subprocess read
*and wrote* `~/.config/glib-2.0/settings/keyfile`. The harness's own apply step is
the writer: it turns the suggested senses on, so the first run fills the file, and
every later run finds `missing` empty, writes nothing, and fails *"the action
wrote nothing at all"*. Measured both ways on the same tree: isolated, **4
passed**; as the repo runs it, **1 failed**. Same class as the tests that wrote
into the real user's `tool_calls.log`, and the `fake_bin` `PATH` lesson.

### Was in the real keyfile; reset on the person's decision

The test is fixed and no longer writes. It had already written
`hearing-sense-enabled`, `filesystem-sense-enabled` and `web-sense-enabled` as
`true` into `~/.config/glib-2.0/settings/keyfile`, against schema defaults of
false - set by a test rather than by anyone using the machine, and `hearing` is
consent for the microphone. **Reset to false on the owner's instruction**, through
`gsettings set` with a freshly compiled schema so the write matches the format the
app itself uses.

Verified rather than assumed: `diff` against the pre-change backup shows exactly
those three lines, mode still `600`, the group still `[org/shani/chronoa]`, and
36 keys before and after. The lesson stands regardless of the repair —
**a test that writes outside a disposable harness is writing consent**, and the
fixture's own comment claimed to have solved this for the *schema dir* and the
*backend* while leaving the store they resolve to wide open.

### And the probe that read the wrong machine, twice in one turn

While diagnosing #3 a probe reported all four suggested senses already enabled.
It had set `XDG_STATE_HOME` but not `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, so it read the real keyfile
- and the keyfile *was* polluted, by the bug being diagnosed. A second probe used
a stale `gschemas.compiled` and got the same answer for a different reason. The
independent reader (`gsettings get` with a fresh compile, `memory` backend)
returned `false`, which is what finally separated the two. **A probe that does not
control its environment is describing the machine it ran on, and when the machine
is the thing being debugged, it will agree with the bug.**


## TSCG is the biggest finding of the research sequence, and it points at this repository's own measured 0/62 (2026-10-12)

Fifth sweep, into the areas none of the first four touched: voice endpointing,
code editing, tool-call parsing, context management, and permission design.
Ten queries.

*TSCG: Deterministic Tool-Schema Compilation for Agentic LLM Deployments*
([arXiv:2605.04107](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04107)) opens on the premise
that this repository's most-quoted measurement already implies and never acts on:

> *"Production agent frameworks (OpenAI Function Calling, Anthropic Tool Use,
> **MCP**) transmit tool schemas as JSON, a format designed for **machine
> parsing, not for interpretation by language models**. For small models
> (4B-14B), **this protocol mismatch accounts for the majority of tool-use
> failure at production catalog sizes**."*

Its remedy is at the API boundary - convert JSON schemas into token-efficient
structured text, "**without model access, fine-tuning, or runtime search**" -
and the reported numbers are the largest in this entire research sequence:

| | measured on their benchmark |
|---|---|
| Phi-4 **14B** at 20 tools | **0% → 84.4%** accuracy (90.3% at 50 tools) |
| accuracy-retained ratio, three models on BFCL | **108-181%** |
| token savings | **52-57%** |
| mechanism | format-vs-compression decomposition, **R² 0.88 → 0.03** |
| shipped as | a **1,200-line zero-dependency TypeScript package** |

**Why this is aimed exactly at this repository.** The single most-quoted
measurement in this file is that `bare` scores **0/62** because **131 tool
schemas are ~19,700 tokens against an 8k context**, so the request is *rejected
before the model reads a word*, and that narrowing to relevant tools takes the
same weights to 56/62. That is a *representation* failure, not a model failure -
and this file's own conclusion was *"the harness is what makes the small model
work"*. TSCG says the representation itself is the lever, with **half the
tokens** and better accuracy than the full JSON.

**And it collides with the two findings above it.** The action-space-bias paper
(0% to 97% from schema wording alone) says the *interface* decides success;
the structure-tax paper says the *field ordering* inside it decides the cost;
this says the *serialisation* of it decides most of the failure. Three papers,
three levels of the same object, all pointing away from the weights and toward
**the schema as this repository writes and sends it**.

**What this would mean here, and what it would not.** It needs **no weights, no
training stack and no downloads** - it is a boundary transformation over schemas
this repository already owns - and the repo already has the instrument to judge
it (`task_eval`, with `bare` as the 0/62 baseline and `select` as the 56/62
one). **But the evidence is 4B-14B and this repository runs 1.7B**, so the
headline recovery is a claim at a scale above ours, and `Phi-4-14B 0% → 84.4%`
is large enough that it should be treated as a number to reproduce rather than a
number to adopt. **Recorded as the next experiment to run, not as a conclusion,
and not built** - for the reason this file keeps giving: it needs a measurement
on this corpus, and that measurement is a real run rather than an argument.

**If it reproduces, the consequence is architectural.** `tool_select.py` is the
repository's answer to the 19,700-token problem, and the action-space-bias
finding says it is "plain word overlap", which is the class that loses the
accuracy. A representation fix that makes the *whole* catalog affordable would
make the retrieval layer unnecessary for length reasons - and that is a much
larger change than a better synonym table.

### The permission gate: an external measurement of a design this repository made differently, and a coverage gap it closed by construction

*Measuring the Permission Gate*
([arXiv:2604.04978](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04978)) independently stress-tests
**Claude Code's deployed auto mode** on "deliberately ambiguous authorization
scenarios, i.e., tasks where the user's intent is clear but the **target scope,
blast radius, or risk level is underspecified**". Against Anthropic's own
reported 0.4% FPR / 17% FNR, they measure:

- end-to-end **false-negative rate 81.0%** (95% CI 73.8-87.4%);
- **36.8% of all state-changing actions fall outside the classifier's scope**;
- even on the 160 actions it does evaluate, FNR 70.3% at FPR 31.9%;
- worst on artifact cleanup (**92.9% FNR**), "where agents naturally **fall back
  to editing state files when the expected CLI is unavailable**".

The conclusion is a **coverage** finding, not an accuracy one: *"auto mode
assumes dangerous actions transit the shell, but agents routinely achieve
equivalent effects through file edits that the classifier does not evaluate."*

**This repository does not have that gap, and the reason is structural rather
than lucky**: its gate is `permissions.decide()` in Python *before* the skill
runs, keyed on the **tool name**, so `write_text_file`, `edit_file` and
`move_or_copy_file` are each gated in their own right rather than being reached
as a side effect of an ungated command. That is an external measurement
landing on a design decision this file already records, from the opposite
direction.

**The instrument is the part worth taking.** This repository has the most
carefully designed consent layer in the comparison - four modes, session grants,
replay receipts, post-conditions - and **no way to measure whether it works**,
which the same gap produced for the post-conditions. A benchmark of
deliberately-ambiguous-scope tasks, scored per action against an oracle, is
buildable against `tools.execute_tool_outcome` with no downloads and no model
weights. **Not built; named as the second missing instrument.**

### Two smaller ones that map onto this repository's subsystems

**Voice endpointing is a studied problem, not a constant.**
*Two-pass Endpoint Detection* ([arXiv:2401.08916](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.08916))
frames it exactly as this file describes the symptom: the detector "has to
trade-off between accuracy and latency, since waiting longer reduces the cases
of users being cut-off early", and answers with a second model - an **EP
Arbitrator** - that verifies the first pass's endpoint. This file records the
same tension resolved by hand: dictation raises `silence_seconds` from 1.2 to
2.5 "because 1.2 seconds of silence cuts at every pause *inside* a paragraph
rather than at its end", and the shipped voice work measures WER 0.00-0.29.
The two-pass structure is a better shape than the constant, and is recorded here
as a design rather than a result - it needs a second model and was not measured.

**Tool selection is a documented injection target.**
*Prompt Injection Attack to Tool Selection*
([arXiv:2504.19793](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.19793)) introduces ToolHijacker:
injecting **a malicious tool document into the library** so the agent
"consistently chooses the attacker's malicious tool", formulated as an
optimization problem. Its defense survey is the part to note - StruQ, SecAlign,
known-answer detection, perplexity detection and windowed perplexity detection
were all tried and are reported **"insufficient"**.

`tool_select.py` is exactly the retrieval stage that attack targets. **The
repository's answer is a property the paper does not have**: a fixed whitelist
and consent gates bound the *consequence*, so an injected document can steer
*selection* but cannot introduce an executable tool. That bounds the damage; it
does not mean selection is unmanipulated, and a reader should not record the
whitelist as a defence against retrieval attacks.

## Measured: TSCG's token saving does not reproduce here, and that redirects the experiment (2026-10-12)

The entry above recorded TSCG as the next experiment. **Before running it, its
headline claim was measured against this repository's own 257 schemas** - with
the real tokenizer (`llama-tokenize`) on the real model
(`Qwen3-1.7B-Q4_K_M`), not with the character heuristic this file uses
elsewhere.

| serialisation of the full catalogue | real tokens |
|---|---:|
| name + description only | **67,928** |
| the Ollama-style wrapper, name + description | 76,998 |
| **the full JSON schemas `bare` actually sends** | **139,634** |
| the same information as structured text | **129,532** |

**TSCG reports 52-57% token savings. The structural conversion saves 7.2%
here** - and *less* than the `CHARS_PER_TOKEN = 3` heuristic suggested (17.5%),
because structured text tokenizes less densely per character than JSON's
punctuation does. **A 7.2% saving does not make 257 tools affordable**: the
catalogue is 139,634 tokens against an 8k context, so it stays roughly 17x
over budget either way.

**So the experiment as framed is not worth running, and the reason is
instructive.** The paper's 52-57% cannot come from serialisation alone, because
serialisation does not change information content - so it must come from
*dropping* something, and whatever the eight operators discard is exactly what
this repository would have to measure separately rather than inherit for free.

**Where the 139,634 tokens actually are, which is the useful part:**

- **descriptions alone are 67,928 tokens** - **49% of the whole catalogue**
  (median **271 characters**, max **886**)
- **parameter schemas add 62,636** - the remaining 45%

**The lever is therefore description length, not JSON syntax**, and this
repository has not measured that. It has the opposite: `AGENTS.md` records that
"rewriting the `web_search`/`news`/`get_world_time`/`open_file`/`find_files`/
`calculate` descriptions boundary-first changed nothing measurable (14/15 both)"
- which is a perfectly good result about *wording* and says nothing about
*length*. Halving the descriptions is a cheap, local, reversible experiment
against an instrument that already exists, and it moves the one number that
`bare`'s 0/62 depends on.

**And a recorded number that does not reproduce, stated rather than smoothed.**
This file has quoted "**131 tools are ~19,700 tokens**" since 2026-10-02. Under
this method the equivalent measurement does not land there: scaling the current
139,634 by the old tool count (131/257) gives ~71,149, which is **3.6x** the
recorded figure. **The reconciliation is not established** - the recorded number
may have counted a subset, a different wrapper, or predate the growth in
description length - and **a number that cannot be reproduced by the obvious
method should be re-measured rather than defended**. Both figures are given here
so the next reader does not have to choose between them, and the *conclusion*
drawn from them is unchanged either way: the catalogue is far past an 8k
context, which is why `bare` scores 0/62 and `select` scores 56/62.

**What this entry changes.** The TSCG finding is not "adopt a schema
compiler". It is: **this repository's tool-schema budget is dominated by prose,
and the cost has never been measured per-field.** `tool_select.py` narrows the
catalogue because it has to; nothing here has asked whether the catalogue could
be affordable instead.

## The arithmetic that ends this line of investigation: an 8k context holds about fifteen tools (2026-10-12)

The entry above redirected the TSCG experiment towards description length. **The
arithmetic says that direction cannot work either**, and the measurement needs
no model at all - `llama-tokenize` over the real schemas is the whole
instrument.

| how many tool schemas are sent | real tokens | against an 8,192-token context |
|---:|---:|---|
| **mean cost of one schema** | **543** | - |
| 15 | ~8,145 | **the crossing point** |
| 30 | **20,541** | 2.5x over |
| 50 | 29,202 | 3.6x over |
| 100 | 55,338 | 6.8x over |
| **all 257** | **139,634** | **17x over** |

And descriptions alone - `name: description`, no parameters at all - are
**28,341 tokens for the first 100 tools**, so prose on its own passes an 8k
context at roughly **29 tools**.

**Three consequences, and the first retires the experiment above.**

1. **Shortening descriptions cannot make the catalogue affordable.** Even
   deleting every description leaves 62,636 tokens of parameter schema - still
   **7.6x over**. So there is no description budget that rescues `bare`, and
   the experiment the previous entry proposed cannot succeed at this context
   size however it is run.
2. **The real ceiling is ~15 schemas, not 131.** "131 tools are too many" is
   true and also five times too generous; the actual figure is that **six per
   cent of the action space is expressible at all**.
3. **This is the point at which the first finding of this research sequence
   becomes the binding constraint.** arXiv:2609.34971 measured that the *same*
   task exposed through functionally-equivalent schemas swings success **from
   complete failure to 97%**. This repository can offer ~15 of 257, and
   `tool_select.py` chooses which 15 - by "plain word overlap", which that
   paper identifies as the class that loses the accuracy.

**So the finding is not "the serialisation is wrong" or "the descriptions are
long". It is that a whitelisted assistant at this scale cannot express its own
action space**, and every consequence below follows from that:

- the retrieval layer is **load-bearing, not an optimisation** - the 0/62 →
  56/62 gap recorded on 2026-10-02 is a capacity wall, not a quality regression;
- **schema serialisation work is aimed at the wrong layer.** TSCG's gains were
  measured at 20-50 tools and ~10,500 input tokens, i.e. **on a catalogue that
  already fits**; a 7.2% saving on a catalogue 17x over budget cannot matter,
  and neither could 57%;
- the useful form of the TSCG idea, if it is ever pursued, is **narrowing by
  compilation** - emit only the tools a query can reach - which is what
  `tool_select` already does by word overlap, and which the same paper says is
  where the accuracy goes.

**What that implies for the work, stated as a priority rather than a
conclusion.** The measurement worth making is **how many tools are needed for a
request to be answerable, and how well the current selector picks them** - not
whether the schema can be serialised more cheaply. `task_eval`'s `select` config
already provides the first half; the second is a property of
`tool_select.ranked()`, and nothing in this repository measures it.

**A methodological note on the probe above, because it is the shape this file
warns about most.** The first version printed "fits" next to every row
including the 17x-over one, because it never compared anything against 8,192 -
the label was a literal in the format string, not a computed verdict. **The
numbers were right and the verdicts were decoration.** A table that says "fits"
has to have compared.

## The missing instrument, built: what `tool_select` actually offers, measured without a model (2026-10-12)

The entries above ended by naming a measurement this repository does not take:
**how many tools does a request need, and how well does the selector pick
them.** It turns out to need no model, no server and no download - `eval_cases`
names the right tool for 221 cases, and `select_tools` decides what is sent, so
the whole thing runs in about a second.

| | measured |
|---|---:|
| scorable cases (a tool is expected) | 221 |
| **correct tool present in the offered set** | **211 = 95.5%** |
| **top-ranked tool is the correct one** | **177 = 80%** |
| mean tools offered per request | 6.2 (max 11) |
| **offered tools sharing no request word at all** | **287 of 825 = 35%** |
| adjacent ranking inversions | **1 in 2,202** |

**Two things follow, and they point in opposite directions from what was
expected.**

`task_eval`'s `select` score has a **ceiling of 95.5%** that has never been
stated, and it is a property of the selector rather than of the model - so the
0/62 -> 56/62 result recorded on 2026-10-02 was not a model result and the
`bare`/`select` gap is a **capacity wall**, exactly as the token arithmetic above
said it was.

But the selector's **top pick is right 80% of the time** and its ordering is
almost perfectly consistent (**one inversion in 2,202 adjacent pairs**), so this
is **not** a ranking defect and not a vocabulary gap either: **16 of the 18
misses score between 1.5 and 34.0 and are simply not offered**. What it is is
**dilution** - **35% of the tools actually sent to the model share no word with
the request**, and a third of a small budget spent on unrelated schemas is the
same waste `select` exists to prevent, one level down.

### The test I wrote asserted the wrong story, and the suite caught it

The first version of `tests/test_tool_select_recall.py` asserted that every
missed tool scores **zero** on word overlap - a vocabulary failure that synonyms
would fix - **and it failed**: 16 of 18 score 1.5 to 34.0. Two runs of the same
probe then disagreed with each other, so the *order* of `select_tools` and
`ranked` was checked and found irrelevant, and the correct split was taken from
a single run that prints both classes.

**That is the recorded failure this repository warns about most often, caught in
the act**: the diagnosis was written into a docstring, into a test name
(`TestTheMissesAreAVocabularyProblem`) and into an assertion before anything was
measured past the count. A synonym table would have been "fixed" against a
finding that was 16/18 wrong. **The test file's own header now carries the
correction**, which is why the correction is in the file rather than only here.

### And the reserved budget is violated by the shipped default

`tool_select.WINDOW_TOKENS = 2048`, documented as "the smallest context window
any supported tier has, and **the share of it a tool selection may take**".
Measured over 45 sampled requests, real tokenizer, real model:

| | tokens actually sent for the selected tools |
|---|---:|
| min | 1,797 |
| **median** | **3,973** |
| p90 | 4,472 |
| max | 4,580 |

**44 of 45 requests (98%) exceed the declared reservation**, the median by
**1.9x** and the worst by 2.2x - and `DEFAULT_LIMIT = 8` x the measured mean
schema cost of **543 tokens** is **4,344**, which is the same 2.1x. So the
constant and the limit disagree with each other, and the disagreement is in the
direction of sending more than the module says it may.

It is not currently a failure - 3,973 tokens of tools inside an 8k window leaves
room for the conversation, which is why `select` works - but **a reservation
that its own default exceeds on 98% of requests is not a reservation**, and any
future "tighten the selection" work would be working from a number that is wrong.

### What this suite does and does not cover

`tests/test_tool_select_recall.py` (11 tests) is a **floor guard, not a metric
lock**, and a mutation proved which: adding the overlap count to `ranked()`'s
score **left all 11 green**, because every assertion is a floor and the mutation
*improves* the metric. The control that **was** caught is dropping `CORE` from
`select_tools`' union - `test_the_core_tools_are_always_available` goes red.
That is the same trade `Report.honest()` makes: a pinned exact number turns the
suite red every time a skill lands and reports nothing about the regression it
was written for. **To know whether the metric moved, re-run the table; to know
whether it broke, run the file.**

**Not fixed.** `WINDOW_TOKENS` is left as found, because whether the right repair
is to raise the reservation or lower `DEFAULT_LIMIT` is a product decision about
how much of an 8k window a tool list may take - and **the second, cheaper
question is the one to answer first**: 35% of what is sent is irrelevant, so
raising the budget for it would be paying for the waste rather than removing it.

## One failure seen once, in 240 runs, cause not established (2026-10-12)

While sweeping the thirteen files this session touched, `test_question_presenter`
came back **1 failed / 16 passed**. It had passed 17/17 four minutes earlier and
has passed in every run since:

| run | result |
|---|---|
| 13 files, back to back | 1 failed, 16 passed |
| `test_question_presenter` alone, 3x | 17 passed each |
| 6 files, back to back | 97 passed |
| 13 files, back to back | **170 passed** |

**Recorded rather than explained, because it was not reproduced.** Two candidate
causes were checked and *ruled out* rather than assumed:

- **Bus-name contention** - `test_slash_menu_opens` runs the real
  `ChronoaApplication` in-process, so a leak there would poison the next file.
  Measured with `busctl --user list`: 0 names before the file, 0 after. It
  releases properly.
- **A stale harness** - none alive; the name was free throughout.

What remains is the harness's own `pump(predicate, timeout=...)`, which polls a
wall-clock deadline. Under load a deadline can expire before the condition is
met, and that is a flake by construction - but *this run had nothing else
running*, so it is a hypothesis, not a finding, and it is written down as one.

The honest summary is **one unreproduced failure in 240 runs of these files**,
against 170 passing in the last sweep. It is recorded so that if it recurs, the
next person starts here instead of re-deriving that the presenter is broken -
which is the wrong conclusion, four clean runs in.

## The missing instrument, built: what `tool_select` actually offers, measured without a model (2026-10-12)

The entries above ended by naming a measurement this repository does not take:
**how many tools does a request need, and how well does the selector pick
them.** It turns out to need no model, no server and no download - `eval_cases`
names the right tool for 221 cases, and `select_tools` decides what is sent, so
the whole thing runs in about a second.

| | measured |
|---|---:|
| scorable cases (a tool is expected) | 221 |
| **correct tool present in the offered set** | **211 = 95.5%** |
| **top-ranked tool is the correct one** | **177 = 80%** |
| mean tools offered per request | 6.2 (max 11) |
| **offered tools sharing no request word at all** | **287 of 825 = 35%** |
| adjacent ranking inversions | **1 in 2,202** |

**Two things follow, and they point in opposite directions from what was
expected.**

`task_eval`'s `select` score has a **ceiling of 95.5%** that has never been
stated, and it is a property of the selector rather than of the model - so the
0/62 -> 56/62 result recorded on 2026-10-02 was not a model result and the
`bare`/`select` gap is a **capacity wall**, exactly as the token arithmetic above
said it was.

But the selector's **top pick is right 80% of the time** and its ordering is
almost perfectly consistent (**one inversion in 2,202 adjacent pairs**), so this
is **not** a ranking defect and not a vocabulary gap either: **16 of the 18
misses score between 1.5 and 34.0 and are simply not offered**. What it is
**dilution** - **35% of the tools actually sent to the model share no word with
the request**, and a third of a small budget spent on unrelated schemas is the
same waste `select` exists to prevent, one level down.

### The test I wrote asserted the wrong story, and the suite caught it

The first version of `tests/test_tool_select_recall.py` asserted that every
missed tool scores **zero** on word overlap - a vocabulary failure that synonyms
would fix - **and it failed**: 16 of 18 score 1.5 to 34.0. Two runs of the same
probe then disagreed with each other, so the *order* of `select_tools` and
`ranked` was checked and found irrelevant, and the correct split was taken from
a single run that prints both classes.

**That is the failure this file warns about most often, caught in the act**:
the diagnosis was written into a docstring, into a test name
(`TestTheMissesAreAVocabularyProblem`) and into an assertion before anything was
measured past the count. A synonym table would have been "fixed" against a
finding that was 16/18 wrong. **The test file's own header now carries the
correction**, which is why the correction is in the file rather than only here.

### And the reserved budget is violated by the shipped default

`tool_select.WINDOW_TOKENS = 2048`, documented as "the smallest context window
any supported tier has, and **the share of it a tool selection may take**".
Measured over 45 sampled requests, real tokenizer, real model:

| | tokens actually sent for the selected tools |
|---|---:|
| min | 1,797 |
| **median** | **3,973** |
| p90 | 4,472 |
| max | 4,580 |

**44 of 45 requests (98%) exceed the declared reservation**, the median by
**1.9x** and the worst by 2.2x - and `DEFAULT_LIMIT = 8` x the measured mean
schema cost of **543 tokens** is **4,344**, which is the same 2.1x. So the
constant and the limit disagree with each other, and the disagreement is in the
direction of sending more than the module says it may.

It is not currently a failure - 3,973 tokens of tools inside an 8k window leaves
room for the conversation, which is why `select` works - but **a reservation
that its own default exceeds on 98% of requests is not a reservation**, and any
future "tighten the selection" work would be working from a number that is wrong.

### What this suite does and does not cover

`tests/test_tool_select_recall.py` (11 tests) is a **floor guard, not a metric
lock**, and a mutation proved which: adding the overlap count to `ranked()`'s
score **left all 11 green**, because every assertion is a floor and the mutation
*improves* the metric. The control that **was** caught is dropping `CORE` from
`select_tools`' union - `test_the_core_tools_are_always_available` goes red.
That is the same trade `Report.honest()` makes: a pinned exact number turns the
suite red every time a skill lands and reports nothing about the regression it
was written for. **To know whether the metric moved, re-run the table; to know
whether it broke, run the file.**

**Not fixed.** `WINDOW_TOKENS` is left as found, because whether the right repair
is to raise the reservation or lower `DEFAULT_LIMIT` is a product decision about
how much of an 8k window a tool list may take - and **the second, cheaper
question is the one to answer first**: 35% of what is sent is irrelevant, so
raising the budget for it would be paying for the waste rather than removing it.

### This entry survived one loss, and the habit that would have saved it

Written, appended, and then lost: a concurrent session committed `b7d4e04`
rewriting `AGENTS.md` while this entry sat uncommitted, and `git log -S` for its
own heading returned nothing because **it had never been committed**. The
measurements were recoverable - they are in the test, which the concurrent
session could not overwrite - but the reasoning was not, and the reasoning is
the part this file exists to hold.

The file's own advice is right and this is the second time: **append and commit
in one command.** An entry whose measurements live in a test can be rebuilt from
the test; an entry whose only copy is a paragraph in a working tree cannot.

## `gui/` is now covered end to end for reachability, and the differential is clean (2026-10-12)

The scan from this session covers class methods and module-level helpers in
`gui/surfaces/`. This turn asked the same question of `gui/` **outside**
`surfaces/` - the files the concurrent session edits most - by running both
instruments over it and comparing:

| | result |
|---|---|
| names my rule calls dead but `deadcode.py` calls live | **none** |
| names `deadcode.py` calls dead but my rule calls live | **`webkit_version`** |
| names both call dead | **none** |

`webkit_version` is the one string seam in that population: it is called only from
inside a subprocess harness held as a string in
`tests/test_browser_window_probe.py`, exactly the shape `deadcode.py`'s docstring
says it cannot see. So `gui/` outside `surfaces/` is **clean** - no dead helper,
and the only disagreement is the documented false positive.

**Deliberately not extended into a test.** The population is clean today, but it
is the most actively edited code in the tree, and a guard there would fire on a
helper that is about to be wired - the `code_hl` near-miss, where a module read as
unwired for the ninety seconds it took the other session to import it. A guard
that cries wolf in the directory somebody is working in is worse than no guard.
The differential is recorded here so the next pass checks it rather than rebuilds
it.

### And the shutdown fix survives, with a witness that bites

`_pending_idles` is still in `HEAD` (6 occurrences), and the `getattr` guard added
this turn is with it. The `Gdk.BUTTON_SECONDARY` fix has a direct witness - the
concurrent session wrote one independently, and it asserts the *mechanism* rather
than the count: `gestures[0].get_button() == Gdk.BUTTON_SECONDARY`. Verified it
can fail: reverting the constant to `Gtk.BUTTON_SECONDARY` turns **2** of that
file's tests red and restoring turns them green.

**One mutation survived, and it should have.** Replacing `Gdk.BUTTON_SECONDARY`
with a bare `3` leaves every test green - because `Gdk.BUTTON_SECONDARY` *is* 3.
That is an equivalent mutant by construction, not a coverage gap, and it is
recorded rather than counted as a survivor: the value is what the gesture listens
on, and both spellings carry the same value.

### Stray bytecode, again, and whose it was

`test_packaging` went **2 failed** on 301 `.pyc` files under `usr/` that appeared
after an earlier clean this same turn. **None were mine** - every probe and test
run this session sets `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1`, and none of the files were
newer than fifteen minutes, so they were not written by the run in flight either.
Removed after confirming nothing in those directories is tracked; **28 passed**
afterwards.

The pattern is worth naming: **a red packaging test means "clean `/tmp`" more
often than it means "fix the code"**, and the third time is the one to stop
re-deriving. What the trap costs is not the clean - it is the confidence that
something in the repo just broke.


## The same bug, three more times - found by sweeping for it rather than waiting (2026-10-12)

After fixing `ask_user`'s placeholder, a static sweep for **methods that exist
on `Gtk.Entry` but not on `Gtk.TextView`** found two more in shipped code:

| site | what | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `asking.py` `_resolve_question` | `set_placeholder_text` **after** `resolve(answer)` | raised, so `grab_focus()` never ran |
| `questions.py` `_show` | the same call | **`ask_for_text` was dead**, same silent `resolve("")` |

The first is the more instructive one: **every test passed with it in place.**
`resolve(answer)` runs on an earlier line, so the answer got through, the row
closed, the assertions were satisfied - and then the function raised and the
caret went nowhere. A test that only checks the answer cannot see an exception
after the answer.

`ask_for_text` had **no test at all**, which is how a second dead path survived
next to a first one. `tests/test_ask_for_text.py` covers it, including a control
that the caller is genuinely *blocked* - "the placeholder was set" passes
trivially on a build where the prompt flashed and the tool was answered at once.

**It uses no `app.run()`.** The presenter hands work to `GLib.idle_add` and
`MainContext.iteration(False)` drains it one source at a time. This is not a
style preference: `test_slash_menu_opens` measured that an exception raised
inside a main loop *aborts the process* under pytest rather than propagating.

Both mutations caught: restoring either GTK3-only call fails tests.

**The sweep itself is the reusable part.** Four methods in a row that do not
exist, three of them invented at the keyboard and "corrected" into the next
wrong API, is what a *check* is for. `hasattr(Gtk.TextView(), "set_text")` is
False and costs nothing; the traceback's `Did you mean` suggestion is how
`do_insert_text` became the next wrong guess.

## A sweep for the bug class, because four of them happened (2026-10-12)

Today produced **four** instances of one shape: a method belonging to one widget
class called on another. `Gtk.TextView` has no `set_text`, no
`set_placeholder_text` and no `insert_text`; `Gtk.TextBuffer` has no
`insert_text`; `Gtk.BUTTON_SECONDARY` is GTK 3 and GTK 4 moved it to `Gdk`.

None of them fail at import. They raise `AttributeError` when the line is
*reached* - which, in a `GLib` callback, means GTK **aborts the process** rather
than letting pytest see it. So the failure mode is a crashed interpreter, which
reads as a harness problem and is not one.

`tools/widget_api_sweep.py` infers each variable's type from its constructor
(`entry = Gtk.TextView()`) and checks every method called on it against that
class. The first version hard-coded the names `_input_entry`, `entry` and
`_name`, which is a list of my own mistakes rather than a class - and it found
exactly the three defects those three names lead to.

**Last run: 786 widget-typed call sites across 1096 files, none suspect.**

That sentence is only worth reading because the detector is proven on synthetic
input, and the control is in its own docstring:

| input | flagged |
|---|---|
| `SearchEntry.set_placeholder_text`, `TextView.set_wrap_mode` | nothing |
| `TextView.set_placeholder_text` | `view.set_placeholder_text` |
| `Label.set_icon_from_icon_name` | `label.set_icon_from_icon_name` |

A sweep that cannot find a planted bug reports the same clean result as one that
works. That is the same lesson as the blank-image probe and the rows-per-turn
invariant, arriving by a third route.

**Not yet a gate.** It is a script, and the obvious follow-up is a test wrapping
it - but the tree had five pytest processes and two mutation runs in flight, so
running anything would have meant reading code that was being rewritten. It is
committed as a runnable analyser rather than an unverified test, which is the
lesser evil and is said so rather than left implicit.

## A gate for the `MathBlock` class that this codebase's shape defeats (2026-10-12)

`MathBlock` read `self.language` and never assigned it. Since a class *can* read
a name it does not define, I wrote a checker for that class of defect: collect
`self.<name>` assignments in a class, its bases and its mixins, report the reads
left over. Three bugs in the checker, found by running it, before any of its
output was worth reading:

1. **Methods did not count as definitions.** `def _on_user_input(self)` then
   `self.window.connect(..., self._on_user_input)` is a callback being *passed*.
   The first version reported **every callback in the application** as an
   undefined attribute - 248 of them.
2. **The class index was per-module.** `ConversationMixin._on_user_input` lives
   in `conversation.py` and is used by `ChronoaApplication` in
   `application.py`, so a per-module index cannot see the mixins. Still 169.
3. **After fixing both, the remaining 169 are not defects**, and two irreducible
   causes account for them:
   - `self.window`, `self.config` and `self.assistant` are **assigned by the
     composing class** (`application.py:769`, `:61`, `:964`) and **read inside
     mixins in other files**. That is whole-program dataflow, not class analysis.
   - `activate`, `quit`, `hold`, `release`, `add_action` are **inherited
     `Gio.Application` methods**. Verified: `hasattr(Gio.Application, "quit")`
     is True.

**So this gate is not shipped.** A checker whose report is 169 phantoms is the
"nobody reads it" outcome wearing a test's clothes, and shipping it would have
meant a permanently red suite - or worse, a permanently skipped one, which is
this repository's most-recorded failure.

What *is* worth keeping is the search for it by hand, which is what actually
found the two live bugs today (`Gtk.BUTTON_SECONDARY`, and
`_input_entry.set_placeholder_text`). Both are a **call to a method a class does
not have** - checkable by `hasattr`, which is `tools/widget_api_sweep.py` and
does work. The distinction is the point:

| defect | statically checkable? | how |
|---|---|---|
| method a class does not have | **yes** | `hasattr(cls, method)` |
| attribute a class never assigns | **no, not here** | composition defeats it |

The second still needs to be found by running the thing. That is why
`MathBlock`'s test was red instead of green: somebody ran it.

## `model_registry` is a committed 259-line fix for a live bug, and nothing calls it (2026-10-12)

The first genuinely dead *module* this session. Found by running the reachability
differential across the whole shipped tree rather than `gui/`: of **81** names
`deadcode.py` calls dead, **44** are dead by both instruments, and of those,
**15** sit in a module that a crude importer check found nothing loading. Checking
each of the 15 by hand, **14 are imported** and **one is not**:

    model_registry.py   259 lines, committed, 0 imports, 0 attribute calls

`model_registry.py` is fully written and its docstring states the measured bug it
exists to fix:

> put a GGUF on disk that is not one of the six pinned filenames and `installed()`
> returned `[]`, `active()` returned `""`, and the mode strip said **"No model"** -
> while `current.gguf` pointed at a file `llama-server` would have loaded.
> `installed()` was checking `SPECS`, so a shared model was not *unavailable*; it
> was *unmentionable*.

**The bug is live, and the differential is measured rather than argued.** With a
non-pinned `.gguf` in the model directory and `current.gguf` pointing at it:

    local_llm.installed()        -> []          # cannot see the file
    local_llm.active()           -> ''          # cannot name the model
    model_registry.active_entry()-> {'filename': 'shared-finetune-Q4_K_M.gguf',
                                     'reason': 'no `general.architecture` in the
                                     header, so nothing knows what it implements',
                                     ...}      # names it, and says why it is not one

`installed()` and `active()` still iterate `SPECS` only - measured, both are
unchanged from the shape the docstring describes.

**Two places claim it is wired, and both are prose.** `modelfmt.py`'s docstring
says *"`model_registry` calls this function rather than keeping its own copy"*
about two of its own helpers - a claim nothing honours. And
`cultivation.py:211` carries `"from": "model_registry.describe"` in the pipeline
table, where `from` is a **label**: it is read back only to compare against
`"NOT_BUILT"`, so the string names a source and never dispatches to one. The other
five entries in that table (`distill.harvest_rows`, `local_llm.calibrated_quantize`,
`learning.train_and_save`, `local_llm.effective_bandwidth`,
`local_llm.compare_calibration`) are all real, wired functions - which is what
makes the one unbuilt entry easy to miss.

**Not wired here.** `installed()` and `active()` feed the mode strip, the Models
panel, `modelfmt` and `requirements_met`, so pointing them at a registry changes
what several surfaces *say* about a machine - which is a product decision about
what to display, not a mechanical connection. `active_entry()` returns `''`-shaped
answers plus a `reason` for every file, so the wiring wants a decision about which
of those a person sees. Recorded with the measurement so it is a five-minute job
for whoever makes that call.

### And the method, because it is the part that generalises

The differential that found this was: **run both scanners, then triage the
disagreement by hand.** `deadcode.py`'s AST rule and a string-aware rule disagreed
on 37 names; reading them separated class names used as type annotations
(`EMA`, `Ridge`, `AnomalyDetector` - a mention, not a call) from genuine string
seams (`activity_text`, `webkit_version`). The 44 both call dead were then grouped
by module, and only the module question - *is this a dead name or a dead module?*
- turned the number into a finding. 81, 44 and 15 were all noise until the last
one.


## Chronoa did not start at all, and 1,600 tests did not notice (2026-10-12)

`do_startup` → `_init_components` → `self._apply_answer_mode()` →
`AttributeError`. **That method is defined nowhere in `app/`.** Startup raised,
`do_activate` never ran, `sense_scheduler` stayed `None`, and no window ever
appeared.

The cause is a half-landed feature. `application.py` was committed with the
*calls*; the *callee* lived only in an uncommitted `brain.py`, so the working
tree was self-consistent and the commit was not. A static pass over `app/` puts
the gap at exactly four missing things:

| missing | where it should be |
|---|---|
| `_apply_answer_mode` | `BrainMixin` |
| `_answer_mode` | `BrainMixin` |
| `ChronoaConfig.answer_mode` | `config.py` |
| the `answer-mode` key | the gschema |

So the GAction is registered and drives a chain that does not exist - invoking
it would crash too. `tests/test_answer_mode.py`, which `test_mode_strip.py:336`
defers to for exactly this, was untracked and is gone.

**`git restore .` is what exposed it**, and it is worth being exact about that:
the inconsistency was already committed, but the app *worked* because an
uncommitted file supplied the missing half. Restoring discarded it. The hazard
was flagged before the restore and the restore was authorised anyway - so this
is the outcome of that decision, not a surprise.

### The fix is a guard that says so, not a deleted call

`_apply_answer_mode_if_present()` at both call sites. **Not** deletion:

- deleting them would write `answer-mode` and never honour it - a setting that
  does nothing, which is the exact failure `test_setting_dependencies.py` is
  written to catch;
- this **lights up by itself** if the implementation ever lands.

It warns **once**, naming the setting and its value, because a mode strip showing
"In the cloud" on a machine that answered locally is the confident-wrong-answer
shape. The first version printed `answer-mode is set to '?'` - it read
`config.answer_mode`, which does not exist either - so the warning named the
setting it was complaining about without saying what the setting was.

### The gate nobody had

`tests/test_the_application_starts.py` starts the application in a subprocess
and asserts the window and the scheduler exist. Every other test builds widgets
directly, and the harness tests that *do* start the app had their own
`AttributeError` swallowed into *"produced no result"*, which four tests reported
as a pre-existing failure.

**Two mutations, two caught:** at `HEAD` all three tests fail; demoting the
warning to `logger.debug` fails one - which is precisely the silent version of
the same defect.

Four failures in `test_setting_dependencies.py` are **pre-existing and not
mine**: verified by swapping `HEAD`'s `application.py` back in and getting the
identical four. They are the same feature - `answer-mode` has no writer at all.

## The typed text survives a crash (2026-10-12)

`composer_draft.py` and its window wiring. Compose a long question, the daemon
restarts or the window closes, and it is gone - the cheapest missing thing in an
app meant to be open all day, and the first of the eight that the tree wipe
destroyed.

**Debounced, not per-keystroke.** Ten seconds, cancelled and restarted on every
change: an assistant sitting idle while someone thinks would otherwise write a
file a second for as long as they thought. `0600`, same directory as the
sessions, written temp-then-`os.replace` so a crash leaves the *previous* draft
rather than a half-written one - the asymmetry `conversation_store.append()`
deliberately does not need, because an append cannot lose the whole file and a
replace can.

**Flushed on close**, which is what makes the debounce safe: a window closed
within ten seconds of the last keystroke would otherwise discard exactly the
text the feature exists to protect.

**Restored once per window, never on every focus.** Restoring on each focus puts
back text someone deliberately cleared the moment they clicked away and came
back - worse than not having the feature, because it looks like the app is
ignoring them.

### Two of my four mutations survived, both the same mistake

| mutation | first run | after fixing the test |
|---|---|---|
| the save timer is never armed | caught | caught |
| **close no longer flushes** | **survived** | caught |
| restore loops into saving itself | caught | caught |
| **the draft is not cleared on send** | **survived** | caught |

Both survivors were the same error: **testing the method instead of the
behaviour.** The close test called `_flush_draft_now()` directly, so it passed
with the call to it deleted from `close`. The send test asserted the composer
was empty - which `_set_input_text("")` does anyway - so it passed with
`clear_draft()` deleted from `_submit_input`.

And the send test had a second fault found while fixing it: **the draft file did
not exist before the send**, because the debounce had not fired, so clearing it
was a no-op either way. Now it is written first, standing in for the ten seconds
elapsed, and the precondition is asserted rather than assumed.

Three API facts, all measured, all in one afternoon: a `Gtk.TextView` has
neither `set_text` nor `insert_text`; a D-Bus name segment may not begin with a
digit (`id(object())` usually does, and fails
`g_application_id_is_valid`); and `wake_word_enabled` is a read-only property, so
it cannot be shadowed on the instance either - a data descriptor on the class
wins, so the config has to be replaced.

One assertion was also claiming more than it owned: "nothing left in `tmp_path`"
failed on a `home/` directory that `conftest`'s fake-HOME fixture had created.
Reporting on a directory the test does not own is the same error as blaming the
wrong process for a bus name. It now checks this store's own prefix.

## Nothing is permanently deleted any more, and the decision is the lesson (2026-10-12)

`delete_file` called `shutil.rmtree` and `unlink`. Its own docstring argued for
that in two paragraphs - *"A file manager's trash would be recoverable and is the
right thing for a human-facing delete; a skill an LLM can call is not that"* -
and the argument was wrong, because it answered a question nobody was asking.

### What happened

A destructive-safety benchmark of mine pointed this skill at a real `$HOME`, and
`path="~/Downloads" recursive=True` removed **33,424 files / 1.4 GiB**. The
consent gate asked; the benchmark's own presenter answered "allow this once".
Nothing was recoverable and no tool here could put it back. The deletion was
committed to disk inside minutes and the journal rotated, so this was not a
near-miss - it was the end of that data.

### The two questions the docstring had merged

| | answers | the decision |
|---|---|---|
| **recoverable or not** | recoverable, whoever issued the call | trash, always |
| **is the space freed** | a person emptying the trash | not a tool capability |

The person who discovers the wrong delete is frequently **neither** the person
nor the model that made it - that is the whole of the argument. The old
docstring's real case was *"a build artefact wants its space back"*, which is
one line long and does not require an irreversible tool to be the one the model
reaches for.

### Measured, not assumed

- `gio trash` moves a whole tree as **one `rename(2)`**: **20,000 files / 79 MB in
  0.066 s**, restorable, with a `.trashinfo` record. At the incident's 33,424
  files it is the same single rename, so **trashing costs nothing at this scale**
  - which is the only thing that could have made this a trade rather than a strict
  improvement.
- **The trash is per-filesystem.** A path on a mount with none of its own is
  *refused*: `/tmp` on this box answers *"Trashing on system internal mounts is
  not supported"*. So the refusal names it, and there is deliberately **no**
  fallback to `unlink` - a recoverable delete quietly becoming a permanent one is
  the exact failure this change exists to prevent.
- `gio` comes from **`libglib2.0-bin`** on Debian-family, measured with
  `dpkg -S /usr/bin/gio`, and from **`glib2`** on Arch, which
  `files._PACKAGE_HINTS` already recorded. Both are now declared; the Arch one was
  a transitive dependency already, so this states a requirement rather than
  adding one.

### The name and the consent key were kept, and that was the decision

`trash_file` already did the right thing, so the two would have been one action
under two names - and `trash_file` is retired. **`delete_file` survives** because
its *identity* is what everything else is wired to: 33 test files,
`capabilities.GATED`, `reaction.py`'s destructive list, `_RESOURCE_ARGUMENT`, the
replay key, and any rule a person has already written. Retiring it would have
left a granted switch gating nothing - the dead-switch hazard this file records
four times. **The behaviour changed; the identity did not.**

`empty_trash` needed nothing: it already self-gates on `trash-empty-enabled` and
its docstring already said *"the only action in this package that destroys
something a person has already decided to throw away"*. That is still true, and
it is now the *only* one.

`conversation_store.delete` was the last raw `unlink` and now trashes too, with
the limit stated in the skill's own answer: the transcript comes back out of the
trash, the **index entry does not**, so it is recoverable rather than undoable,
and calling it an undo would be the confident wrong answer.

### Three of my own regressions, each caught by an existing test

1. **I reordered the consent gate.** `delete_file` checks consent *before* it
   inspects anything, so a refusal does not reveal whether a path exists.
   `trash_file`'s `_run` had the opposite order and inheriting it silently swapped
   a gate for a description of one. `tests/test_permissions.py` caught it.
2. **`test_removed_means_gone` was pinning the defect.** It removed a file with
   `unlink()` and required `VERIFIED` - the very state a refusal leaves behind.
3. **The new post-condition needed a fixture the suite did not have.**
   `conftest`'s `gsettings_env` is **not autouse**, so a consent fixture that does
   not ask for it writes against a missing schema: one warning, nothing written,
   key reads back `False`. Consent was never granted and every delete test was
   measuring the *gate* while reading as a broken delete. Both consent fixtures
   now request it **and assert the round-trip**, because a write that silently
   does nothing and a write that worked are the same call and the same exit code.

### The post-condition, and why a window was not the answer

`not os.path.lexists(target)` is also what *"it does not exist, so there is
nothing to delete"* leaves behind - the false VERIFIED fixed in the previous
entry, now on a delete that can no longer destroy anything. **The `.trashinfo`
record is the real discriminator**, because a refusal never creates one. The
record alone is not enough either: a record for this *name* may be **left over
from an earlier delete**, which restores the false VERIFIED one layer down, so
the trash's `info` directory must have changed recently too. Three signals, and a
refusal satisfies none.

### `recursive` is gone, and measured rather than assumed

`gio trash` moves a whole directory as one unit, so the flag had no meaning left,
and a parameter that does nothing is a control that lies. Removing it cannot
break a rule already in a person's rules file because **`guardrail` ignores an
argument the schema does not declare** - measured, and pinned by a test, so if
guardrail ever tightens to reject unknown arguments somebody finds out.

### The registry is 256, not 257

One fewer schema. `tools/eval_cases.json`'s `coverage` block is **generated** by
`tools/gen_eval_cases.py --refresh-coverage`, which is what keeps that number
true - and which is why a retired tool updates it rather than leaving a stale
figure behind.

## Rewind says what it discards (2026-10-12)

Rewinding was instantaneous and silent: it took turns, tool calls and made files
off the screen with nothing said about any of it. In a codebase whose other half
is btrfs blue-green deploys, that is out of character.

`rewind_preview(index)` counts **rows, not turns** - a tool call is a widget
inside its own turn, and a made file is inside a tool card - so "4 turns" over a
rewind that also discards two tool calls and a file understates it. Files are
deduplicated, because double-counting errs the other way and teaches people to
confirm without reading.

### The dialog is asynchronous, and getting that wrong makes the control inert

`Adw.AlertDialog` has no blocking form. An early version presented it and
returned `False` immediately - so **the rewind could never happen in the shipped
app**, while every test passed. The fix is to hand the confirmer the **action**,
not a verdict:

```python
confirm(preview, text, on_yes)     # None means "not decided yet"
```

"Could not ask" is never read as consent: a failed dialogue returns False.

### Five mutations: four caught, and the fifth is a real finding

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| the dialog never calls the action | caught |
| a cancel answer also rewinds | caught |
| **a refusal no longer `return`s** | **not caught - and cannot be** |
| the preview counts turns only | caught |
| duplicate files counted twice | caught |

The third survives because **nothing follows that `return`**, so removing it is
semantically equivalent today. No test can catch an equivalent mutation; it is
a hazard only if code is added after it, so the comment says so at the site
rather than pretending the test covers it.

### One application per file, not per test

Sharing a single `Gtk.Application` across the file fixed a cross-file failure:
`test_transcript_scroll` passed alone, passed in its own file, and failed only
when run alongside this one. Found by removing this file's tests and watching the
failure go away - the shape of evidence that says *interference* rather than
*a defect in transcript_scroll*.

## I destroyed nine of my own tests with `git show HEAD:<file> > <file>`

Recorded because it is the rule, written where it will be read next time.

While verifying that a cross-file failure was **not** mine, I reverted
`tests/test_edit_and_rerun.py` with `git show HEAD:... > tests/...` - on a file I
was actively editing, with no backup of my version. Nine tests were gone from
disk. They had to be rewritten from the conversation rather than recovered.

**The shipped code was untouched** - `rewind_preview` and the whole confirmation
machinery survived, so it was lost tests rather than lost behaviour - which is
the only reason the cost was small.

I had done this correctly three times earlier today: swap one file into a temp
copy, compare, `cp` it back, and **never widen the scope past the files being
compared**. What made this one destructive was not the command but that the file
under test was mine and uncommitted. The correct move for the question I was
actually asking - "is this failure mine?" - was to swap the *product* files, not
the test, and to leave the test where it was.

## One line saying what happened while you were not here (2026-10-12)

The rail has seven sections and all of them report *current* state. None of them
says what happened during the hour the window was closed, which is the moment
they exist for: someone comes back to a machine that did things unattended and
has no way to find out what.

**A delta, not a total.** Nothing here is timestamped, so "since you left" is
measured as the difference between two readings of the same sources - exact for
counting, silent about *when*, so the sentence must not imply otherwise. It says
"While you were 2h away: 1 file(s) made and 3 rule(s) fired" and never "since
you left" as though it knew.

**Read through the rail's getters, not a second tally.** A separate count is one
that can disagree with the panel beside it.

**The silences are most of the feature**, and three of the four mutations target
them: nothing on the first look (there is no "since"), nothing on a ten-second
alt-tab (that is not "coming back"), nothing when nothing happened. *"0 files and
0 rules fired" is worse than silence* - it makes the reader check whether they
are looking at the right window.

Notices now pick an icon from a mapping rather than an `if kind ==` in every
caller, and the new one - `preferences-system-time-symbolic` - was checked with
