`rglob` against Adwaita, because the sibling test that passes for icons missed two
bad names earlier today.

### A mutation that cannot be caught, because the code says the same thing twice

`previous is None` and `left_at is None` are **the same case** - the snapshot
carries both - so a mutation deleting the first guard passed all nine tests. It
is not a missing test; the two conditions are redundant. Both are now stated in
one `if` with the reason written at the site, because "an un-caught mutation"
recorded nowhere becomes "an un-caught mutation" read as coverage.

**Also recorded from writing it:** `window.py` has no `from __future__ import
annotations`, so an import inserted on that anchor put nothing there and left
`time` undefined - caught by pyflakes, but only because the file was read back.

## A rail row that clicked nothing, and named nothing

Three call sites of `_Section.link(text, detail, surface, on_open)` passed an
**icon theme name in the `surface` slot**. `link` had lost its `icon` parameter
at some point; the call sites kept passing one.

Nothing raised. The row rendered, the tooltip read *"Open the
preferences-system-symbolic panel"*, and clicking it asked the window for a
surface named `preferences-system-symbolic` - which does not exist. A third bug
of the same shape was already recorded in that function's comment: the previous
fix for a *duplicate* `surface=` keyword had deleted the keyword and kept the
icon, converting a loud `TypeError` into a silent lie.

- **Fixed** by restoring `icon` as a named parameter (`link(..., icon=...)`) and
  giving all five rows a surface that exists: `diff`, `artifact_store`,
  `triggers`, `senses`, `goals`.
- **Gated** by `test_every_rail_row_opens_a_panel_that_exists`, which clicks
  every button in the rail and checks the name against
  `surfaces.available_surfaces()` - read live, not a hand-copied list, because a
  copied list drifts and then asserts nothing.

**The gate did not bite at first, and that is the part worth keeping.** With a
made-up artifact path (`/tmp/opencode/one.png`, which does not exist) the Made
section renders nothing, so restoring the Made row's bug under it passed -
**1 mutation survived, because the row under test was never built.** The fix was
to make the fixture create a real file, and to add
`test_the_made_section_is_actually_under_the_gate`, which asserts the row
exists so the gate's coverage is visible rather than assumed.

### Two checkers I wrote and then threw away

**A static scan of `link(` call sites.** It reported every surface as unknown
because it compared the literal `'"diff"'` against the unquoted name `'diff'` - a
check that cannot pass is not a check. Fixed the quoting, and it then flagged
`self._icon_for(p)` and `'detail'` - it mis-parses any multi-line call, because
the regex terminates at the first `)` it meets. **Dropped in favour of the
runtime gate**, which cannot mis-parse: it clicks the button and reads what
actually happened.

**`widgets.py` in the mutation harness.** The harness copied
`shani_chronoa/widgets.py`, which does not exist - it is `gui/widgets.py` - so
every mutation reported `No such file or directory` and *looked* like it had
passed.

### Editing without an assert

Three edits in the Sensing patch used bare `str.replace` with no count check. One
of them - adding `_fill_senses` to `refresh()`'s filler list - silently did not
match, so the section was built and never filled, and **ten of fifteen tests
failed**. A silent no-op edit reads exactly like a bug in the thing being
tested; the cost of `assert s.count(old) == 1` is one line.

### Snapshot testing while another session mutates the tree

`conftest` refuses to run while a mutation run is live, which is correct. The
way to keep working without fighting it: `cp -r usr tests /tmp/opencode/snap/`
- **preserving the `usr/lib` + `usr/share` layout**, because `conftest` computes
`SCHEMA_SRC = REPO_ROOT/"usr/share/glib-2.0/schemas"` and flattening it gives a
`glib-compile-schemas` failure that looks like a schema bug. Verify the copy
carries your markers with `grep -c` before trusting any result from it, and run
mutations *there* - mutating the real tree while another session rewrites it is
how you ship someone else's mutation.

## A ruler for long conversations, and four GTK facts that cost a morning

The minimap (`gui/minimap.py`) is one tick per turn, coloured by role, with the
viewport drawn on it. `visible_turns()` and `scroll_to_turn()` already existed,
so the data was there and nothing was drawing it.

**The window needed a way to know a turn arrived.** The transcript emitted no
signals at all, so `TranscriptView` grew a `turn-added` signal emitted at both
append points. The alternative - re-deriving the turn count on every scroll
tick - is work proportional to the whole conversation, on every pixel of
scrolling, to learn something that changed once.

**The viewport arithmetic is a module-level function on purpose.**
`visible_turn_range(value, upper, page_size, spans)` takes five numbers and
returns two, so each edge has a hand-worked answer in the tests. The one that
motivated it: GTK hands back a `value` up to a pixel or two past
`upper - page` during a fling, and an unclamped comparison reports **the last
turn as not visible** - at exactly the bottom of the conversation, which is
where you notice.

### Four GTK4 facts, each found by a test that could fail

- **`self._remove` does not exist.** `TurnMinimap.set_turns` cleared its ticks
  with `self._remove(...)`, a GTK3 name. Every unit test called `set_turns`
  exactly once, so the clearing code never ran until the *wiring* test added a
  second turn - and then **PyGObject swallowed the `AttributeError`** raised
  inside the signal handler, so the map stayed one tick wide and reported no
  error. Fixed to `remove()`; `test_rebuilding_replaces_the_ticks_rather_than_
  appending` now runs that path on its own.
- **`get_children` does not exist** on a GTK4 `Box`. The startup probe used it
  inside a `try`, caught its own `AttributeError`, printed `-1`, and the
  assertion below reported a *wiring* failure rather than the missing method.
- **`type(child).__name__` is `"Button"`, not `"GtkButton"`.** Counting
  `"GtkButton"` found nothing in a map full of ticks. Only plain Python classes
  report their own name (`"TurnMinimap"`), so a name-based check works for our
  widgets and silently finds zero for GI's. **Use `isinstance`.**
- **`get_accessible_property` does not exist** on this build, so an accessible
  label can be written but not read. `test_the_minimap_itself_is_one_focus_stop_
  with_a_label` records `update_property` instead - the repo's existing pattern
  in `test_mode_strip.py`.

### The connection that no test covered

`self._transcript.connect("turn-added", self._on_turn_added)` in `__init__` was
covered by nothing: the wiring tests bind the methods to a stub and do their own
`connect`, so **deleting the line left all of them green** (mutation-confirmed).
The only place the real `__init__` runs is the startup probe, so the probe now
reports `MINIMAP`, `MINIMAP_TREE`, `MINIMAP_SCROLL` and `MINIMAP_TICKS` - it
adds a real turn to the real window and counts the ticks. All four now kill
their mutation.

Two of those assertions were written wrong first and had to be fixed before they
meant anything: the tree walk followed `get_parent()` **up** from the window
(where there is no parent) instead of down through children, so it reported a
correctly attached widget as dropped.

## answer-mode: the warning was the bug, and the missing method was already written

`_apply_answer_mode` was missing while **two callers and a warning** existed for
it. The warning was not merely useless - **it was false**:

> answer-mode is 'cloud' but _apply_answer_mode is not implemented in this build,
> so the choice is not being applied - the model will answer as it did before
> that setting existed

while `brain.py` was reading `privacy-mode` and `cloud-fallback-enabled` on
**every turn**. The setting did govern what left the machine; what it did not do
was move the engine off the one already loaded.

**The method was already written.** `BrainMixin.select_llm(what)` is documented
as *"Switch the answering engine now"* - it was written for the Models panel and
had **no product caller at all**. So landing this was wiring, not invention, and
the thing I had refused to guess at in an earlier session was already settled by
a docstring and a test suite.

**The mapping is the strip's own labels.** `_ModeStrip._EGRESS` offers four rows
that reduce to the three values the gschema now declares:

| row | stored | engine |
|---|---|---|
| Nothing leaves | `local` | local |
| This machine answers | `local` | local |
| This machine, then cloud | `local-cloud` | **local** |
| Cloud | `cloud` | cloud |

`local-cloud` maps to *local* deliberately: "answer here when you can, reach a
provider when you cannot" is *start* local, and the fallback is
`_maybe_enable_cloud_fallback`'s job. Mapping it to cloud would answer every
question remotely while the chip said "This machine, then cloud".

**Switching only when it would change something** - rebuilding a cloud chain on
every startup to arrive at the engine already running spends a provider's rate
limit to learn nothing. **A refusal is logged and the engine left in place**,
never reported as a success.

### The guard test stopped testing anything

`test_a_missing_applier_warns_rather_than_failing_silently` relied on
`_apply_answer_mode` being defined nowhere, so the guard took its missing
branch. The moment the method landed, `getattr` found it, called it, warned
about nothing - and the test failed **for having been right**. The guard's
missing branch is now reached by shadowing the method with `None`, which is the
only way to exercise a `hasattr` guard whose method exists.

`tests/test_answer_mode.py` (destroyed once already, by my own
`git show HEAD:<file> > <file>`) asserts both directions: the warning does not
fire while the method exists *and the guard actually calls it*, and it still
fires when the method is genuinely gone. **Insurance that is only ever checked
in the present case cannot tell a working guard from a dead one.**

### A comment that described a path the code cannot take

The first draft said the empty-mode branch was the ordinary startup and that
guessing `local` would override a legitimate cloud chain. The gschema gives
`answer-mode` a default of `'local'`, so `config.get` never returns empty in the
real application - the branch is reachable only from a config whose compiled
schemas predate the key. Corrected in `7a59930`; a comment that describes a path
the code cannot take misleads whoever reads it next.

## The chunk-runner bytecode fix was a no-op, and the trap has one source (2026-10-12)

Correcting a claim made earlier this session, because it was measured badly and
then asserted confidently.

`tools/run_suite_in_chunks.sh` was changed to set `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1`, and
the report said *"proved by measurement: run a chunk with the flag in place and
the `.pyc` count under `usr/` does not move (36 before, 36 after)"*. **That
measurement could not have failed either way**, which is the negative-control trap
this file records more than any other. Run without the flag, the same count is
**0 before, 0 after** - identical.

The decisive experiment, run as a comparison rather than as a single arm:

| run | `.pyc` written under `usr/` |
|---|---:|
| `python3 -m pytest tests/<file>.py`, no flag in the environment | **0** |
| `python3 tools/gen_capabilities.py`, no flag | **312** |

So **the pytest path never wrote bytecode**: `tests/conftest.py:38` sets the
variable at module scope, and pytest imports every conftest before it imports any
test module, so the package is always compiled after the flag is set. The whole
source of this trap is **standalone `tools/*.py` runs**, which import the package
with no conftest involved at all.

The flag in the chunk runner stays - it is harmless defence against a future where
conftest's guard is moved or a tool is imported earlier - but it is not the fix,
and it was recorded as one. **A measurement that would read the same whether the
change worked or not is not a measurement of the change.**

The six hand-cleaned `__pycache__` directories this session were all standalone
`tools/` runs, mostly this session's own probes. The habit is the only durable
answer available: `pytest-env` is not installed, so `pytest.ini` cannot set the
variable, and a root-level `sitecustomize.py` that `site` would auto-import is
magic nobody would expect to find in this repo.


## Comparing two conversations, and what was chosen *not* to compare

The last of the approved main-UI features. `conversation_diff.py` holds the
comparison; `gui/surfaces/compare.py` is the panel; both are new.

**Assistant text is not comparable, and comparing it is worse than useless.**
The same question answered twice gives two different answers, so a diff over the
assistant's half reports every turn as new on *every* comparison. A panel that
says "everything is different" every time is a panel nobody opens twice. What
*is* comparable is what the person asked, and "have I already asked this?" is
the question a conversation list cannot answer.

**Matching is on normalised text - NFKC, casefolded, whitespace collapsed,
trailing punctuation dropped.** A diff that calls "What's the weather?" and
"what's the weather ?" two different questions teaches the reader to distrust it
on the first comparison. **NFKC rather than NFC** because a question typed on a
phone and the same question pasted from a web page routinely differ by more than
one accent form.

**Repeats are counted, not collapsed.** A set-based diff hides that a question
was asked three times, which is exactly what someone re-reading an old
conversation wants to know.

**Order is preserved within each side but is not a difference.** The order
questions were asked in is the order of the work, so `only_old` and `only_new`
keep it. But a question asked earlier in one conversation and later in the other
is the same question, and `identical` ignores order - a panel reporting that as
four changes would be reporting on a reordering.

### Three tests that could not have failed

Each of these passed against a mutation that broke the behaviour it names. All
three are the same mistake wearing different clothes - **test data chosen
without checking it could distinguish the two behaviours.**

- **"first, second, third" is in alphabetical order**, so sorting the unique
  questions changed nothing and *two* mutations survived. The test now asks in
  the order `zebra, apple, mango`.
- **The ordering test checked `only_new` alone**, so sorting `only_old` was
  invisible. An asymmetry that is genuinely wrong.
- **`set_selected(99)` is clamped by GTK**, so the out-of-range state the test
  named was unreachable and removing the clamp in `_selected` passed. The index
  now comes from a stand-in that returns 99.

And **two substring/membership slips of my own**: `'"Only in the later" in
labels` against a *list* asks for an element equal to the whole phrase, and the
element is `"Only in the later (1)"`. Both failures showed the panel rendering
exactly the right thing.

### A real defect the panel test found

`NO_QUESTIONS` said *"One of these asked nothing"* but fired only when **both**
sides were empty. A conversation consisting of nothing but a system prompt,
compared against a real one, reported "Earlier asked 1 question(s); later asked
0" and three groups of "None" - true, and useless. The count line was right and
said nothing.

The selectors and the results also live in **separate boxes now**: the first
version cleared results by index (`children[2:]`), assuming the two drop-downs
are always first. Reordering the layout by one row would have deleted a control.

## Two defects the Compare panel's own tests could not see

Both were found by asking *what does this code ask the real application for*,
rather than by reading the code again. The fixture was a stub built to match
the guess, so every test passed against a panel that would not have worked on
any machine.

**The panel guessed at attributes the application does not have.**
`_store_root` looked for `_conversation_root`, `conversation_root`,
`_sessions_root` and `session_dir` on the app. `ChronoaApplication` has **none
of them** - every caller in `app/` and in `gui/surfaces/conversations.py` asks
`conversation_store.session_dir()`. So the panel resolved no root and rendered
**"Could not read your conversations" on every machine, forever**. Now it asks
the module function the way every other caller does, and the override a test
uses is spelled `_test_conversation_root` so a stub cannot stand in for the
real answer again.

The witness is `test_the_app_has_the_root_this_asks_for`, which constructs a
bare `ChronoaApplication` and asks *it* - not a stand-in, and not the fixture.
`test_the_root_the_panel_asks_for_is_where_conversations_are_written` reads the
store's own answer so a rename cannot leave this panel reading an empty store.

**The listing was a second answer to a question that already had one.** It read
the raw index and reimplemented the newest-first sort and the untitled-conversation
name. `conversation_store.list_sessions()` has done both since it was written.
Two implementations of "what is this conversation called" is two that drift, and
the panel's would have been the one nobody looked at.

**`content` is not always a string.** A question sent with a screenshot is
stored as a list of parts, and `normalise` returned `""` for a list - so every
multimodal question vanished from the comparison, and a conversation of them
read as one that had asked nothing. That is the confident-wrong-answer shape
wearing a comparison panel's face. The store hits this in
`conversation_store._text_of`; `content_text()` is the same rule, spelled out
here rather than reaching for a private name.

### The pattern, named

Three of this feature's checks failed for the same reason: **test data or a stub
chosen without checking it could distinguish the behaviour from its opposite.**

- a fixture app carrying the attribute the code guessed at;
- "first, second, third", already alphabetical, so sorting changed nothing;
- `set_selected(99)`, clamped by GTK, so the state the test named was
  unreachable.

A test that cannot produce the failure it describes is not evidence. The check
that catches this class is cheap and belongs in the same file: *build the real
thing and ask it*, rather than building a thing shaped like it.

## deadcode.py's count is a ceiling, and five live names are inside it (2026-10-13)

Re-run today: **80** dead names across 44 modules. The number moves - 79, 81, 81,
80 across four runs this week - and the *triage* has not changed in any of them:
**no module is entirely dead**, every name is a dead name inside a live module.
The framing that would be wrong is "80 dead names", and the framing that is right
is the module question.

**But the count is a ceiling, not a measurement, and the reason is now verified in
five specific places.** `tools/deadcode.py` documents its own rule - *"String
constants are not scanned, which is what removes the prose false positives"* - so
any name reached by a **string** reads as dead to it. Of today's 80, **32 appear
quoted somewhere** in the package or tests, which is an upper bound on how many
are live that way.

Verified live by string, each read out of the code rather than inferred:

| name | the mechanism |
|---|---|
| `show_devices` | `phone_link.py:370`'s `getattr` string tuple |
| `speaking_row` | `voice.py`'s `_FORWARDED` `setattr(page, name, getattr(...))` |
| `webkit_version`, `activity_text` | called inside subprocess harnesses held as strings in two test files |
| `context_report` | `gui/window.py:1978`'s `getattr(assistant, "context_report", None)`, then **called** - `report() if callable(report) else None` |

`context_report` is the newest and the most instructive, because it is *fully
wired and displayed*: `assistant.py:841` computes the `context_meter.Report` on
every request, `_rail_context` reads it through that `getattr`, and window.py:1602
passes it to the rail as `get_context=`. 34 tests across the context-meter and
now-rail suites pass on top of it. A scanner reports it dead because the seam is a
string.

**And the bound is not the count either** - a quoted name can still be dead.
`set_suggestion_handler` appears quoted exactly once, in a `window.py` docstring
explaining its sibling's pattern, and has no caller of any kind. Quoted means
*check*, not *live*.

So the honest statement of what `deadcode.py` produces today is: **80 names an
AST attribute scan cannot reach, of which at least five are demonstrably live, and
none of which is a dead module.** The five cost nothing to find and each would
have been "fixed" by someone trusting the number.


## Found by reading the diff, not by a failure: a comment that denied its own code

`_on_turn_added` was documented **"Appended rather than rebuilt: a turn arriving
does not move the ticks that are already there, so there is nothing to redraw"**
and the line under it called `set_turns`, which **removes and recreates every
tick**. Three consequences, none of which any test could see:

- **O(turns) per turn**, so quadratic over a conversation - the worst possible
  place for it, because the cost is paid on the UI thread while a reply is
  streaming.
- The **highlighted tick widget was replaced outright**, so the viewport
  highlight silently moved onto a fresh tick that did not carry the class until
  the next `set_viewport`.
- Every existing test **counted** ticks, and a rebuilding map and an appending
  map have identical counts. Counting cannot see this; **identity** can.

`TurnMinimap.append_turn(role)` now adds one tick, and the tests compare widget
objects (`after[:len(before)] == before`) rather than lengths.

**The fix for that had a bug in it, and a test caught the bug rather than the
first measurement.** `_built` was set just before the tick-append loop - which
the empty-map branch returns *before* - so it stayed False forever on an empty
map, and every `append_turn` re-ran `set_turns(())`, clearing the tick the
previous call had added. Measured: **two appends left one tick.** The flag moved
above the empty case.

### The general lesson, twice over

A test that counts things cannot see anything about *which* things. Every
minimap test asserted a length; none asserted identity, and the length was
correct throughout a quadratic implementation. When the question is "did this
change the thing or make a new one", the assertion has to be `is`, not `len`.

## Two more defects the same review found, both invisible to counting

**The map rebuilt every tick on every turn** - recorded above. The second is a
layout bug that needs the *stylesheet* to see, which is why no widget unit test
caught it: a `Gtk.Button` is mostly theme padding, so with `min-height: 3px` the
map's **minimum** height was about four pixels a tick, and GTK **cannot
allocate a widget below its minimum**. Measured at the largest conversation the
store allows (`MAX_LOADED // 2` = 250 turns, a user and an assistant each):

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 4 turns | 23px | 15px |
| 40 turns | 167px | 87px |
| **250 turns** | **1007px** | **507px** |

1007px is a hard floor on the column. A 900px window cannot honour it, so the
composer is pushed off the bottom of a conversation that is well inside the
cap. Fixed with `min-height: 1px` plus `vexpand` on the map and on each tick:
the floor becomes one pixel a turn, and `vexpand` hands the rest of the height
to the ticks either way - four thick marks filling a tall column, or thin ones
that fit.

**`test_a_full_conversation_still_fits_the_window_height` derives the turn
count** from `MAX_LOADED // 2` rather than typing in a number. A hardcoded 400
passes today and quietly stops being true when the cap moves - a test that
asserts a fact about the world has to recompute that fact from the world.

The measurement loads the real stylesheet first, because the size being tested
only exists once the CSS is applied. A test that measured the widget without it
would have measured 35 pixels a tick and passed.

## Two more from reading the Compare panel, both about claims it makes

**Two conversations generated from the same first question have the same
title**, and the pair of drop-downs then read "Fix the build" twice - so which
two are being compared is unknowable. That is the common case, not an edge one.

The fix does **not** add a date. There are already three `_when()` functions in
that package, each formatting a different type of thing, and a fourth would be
duplication; importing the Conversations panel's private is the same mistake
`conversation_diff` avoided by spelling out `content_text` rather than reaching
for `_text_of`. The label carries the **message count** instead - `list_sessions`
already had it, so this adds no formatting of its own, and conversation length
is what you want to know when choosing what to compare.

**`conversation_store.load()` keeps only the last `MAX_LOADED` (500) messages
and says nothing.** That is right for opening a transcript and wrong here:
this panel exists to answer *"have I asked this before?"*, and a question asked
forty turns before the window opens is reported under **"Only in the later"** -
a confident *you have not asked this before*, built out of a message the reader
never had. The counts have the same problem, more quietly.

So the truncation is **detected, not inherited**: the file's own non-blank
lines are counted against what `load()` returned, and the panel says which side
was cut and that a question listed as new may have been asked earlier. One
extra pass over a file the panel has already read, and it needs no change to
`load()`.

A failure and a truncation look the same to a reader and mean opposite things -
"nothing here" versus "not all of it" - so an unreadable conversation is
explicitly **not** reported as truncated.

## The mode strip now checks itself against the engine that is answering

Landing `_apply_answer_mode` created a gap rather than closing one. The strip
answers *"what is Chronoa allowed to be"*; the Models panel answers *"what is
answering"*. That split is deliberate and still right - but until the applier
existed nothing **moved**, so the two could not disagree and nothing was
watching for it. Now they can, and the direction that matters is the privacy
one: a person who chose **Nothing leaves**, with a cloud provider answering, and
no line anywhere on screen saying so.

`_note_engine_disagreement()` runs at the end of every `refresh()` and says so
only when the disagreement is a **failure**:

| chosen | answering | a failure? |
|---|---|---|
| Cloud | this machine | **yes** - you asked for a provider |
| This machine, then cloud | this machine | no - that is the point of it |
| This machine, then cloud | a provider | no - "when you cannot" |
| Nothing leaves / This machine answers | a provider | **yes** - the privacy promise |

**The first version got two rows of that table wrong**, and both were caught by
running it rather than reading it:

- it asked *"did the user want cloud?"* and counted `local-then-cloud` as
  wanting it - so it flagged a local engine under the one mode whose entire
  description is *answer here*;
- it cleared the mark only on `local`/`local`, so a cloud engine that caught up
  with a cloud choice stayed flagged **forever**. A warning that cannot clear is
  noise, and noise is how a real warning stops being read.

The refusal reason is read from `app._answer_mode_problem`, which
`_apply_answer_mode` now records. **The engine already produced a sentence saying
what went wrong**; a second guess beside it would be a second answer to the same
question.

The mark is a **css class and a tooltip, not a seventh chip** - a chip reading
"answering: local" would be read as a seventh permission rather than as an
observation about the one beside it. The tooltip carries the sentence; the rule
carries the finding, because a warning that exists only in a tooltip is a
warning nobody sees.

## Which turn wrote which file

**The gap:** the pre-image ring - the mechanism behind undo - stored
`{path, at, content}` and **no turn**. So the Diff panel knew every change ever
made and nothing could say whose it was. "What did *this* turn do to my
machine" had no answer; the only one available was session-wide, and a
session-wide answer to a question about one turn is not an answer.

That matters more here than in a chatbot. This app writes to your machine, and
the pre-image ring is the only thing standing between it and an unrecoverable
edit.

**The label crosses the subprocess boundary in `argv`, not in memory.** A skill
runs as `python3 -c`, so the only channel to the child is the one the consent
grant already uses: `argv = ["env", KEY=VALUE, ...]`. `execute_tool` now appends
`CHRONOA_TURN=<label>` to that same `env` invocation - *beside* the grant, not
as a second `env`, because two `env` invocations work and make the reader
wonder which one wins.

The child is told **which turn asked, and nothing else**. It is a label in a
log, not a way back into the app; the answer string remains the only thing that
comes back. `TURN_ENV` lives with the reader (the skill) and is imported at the
point of use, so the two ends cannot drift - and a top-level import of a skill
from `tools` is the direction that once handed a skill a half-built module.

**The environment value is treated as text to check, not as an identifier**:
whitespace collapsed, capped at 64 characters. It comes from the environment and
lands in a file a person may read, so a newline in it would put a second line
there.

**Cleared in a `finally` on the turn.** A label left behind attributes the
*next* turn's writes to this one - so the one turn the user cancelled would
appear to have rewritten whatever the following turn did.

### Attribution is never guesswork

An entry with no label - a skill called directly, or a build from before this
existed - **belongs to nobody**. It is not folded into whichever turn asks. A
file listed as changed by a turn that did not change it is worse than no list
at all, and `changes_for_turn` is written to make that impossible rather than
to make the common case convenient. The one file the app itself writes
unattributed stays fully undoable through `recent_changes()`; adding a key to
the ring cost nobody their ability to put a file back.

The footer counts rather than listing: a path is unreadable at that width, the
count is what a reader wants, and Diff is one click away for the names.

## The modes that exist, and the one you could not see

Asked what modes this app has. The honest inventory:

| mode | where it lives | enforced where | on the strip? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Plan mode** | `/plan` | `execute_tool` — the dispatch path, not the prompt | yes ("Read only") |
| **Explore** | Settings → Privacy | `permissions.explore_refuses()` | **no** |
| **Don't ask** | Settings → Privacy | refuses rather than prompting | **no** |

**There is no code mode, no ULW, and no automode.** `dont_ask` is the closest
thing to an auto mode, and it is the opposite of what the name suggests: a call
that needs permission and cannot be asked about is **refused on the spot**, not
performed.

Plan mode is worth reading as a model: it refuses the consent-keyed set,
derived from `capabilities.gated_by` rather than from a second hand-kept list,
and it is enforced in the dispatcher rather than asked for in the prompt -
because a prompt instruction is a promise the model may or may not keep and a
check in the dispatch path is a fact.

### The gap: two of the three were invisible from the window

The strip answers *"what is Chronoa allowed to be"*. It did not answer *"will
it ask me first?"* - and the answer to that can be **no**. So a person who had
set "No questions" in Settings, and then watched Chronoa refuse an action
without asking, had no way to connect the two: the setting lived behind a
Settings window, and the conversation was where the surprise happened.

Now the posture is a chip, placed **before** "what it may change" because it is
the question that decides whether you get interrupted.

Three things it deliberately does not do:

- **It does not say "auto".** "Auto" on a mode strip reads as *it may act
  freely*, which is the opposite of this mode. The word is "No questions" and
  the tooltip says risky calls are **refused** rather than asked about.
- **It does not persist.** `permissions` keeps the posture in memory only, so
  a mode that never asks cannot become the silent default at the next unattended
  login. Putting it on the strip must not make it look sticky, so the tooltip
  says it lasts until the app restarts, and a test fails if `permissions` ever
  grows a `save()`.
- **It does not repeat the mode names.** `_PERMISSION` and `_PERMISSION_KEYS`
  are both checked against `permissions.Mode`, and a test asserts the strip's
  three rows and the action's three keys are the same tuple.

`search-symbolic` was the first icon for the Explore row and **is not in
Adwaita** - the empty box that reads as a rendering bug. `edit-find-symbolic` is,
checked with `rglob` over the theme directory rather than `has_icon`, which has
been wrong before.

## Measuring `explore` before putting it on the strip — and not putting it there

The first version of the permission-posture chip offered three rows, `explore`
among them, beside the "Read only" chip that *is* plan mode. Measured across all
**256** tools with both modes on:

| | blocks | tools neither blocks |
|---|---|---|
| plan mode (`gated_by`, the consent-keyed set) | **92** | 73 |
| explore (`READ_ONLY_TOOLS`) | **168** | |
| both | 77 | |

So two read-only controls on one strip, differing on 168 tools, with nothing on
screen to say which is which. **And explore refuses `ask_user`** - in explore
mode the app cannot ask you a question - along with `backup_status`,
`accessibility` and `alarm`, none of which can change the machine.

That is a **defect in explore's calibration**, not a reason to advertise it.
It stays in Settings, where its stricter meaning is written down, and the strip
carries only what answers a question the strip is for.

**The exclusion is witnessed by the measurement, not by a comment.**
`test_the_reason_explore_is_off_the_strip_is_still_true` re-derives both counts
and asserts explore still refuses `ask_user` and still blocks far more than
plan mode. If that calibration is ever fixed, the test fails and the row
becomes worth reconsidering - instead of a comment in a table quietly rotting
into a false justification.

The strip's two rows are also asserted to be a **subset** of what the action
accepts, not equal to it: Settings still writes `explore`, and the strip is not
the only door.

## The general form of the startup bug is not machine-checkable here, and that is the finding (2026-10-13)

After `_answer_mode` cost eight actions, the obvious next step was a scanner for
the general shape: *a `self.X` load where X is bound nowhere in the class or its
bases.* The existing guard -
`tests/test_sense_labnetworks.py::test_every_name_it_uses_is_imported` - checks
unbound **`Name`s** only, so it structurally cannot see an `Attribute`, which is
the entire difference between what it caught and what it missed.

**Written and measured, it reports 54 files.** Almost all of it is two kinds of
noise, and neither is fixable from inside a scanner:

| noise | example |
|---|---|
| **external bases** | `Gtk.Application`'s `add_action`, `activate`, `hold`, `lookup_action`; `Gtk.Widget`'s `add_css_class`, `append`, `set_tooltip_text`; `BaseHTTPRequestHandler`'s `client_address`, `path`, `send_error` |
| **mixin cross-references** | `VoiceMixin` reading `self._async` and `self._submit`, `BrainMixin` reading `self.config` - bound on `ChronoaApplication`, which the mixin is *mixed into*, never on the mixin itself |

The real defect is in there - `application.py` lists `ChronoaApplication._answer_mode`
- but it is one line in a list that also contains `activate` and `add_action`, and
nobody will find it. **A scanner that reports 54 files is worse than no scanner**,
which is the same conclusion `open_surfaces` reached for skill candidates and
`list-audit.py` reached for name lists: a lead list nobody can work through is a
lead list nobody works.

**What was built instead is narrow and sound:** `tests/test_every_app_action_is_registered.py`
pins the **complete** set of 36 actions by stubbing `add_action` and driving
`_create_actions()` once. It needs no display, it fails on a hole *and* on a quiet
addition, and reproducing the original defect makes every test in it fail.

The reason the narrow version works is the thing the wide one lacks: it asserts a
**consequence** (these 36 names are registered) rather than a **shape** (this
attribute is bound somewhere). A consequence can be checked exactly; a shape in a
codebase with mixins and external bases cannot, short of resolving every base
class outside the repo.


## A plan is data, not a paragraph

Plan mode's refusal tells the model *"describe the steps instead"*, and that
prose was the entire record. So nothing could be ticked off, resumed or
corrected, and approving a plan meant asking again in a new turn and hoping the
model re-derived the same steps from its own text. Meanwhile `goals.py` already
had `PlannedStep`, `depends_on`, `Phase.AWAITING` and a persisted store - and
**nothing connected them.** There were three answers to "where is the plan" in
one codebase, and the one named *plan mode* kept nothing.

Now: `planmode.record_refusal(name, arguments)` at the dispatch site (the only
place that has both the tool and the arguments it wanted), `plan_from_refusals`
in `goals.py`, and the run is parked in `AWAITING` rather than `PENDING`.

### Two properties it had to keep

**The plan is made of the calls that were actually refused.** A model may
describe steps in prose without calling a tool, and then this stores *nothing*.
That is the point, not a limitation to paper over: steps assembled from prose
would be our guess at what it meant, and a stored guess that later executes is
the worst thing this app could hold. A plan that quietly drops the steps it
could not justify is a plan that lies about its own coverage.

**Approving it grants nothing.** `advance()` runs each step through
`tool_executor`, which is `tools.execute_tool` - the same path a typed call
takes, so every consent key, every prompt and every verification still applies.
Verified by running a stored step with plan mode on (refused) and off (not
refused), not by reading the docstring. `plan_from_refusals` writes a
*proposal*; it is not a permission.

`record_refusal` is called from the dispatch site rather than from
`blocked_reason`, because `blocked_reason` is asked "can this tool run" and is
called from tests and from the permission layer's prose - giving it the
arguments would make every one of those calls a plan step.

## Plan mode asks, rather than describing what it would have done

The refusal told the model *"describe the steps instead"* - which hands the
decision to the one party with an interest in being wrong about what you want.
It now puts the call to the user, through `ask_bridge.ask`, with the actual
tool and the actual arguments named in the question. A "Do it now" runs that
call immediately **through the same `execute_tool`**, so consent, sandboxing
and verification all still apply to it - the ask is not a side door round the
dispatch path, it is a question asked inside it.

**Everything that is not an explicit yes is a refusal.** No presenter, a
dismissed prompt, a timeout, an empty answer, an answer that is not one of the
two words - all of them mean *no answer was given*, and the rule this app keeps
insisting on is that an unanswered question is never consent. This change adds a
way for a tool to run that did not run before, so the negative cases are the
whole test file rather than a footnote.

**"Do it now" is the first option.** The common answer to "what would you do
about this?" followed by silence is yes, and a dialog leading with "no" teaches
people that plan mode is a wall rather than a question.

**One "Keep planning" stands for the rest of the turn.** Asking again for every
remaining step turns one question into ten dialogs - the opposite of what was
asked for. The silence *is* the answer; the steps still land in the stored plan,
because a refused step that is not recorded is a step the plan does not mention.
"Do it now" does not silence the next one - that answer was about that call.

**The gate in front of the ask is `blocked_reason`, which is empty when plan
mode is off.** `ask_to_proceed` itself asks and obeys the answer regardless of
the mode, so the thing that stops it being a way to run something unasked is
the refusal check in front of it - which is what the first version of the
off-mode test got wrong, by asserting the wrong function's return value.

### Why asking from `execute_tool` cannot deadlock

`ask_bridge.ask` blocks on a `threading.Event` with a timeout, and `execute_tool`
is synchronous, so asking from inside it looks like a deadlock until you check
where the dispatcher is called. The assistant runs it through
`run_in_executor(None, ctx.run, ...)` (`assistant.py`), so the call is already
off the GTK thread and the main thread stays free to show the dialog.

That is not incidental: the comment at that call records the deadlock it caused
when it did not - the question was answered on 2026-10-08 and only transcribed
at 13:59:23, after the timeout had reported "no option was chosen". The same
thread is why `ask_user` works, so the pattern is established rather than
assumed.

**A refusal is not a validation miss.** The assistant counts results beginning
`ERROR:`, `Not run. ` and `Refused: ` as a malformed call, and stops after
three. A plan-mode refusal begins "Plan mode is on", so it does not count -
which is right, because it is a policy refusal and not a broken call, and the
`LoopDetector` is what catches a model retrying the same tool.

## The three modes, and the four that were there before

Asked for automode / ultracode / ultrawork, then for the minimum. The two
requests pull in opposite directions, so the resolution was to find the
*decisions* inside them and ship three, rather than ship a list of names.

| chip | question | enforced in |
|---|---|---|
| **Plan** - Working / Plan | what would you do? | the dispatch path, and it asks |
| **Auto** - Ask first / Auto | will it stop me to ask? | the permission layer's refusal |
| **Build** - General / Build | what is it working on? | which tools reach the model |

**The strength of each is different, and the file says so.** Plan is a check in
`execute_tool`. Auto is a refusal in `permissions`. Build changes which schemas
reach the model - a strong nudge, **not a gate**. Nothing refuses a general tool
because Build is on, because that would make a Build turn unable to open a
browser and the failure would arrive as "I cannot do that" rather than as the
reason. A mode that hid tools would make some questions unanswerable.

**Build, not Code.** The files people bring this app are often not source - a
`.docx`, a `.csv`, a systemd unit - and "code" promised a programmer's workflow
it does not have. The module is `buildmode.py` as well; a module named
`codemode` implementing a mode called Build is the same mismatch this whole
change is about.

### What was actually redundant

Not the number of modes - **two controls for one axis**. Settings' permission
combo and the strip's chip both set `permissions`, and Settings offered a
third option (`explore`) that **no chip on the strip could show**, so a mode was
reachable only by hunting through Settings. It is now exactly the chip's two
options, with a subtitle for a session already in read-only that says where it
went.

Read-only also stops being a strip chip. It was never really one control: "Read
only" meant plan mode, so a permission and a workflow shared a word, and the
chip could report either. It is `permissions.EXPLORE` in Settings, where its
stricter meaning is written down - and `buildmode.read_only_note()` says so for
anyone who remembers it on the strip.

### The blank icon, again, and this one was mine

Measuring every symbolic name in Adwaita: **it ships no build, tool, hammer,
wrench, construction or gear icon at all.** `system-build-symbolic` and
`applications-development-symbolic` are Yaru names - and so is
`emblem-default-symbolic`, which this strip had been given for the Plan chip's
"Working" row one message earlier. The same empty-box bug this repository has
hit three times, introduced by me while fixing a different one.

## A UX review, and the one thing it turned up

Four chips moved off the strip to the palette, and that created the problem this
found: **a control whose only path is a keyboard shortcut nobody knows about is
a control that is not there.**

Checked, and there is no shortcuts surface - `Ctrl+K` and `Ctrl+F` appear in
this file **only in code comments**. There *is* a `HelpWindow` and a help
button, and it answers *"what can Chronoa do"*; nothing on screen answered
*"what can I press"*. So the four modes that just moved there were reachable by
exactly one person in the history of this codebase: me.

Two fixes, both in the places a new person is guaranteed to look:

- **The empty state names them.** `show_placeholder()` already existed to give
  a new user something to act on, so it now carries
  *"Ctrl+K for anything else · Ctrl+F to find in this conversation · ? for what
  Chronoa can do"* - each described by what it does, because "Ctrl+K" alone is
  not a reason to press it and the word *palette* appears nowhere else in the
  interface.
- **`?` is now bound to help.** It was advertised before it existed, which is
  worse than not advertising it: a person presses it, nothing happens, and
  they learn the interface lies to them.

**`?` is tested as `Gdk.KEY_question`, not `Gdk.KEY_slash`.** The shifted key is
the one delivered with Shift held; the bare slash is what you type into the
composer every time you write a slash command. A check for the bare slash
would open the help window over the thing being typed.

### Still missing, and it is the bigger half

`HelpWindow` is a capability list - what Chronoa can do - and nothing tells you
what *you* can do. The empty-state line covers first run; a person who closes
the app and comes back has no equivalent. The honest version is a keyboard
section in `HelpWindow` built from the same tables the strip and palette use,
so it cannot list a shortcut that was rebound.

## What you can do, next to what Chronoa can do

`HelpWindow` is a capability list: what the assistant is able to do, grouped by
intent with consent state shown. **Nothing on screen answered what the person at
the keyboard can do**, and two of the shortcuts that matter are the only route
to a control that is deliberately not on the toolbar - the four mode chips that
moved to the palette among them.

There is now a "What you can do" group above "Everything Chronoa can do": five
rows, the key in its own column, built into the same `_index` the window's own
filter walks, so searching finds a shortcut like anything else. The empty state
covers first run and this covers every run after it, which is the half that was
missing.

### The shortcuts list is hand-written, and three bugs proved it can't be trusted

The section is five typed rows. Its first comment claimed the list was *read
from the app's actions and could not go stale* - which was false, and was the
same false promise this file has spent all session removing elsewhere. It now
says it is hand-written, and a test is what keeps it honest.

Writing that test found three bugs, all mine, and all failing toward **false
alarm** - which is still an afternoon wasted:

- the table's third field named `show-help` and `turn-stop`, **neither of which
  is an action**; both are keyval handlers. The field is only a search haystack,
  but naming actions that do not exist is how the next reader concludes a
  binding is missing when it is only the label that is wrong.
- `rglob("window.py")` **matches `settings_window/window.py` first**, so the
  test read that file and reported Ctrl+K as unbound when it was looking at the
  wrong `window.py` entirely.
- `package.parent` instead of `package`, pointing the test at a directory a
  level too high.

Each is fixed by naming the file, and the lesson recorded once: **a test that
opens a file by name is only as good as its ability to open the right one.**

## I read a sweep's failures while its chunks were still running, and under-reported by ten (2026-10-13)

A ten-chunk sweep came back with five chunks finished and I collected the failure
list then: **15 distinct failures across 5 files**. Two chunks were still running.
One of them, `chunk_aj`, finished ten minutes later with **11 failures of its
own** - so the true list was **25 across 6 files**, and the ten I missed were all
`test_voice_loop_live.py` (the parallel-flaky live-audio suite AGENTS.md already
documents, so no harm came of it, but only by luck).

**The failure was not the sweep's, it was mine: I treated a partial result as a
complete one.** The chunked runner exists precisely so a crash costs one chunk,
and it prints *"exited"* per chunk - nothing said *"done"*. A chunked run's result
is only a result when every chunk has a summary, which is the same distinction the
mutation runner draws with `N of M sets` and `INCOMPLETE`. It is worth naming
because the cost here was invisible: the missing ten were all flakes, so the
omission changed nothing observable, which is how it would have survived.

Two real defects were hiding in the part I did not stop to read, and both were
fixed after the fact:

- **`compare` could not scroll.** `common.surface()` returns an `Adw.ToolbarView`
  and `build()` put its view straight into the content slot, so the panel's bottom
  was unreachable at any window height. Three of the four panels without
  `common.scrolled` build their own `Gtk.ScrolledWindow`; this one had none. The
  test was written against `inventory`, which had the same defect.
- Both were pre-existing rather than introduced by today's status work - the sweep
  ran against the commit *before* the status slot existed.

**The rule that follows: read a chunked result's chunk count before believing its
tally.** Six finished and a seventh pending is a 15-failure answer that is really
a 25-failure one, and there is no way to tell from the number itself.



## The corpus carried arguments all along, and a scan for the wrong spelling hid them (2026-12)

A `tools/` builder concluded **no corpus case carries arguments** and the whole
model work was re-planned around it: 渡劫 was recorded as blocked because
`ascension_gate` scores right tool *and* right arguments and nothing carried any.
The key is **`args`**, not `arguments`. Measured: **111 of the 220 cases carry
arguments**, over 98 distinct tools, and `task_eval.py:91` reads that key — so
the gate was gradable the entire time and the reason given for not starting was
false. Three places repeated the wrong scan: the builder, its own limit
sentence, and `cultivation.py`.

It is the `price`/`collapse` failure in its purest form — **a scan looks for a
plausible spelling of a word, finds nothing, and the nothing reads as a fact
about the tree.** The tell is that it *agreed* with the conclusion it was
already standing on.

**What it does bound is now measured rather than assumed.** 109 of the 220
declare no arguments, and through the real scorer a model that calls the right
tool with an **empty argument dict** scores as fully correct on all 109 — not a
scoring defect, but it means `Measurement.right` cannot separate an improvement
on the 111 from a vacuous pass on the 109. The gate's headroom is **111 of 220,
not 220**.

**And 渡劫's cost is measured: 15.5 hours per epoch.** torch 2.14.1+cpu, peft
0.21.2, transformers 5.19.0, accelerate 1.15.0 in `cache/cultivate-libs`
(gitignored, none packaged); Qwen3-1.7B safetensors at `cache/models/`.
`tools/lora_timing.py` times a real rank-8 LoRA on `q/k/v/o_proj`: **31.8 s per
optimiser step**, 512 tokens, 8 examples/step, 4 threads, **15.9 GB peak RSS**
(*ru_maxrss* from the kernel, never estimated from parameter counts). One epoch
over the 165 training rows is **15.5 hours**, and that is the optimiser alone,
no evaluation and no checkpointing — a floor. **The conclusion is not "start
it":** on a machine of this class the path is viable and unattended, and the
objection is that one epoch buys a number whose grading population is half
vacuous. The recipe is fixed in the tool with its sources — rank 8, **one
epoch** (arXiv:2506.14126 measures long expert fine-tuning *degrading* a merge;
2508.16082 measures a one-epoch task vector as the negative gradient scaled by
lr), `q/k/v/o_proj`, a seq-cls head not label generation (+2.2–3.3 at 0.6B/1.7B,
arXiv:2607.03801).

### The corpus builder drifted with the machine's own tool-call log

`ranked()` reads `learned_weights()` → `weights_from_tracker(_tracker())` when
its `learned` argument is left at `None`, so the corpus was a function of
**whoever ran the builder and what they had asked for since**. Two builds of one
commit, minutes apart, no edit between them: **212 and 211** positives inside
the offered set. Fixed with an explicit `learned={}` — the point at which "no
learned weights" is said out loud.

### 192 of 204 tools appear exactly once, so a *selector* cannot be trained here

The first framing was a selection corpus and the data retired it: holding out a
request also holds out its tool, so a classifier trained on the rest never sees
a description it has one example of. **Ranking transfers** — every tool is
natural language — and it is what the measurements demand: offered-set recall is
94.5% and the misses sit at rank 8–41, retrieved then crowded out.
`tools/build_reranker_corpus.py`: 220 requests → 1662 pairs, negatives from
`ranked()`'s own top slice because those are the confusers that crowd the answer
out. **Uniform negatives build a corpus the model passes trivially**, and pass
every structural check while training nothing.

### The test-design finding worth more than either

The first test file read the shipped `reranker_corpus.json`, so **five of seven
mutations of the *builder* came back survivors** — a broken builder still leaves
the last good artefact for a test that reads it. Fixtures now build fresh; the
one test that reads the file is `test_the_shipped_file_matches_a_fresh_build`,
which is where "the artefact is stale" belongs.

Two mutations of that set were worth the run on their own: **the truncation
mutation is an equivalent mutant** because `NEGATIVES=12` against
`DEFAULT_LIMIT=8` means truncation never fires, and **the limit check survived
because it asserted `"111" in limit` while the limit names 111 twice.** Both are
the "a check that cannot fail" trap, and neither was visible until a mutation
was aimed at it. 8 mutations, 7 caught, 0 survivors, 1 equivalent.

### Same as above: `tool_select` had dropped tools it ranked first, and said nothing

`log ?in` matched **"login"**, so `wants_a_browser` fired on an ordinary
question, `browse` was protected at **874 of a 1536-token budget**, and
`fingerprint_status` was dropped *despite ranking first*. The conversation path
overrode a first-place match on all 3 turns that took it, and **all 3 were
misses**. Offered-set recall **92.7% → 94.5%** (204/220 → 208/220), 18 tests, 2
mutants caught. Both fixed and pushed (`b134a15`).

### And the budget-aware protection was tried twice and reverted twice

Making `browse`'s protection conditional on it not starving the answer broke the
case the protection exists for — "book the cheapest flight on blazedemo.com" lost
`browse`, the exact failure the module records as measured, and the table went
*down* to 94.1%. **Not shipped.** Score cannot decide it: `browse` ranks *below*
`web_search` in both the case that should be protected and the case that should
not (2.89 vs 21.16). The real discriminator is what the displacement already
removed, and answering it needs to know what the person is asking to *do* —
which is the intent layer the research points at, not another heuristic.

## The deep scan, and the fix it refused

**`Verdict` never reaches the screen.** `verification.Verdict` has four states -
`VERIFIED`, `FAILED`, `UNVERIFIED`, `IMPOSSIBLE` - and the class docstring argues
in detail why each matters. Nothing in `gui/` reads it. And the assistant decides
the card's `ok` by string prefix:

```python
ok = not str(result).lstrip().lower().startswith(("error", "refused"))
```

so a refusal whose wording does not begin with *error* or *refused* reaches the
transcript as a success. That is precisely what `DispatchResult`'s own docstring
warns about: "a refusal starts to look indistinguishable from a success that
nobody checked".

**The fix already exists.** `execute_tool_outcome` returns the verdict as data,
its docstring is written against exactly this failure, and `brain.py` and
`gateway.py` both use it. The assistant was the one caller that had not been
moved.

### It could not be fixed here, and the reason is worth more than the fix

Two attempts, both stopped by the same thing:

- **calling `execute_tool_outcome` alongside `execute_tool` runs the skill
  twice** - a write performed twice because the caller wanted to know whether
  it worked;
- **replacing one with the other moves the seam**, and **58 test files patch
  `execute_tool`** to intercept a turn's tool calls
  (`monkeypatch.setattr(A, "execute_tool", lambda *a, **k: big)`). Moving the
  seam bypassed every one of them: they ran the real skill instead of their
  fixture, and a turn that used to write a stub wrote a real file. One test
  failed loudly; the rest passed while doing something other than what they
  claimed.

That is a worse outcome than the string guess, so the seam stays where the tests
are. What survives is `_tool_ok()`, a named function with the markers read from
one place, the limitation stated, and the reason recorded - rather than an
unexplained expression in the middle of the tool loop where the next person to
touch it has no way to know why it is still a prefix.

**The real fix is a migration, not an edit:** move the 58 patch sites, then move
the seam. That is a change with its own review and its own test run, and it is
not something to slip into a session that also moved three modes onto a strip.

### What else the scan found

- **`model_seconds` was computed and never shown.** Now the footer says
  *"1.2s of it the model"* when the turn took two seconds or more - separating
  thinking time from tool time, which on a local model is the question you ask
  before choosing a smaller tier.
- **No dead GUI code.** Every public method in `gui/` is called by product,
  test or tool - 0 orphans across 1114 files.
- **`budget_seconds` is computed and read nowhere, deliberately left so:** it
  only feeds the over-budget check and showing it would add a denominator
  nobody asked for.

## The model picker row, and three defects that only rendering showed (2026-10-13)

`gui/model_picker.py` was written, and `rows_for()` was verified — **all six
tiers render, the subtitles are right**. The *widget* had never been built.
Writing `tests/test_model_picker.py` found three things, and each of them is a
class this file has already recorded under a different name.

### 1. Three methods were on the wrong class, and the window could not be built

`_model_row`, `_model_word` and `_refresh_model_word` were written inside
`_ModeStrip`. `_model_row()` is called from **`ChronoaWindow.__init__`**
(`window.py:1925`), which does not inherit from `_ModeStrip` — so
`ChronoaWindow._model_row()` was an **`AttributeError` on every window
construction**. pyflakes cannot see it: `self.foo()` inside a method of class A
is a name, not an attribute the compiler resolves.

Found by **building the row and asking for its label**, which is the only thing
that reaches the lookup. The three methods moved to `ChronoaWindow`;
`_model_chip` and `_model_rows` stayed on the strip, where they are used.

### 2. `rebuild()` called a `Gtk.Box` method on a `Gtk.Popover` — shipped

```python
while self.get_child() is not None:
    self.remove(self.get_child())      # AttributeError
```

**`Gtk.Popover` holds one child through a setter and is not a `Gtk.Box`.**
Measured: `hasattr(Gtk.Popover, "remove")` is **False**,
`hasattr(Gtk.Box, "remove")` is True.

It shipped because **`rebuild()` is called from `__init__`, where the child is
still `None`** — so the loop body never ran and construction succeeded. Every
rebuild *after* that raised. And what the method exists for, in its own
docstring, is *"a picker that kept stale rows would say 'answering now' next to
a model that stopped"* — a model downloaded while the window was open. **The
one thing it exists for was the one thing that did not work**, and no shipped
caller calls it, so nothing surfaced it.

`set_child(None)`. The second mutation in the set **restores the shipped line
and fails two tests**, which is the strongest kind there is: not hypothetical.

### 3. The redraw looked for a method on the wrong object, behind a guard

`application._refresh_strip` did `getattr(window, "_refresh_model_word", None)`
— on the **window**, while the method was defined on the **strip**. `getattr`
returned `None`, `callable()` said no, and **the refresh silently did nothing**:
the row kept naming the previous model after a switch. The `callable()` guard
is what made it invisible — *a refresh that does nothing looks exactly like a
refresh with nothing to do*.

The two widgets being separate is real (`_model_row()` appends into the
window's `main_box`, not the strip), so the lookup stays; what was wrong was
which object asked, and the method now lives where the caller looks.

### 4. Two widgets, two tables, two words for one state

The chip read `SPECS` and walked `installed()`; the row read `TIERS`. Rendered
across four machine states:

| machine | chip said | row said |
|---|---|---|
| nothing installed, nothing answering | `No model` | **`the default model`** |
| 1.7B installed and answering | `1.7B` | `1.7B` |
| 8B installed, nothing chosen | `8B` | `8B` |
| **a model nothing describes is active** | **`No model`** | **`ghost-gguf`** |

Two labels for the *absence* of a choice, one of which implies a choice was
made; and "No model" beside a model that is loaded. **The row now asks the
strip's own `_model_rows()`** — the table the chip is drawn from, so the
question cannot be answered twice — and `_model_rows()` names the active key
when nothing else describes it. **All four states agree**, and
`test_the_row_and_the_chip_always_name_the_same_model` is parametrized over all
four so it cannot go quiet.

### 5. `chip_for()` was dead, with a docstring claiming otherwise

It built *a second model button* — bare, no label, different from the row's —
and had **zero callers**. Its docstring said *"Called on every refresh, from the
same place the menu was built"*. Deleted rather than wired: the strip's control
is answered by `_model_chip`, and a dead button whose docstring describes a
caller reads as coverage. **This is the `code_hl` shape** — a function written
and a caller claimed, measured at ninety seconds after the other session
finished wiring it.

### Three of my own test bugs, and the one that matters most

The file's own header records the general finding — *test data chosen without
checking it could distinguish the behaviour from its opposite* — and this file
was no better:

- **The `TIERS` fixture omitted the `" - "` separator** the real labels carry
  (`"Small (0.6 GB) - quick on any computer, for simple requests"`). So
  `rows_for`'s split had nothing to split and my assertion that the title is
  `"Small"` failed against correct code. **The fixture was shaped unlike the
  real data.**
- **The `_choose` test used `ModelPicker.__new__`.** `popdown` is a `Gtk.Popover`
  vfunc, and a Python attribute on an *uninitialised* GObject does not shadow
  it — the call reached the real method and raised *"object is not
  initialized"*. A fixture shaped like the call rather than like the thing
  being called, which is the rule this file states about `meeting.notes`' fake.
- **The "unreadable list" assertion only checked a widget existed.** A
  `Gtk.Label` with an empty string satisfies it. It asserts the *words* now.

**And one assertion of mine was simply wrong**: I claimed the title should be
`"Small"` and the size should go. The size stays — the *sentence* is what will
not fit in a 260px popover, and the size is what a person needs before choosing
something they are about to load. The module was right.

### 6 mutations, 6 caught, 0 survivors

| mutation | |
|---|---|
| `set_child(None)` → `remove()` (**the shipped bug**) | **2 failed** |
| the pick hands over an empty key | 1 failed |
| an absent model says "ready" | 1 failed |
| the answering model does not say "answering now" | 1 failed |
| the row stops reading the strip's table | **3 failed** |
| the row ignores an active key the rows cannot describe | 1 failed |

Run against a **copy** at `/tmp/opencode/snap-mp`, never the shared tree —
the other session was committing throughout and a mutation run that rewrites
product source is a mutation run that ships somebody else's defect.

### And the one fix that could not be made, restated for the next person

The assistant's `ok` is still a string-prefix guess while the dispatcher
computes the real four-state verdict one line earlier. **`execute_tool_outcome`
is the fix and 58 test files patch `execute_tool`** — moving the seam bypasses
all of them, and a turn that wrote a stub wrote a real file instead. That is a
migration with its own review, not an edit, and it is why `_tool_ok()` exists
as a named function carrying the limitation rather than as an unexplained
expression in the middle of the tool loop.

## The permission-posture chip is 3-red at HEAD, and the in-flight rework orphans its test (2026-10-13)

Running `tests/test_permission_posture_chip.py` against a clean `git archive HEAD`
snapshot (not the dirty tree) gives **3 failed, 13 passed**; against the working
tree it is **14 failed**. The eleven extra are the other session's in-flight
`gui/window.py` rewrite, which deletes `_permission_chip`, `_read_permission` and
`_PERMISSION` from `_ModeStrip` outright. But the **three that are red at HEAD**
are a committed defect, not a consequence of that rewrite, and all three are
defects in the chip itself:

- `test_the_posture_offers_exactly_the_three_modes_that_exist` - `_PERMISSION` has
  two rows (`default`, `dont_ask`) but `permissions.Mode` has three; `explore` is
  not offered. So a user on the strip cannot select `explore` at all.
- `test_the_chip_follows_the_posture_settings_changes` - `_read_permission()`
  returns `default` where the test expects it to follow a live `explore`.
- `test_the_tooltip_says_the_posture_does_not_survive_a_restart` - the tooltip
  never says the posture does not persist across restarts.

**The in-flight rework addresses all three** - it replaces the static `_PERMISSION`
table with a menu built from the live permission layer (`app.answer-permission::`,
reading `permissions.get_mode()`), which is exactly what the three tests are
asking for. So the rework is not gratuitous; it is fixing real committed bugs.

**The handoff that matters: committing that rewrite will take this file from
3-red to 14-red**, because the whole test targets the retired `_ModeStrip` chip
attributes. Whoever commits the rewrite should either port the test to the new
menu or `git rm tests/test_permission_posture_chip.py` if the chip is genuinely
gone - not leave it as 14 orphans. I did not edit any of this: `gui/window.py` is
the other session's in-flight file, and the correct fix for the three HEAD-red
failures is the rewrite already under way, not a patch on top of it.

**The transferable lesson: a suite's result depends on the tree it ran against,
so "is it red?" needs the tree named.** The dirty-tree figure (14) and the HEAD
figure (3) pointed at two different problems, and only the snapshot separated
"red because of uncommitted work in flight" from "red because of something
already committed." When a failing count is much worse than expected, running
the same test against `git archive HEAD` is the cheapest way to tell which of
those you are looking at.

## A sweep for "written on one class, called on another" — and it found a second live crash

The picker defect above is a *class* of defect, and pyflakes cannot see any of
it: `self.foo()` inside a method is a name, and which class owns it is a
question of inheritance, not of syntax. So `tools/member_sweep.py` asks it for
every class in the package.

**Result on this tree: 0**, with 2 classes it could not ask about and says so.
**The control is the only reason that is readable** —
`tests/test_member_sweep.py` moves `_model_row` back onto `_ModeStrip` and
requires the sweep to print that name. A checker that has stopped looking prints
exactly what a working one prints when there is nothing to find.

### It found a second crash on its first run, and it was live

`gui/surfaces/artifact_store.py`'s **Clear** button:

```python
def _find_search_entry(self):
    for child in self.get_children():        # Gtk.Box has no get_children
```

Measured by pressing the real button on a real view:

```
view built: _ArtifactStoreView
Clear pressed RAISED: AttributeError: '_ArtifactStoreView' object has no
                      attribute 'get_children'
```

**Clear has raised on every press since it was wired**, and this is the same
GTK3-`get_children` defect this file already records twice — so the record of
the *class* was right and the gate that was supposed to hold it was a grep, not
an AST pass.

The fix is not a GTK4 iteration. `__init__` builds the entry, connects it, and
**then `_find_search_entry` walks the tree looking for it by its placeholder
text** — a second way to answer a question the class already knew the answer
to. It holds the reference now, which is exact and O(1).

### The tree-wide gate is "guarded", not "absent" — and the grep version was wrong twice

The first version grepped for `get_children(` and reported **five** sites. Four
were **comments explaining this very fix**. That is *a scanner whose needle is
in its own input*, met for the fourth time in as many passes, and the fifth was
`activity.py`, which is **correct**: it guards the call with
`hasattr(self._summary, "get_children")`, because `build_summary` returns either
a plain `Gtk.Box` or a `common.group` and only one has the method.

So the invariant is **every `get_children()` call is guarded by an `hasattr` on
the same receiver** — not that the call is absent. Requiring absence would have
failed correct code and been "fixed" by deleting the working guard, which is the
over-fix this file records for `connect`/`emit`. A **planted** call in a scratch
tree is required to be found, so the zero means something.

### Four bugs in the sweep itself, and every one reported a real name for the wrong reason

None of these is exotic; all four are the same trap in new clothes.

| the bug | what it reported |
|---|---|
| `self.x.y(...)` counted as a call on self | `startswith` as a member `ChronoaWindow` must define |
| a `@staticmethod`'s first parameter read as `self` | `text.startswith` on `ChronoaWindow` |
| an attribute *read* counted as a call | `mac` as a method `BluezWatch` must define |
| **only bare-name bases collected** | `Adw.ApplicationWindow` and `Gtk.Window` **dropped entirely** — so two windows reported their own base class's methods as missing |

The fourth is the instructive one: it made the sweep cry wolf about
`set_content`, `add_breakpoint`, `present` and `connect`, and the obvious
response — to believe it — would have been to add methods the classes already
inherit. **A checker that reports a base class's own methods as missing has
stopped resolving the base**, and that is the signal to check the resolver.

### And the base is resolved by asking, not by a list

Every remaining name is asked of the installed library with `hasattr` over the
real `__mro__`, so there is no hand-kept allowlist — which is what this file
keeps getting wrong (`wpctl` three times, the finite check four times,
`_SYNONYMS`, `capabilities._GROUPS`). Two rules that cost a round each:

- **`Adw.ApplicationWindow` must be looked up in `Adw`.** Searching the
  namespaces in dictionary order returned **`Gtk.ApplicationWindow`** — a class
  of the same name, with fewer members — and reported `set_content` and
  `add_breakpoint` as missing from a class that has both.
- **A base it cannot resolve is a third thing, not a finding.** Two classes
  inherit `BaseHTTPRequestHandler`, which is stdlib. Reported as findings that
  is crying wolf about names nobody checked; dropped silently it is an absence
  read as a pass. They are printed as **"could not ask"** and counted in neither
  column.

### My own mutation runner wrote to the shared tree, and reported three survivors because of it

The first run of the check on the new gates reported **3 mutations, 0 caught**.
That is the shape of a result that should make you check the harness before the
code. The runner built its path from a **relative** `usr/lib/...`, so every
mutation was written to the **real repository** while pytest ran against the
snapshot — the snapshot never changed, so nothing could fail, and the tree was
mutated three times plus once more in a probe.

**The `finally` restored every file and `git diff` shows exactly the intended
change** — verified rather than assumed, and the whole point of `finally` plus a
journal. But a harness that mutates the shared tree is the exact thing this
workspace forbids, and it was doing it silently while reporting a clean result.

**A "survivor" is the one measurement whose cause is usually the harness.**
Re-run one by hand in the directory the test claims to be in before believing
it: the same mutation, applied there, failed immediately. Paths, not coverage.

**3 mutations, 3 caught** once the path was absolute.

## A test file written and never run, and the harness that made it look run (2026-10-13)

`tests/test_plan_mode_asks.py` had **13 tests, and every one of them hung for
180 seconds.** The whole file timed out.

```python
def presenter(question, options):
    event = threading.Event()
    event.chronoa_answer = reply          # the answer, on an event
    return event
```

`ask_bridge.ask` does `done.wait(timeout)` and *then* reads `chronoa_answer`
off it - so an event that is never **`set()`** is not an answer, it is a
three-minute wait. `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` is **180**, not the 120 the rest of
this file says, and every test in the file asks exactly one question.

`event.set()`. **13 passed in 0.15 s.**

**The file counted as covered everywhere that counts files.** It was in the
session's "new, mostly unexecuted" list; it was committed; it was pyflakes-clean;
and it was in a batch that *appeared* to run. **A test file that times out tells
you nothing about the thing it was written for**, and every listing that counts
files rather than results reports it identically to one that passes.

**And the batch it was hiding in timed out at the same place**, which is what
finally surfaced it: a 900 s run stopped at test 114 of the batch with one `F`
and no summary. `exit=124` is not a flaky result, it is a hang, and the only
evidence is that the number is there — the same distinction this file draws for
`MutationDidNotParse`.

**3 mutations, 3 caught**, and the fourth is **equivalent by construction**:
removing `ask_to_proceed`'s `if not ask_bridge.has_presenter()` guard leaves all
13 green, because `ask()` returns `""` with no presenter and `""` is not
`"Do it now"` - so the call falls through to the same refusal and the same
record. The guard is kept as the readable statement of a rule the layer below
also happens to enforce, and the file says so rather than growing a test that
passes either way.

## Two false verdicts in one afternoon, and both were concurrency (2026-10-13)

### Five D-Bus timeouts that were my own backgrounded run

`test_model_selector_chip.py` reported **5 failed** — every test in the file —
with `g-io-error-quark: Timeout was reached (24)` and a runtime of **125
seconds**.

It is **5 passed in 0.68 s**. The cause was a pytest run I had backgrounded
earlier and never collected, still alive and holding `dev.shani.chronoa`; the
file builds a real `Gtk.Application`, so its activation was forwarded to the
stale owner and never ran locally. **25-second waits, five of them.**

This is the recorded mechanism - `test_setup_button_is_reachable` documents it
with *"measured with three concurrent suites live"* - and it is the **fourth**
time this session that concurrency was the answer, after `GSETTINGS_BACKEND`,
`fake_bin`'s `PATH` and `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`. **The 125 s against 0.68 s is the
tell**: a test that takes two minutes when it takes one is waiting on something,
not computing something.

**Both of my own PIDs, killed by number** (102112, then its child 102118 — `kill`
on the parent left the pytest running, because it was the *shell* that was
signalled). The user's `shani-chronoa-overlay` (77892) was left alone, which is
the only reason it is still running.

### And a snapshot that was not a faithful copy

The other files were run in `/tmp/opencode/snap-ms` while the real tree was
locked by the other session's mutation run — the sanctioned approach. One file
failed there and passed in the real tree:

> `the default is qwen3-1.7b but only [''] is installed`

**`cache/` is gitignored, so the snapshot never had it** - and `local_llm`
reads the model directory to answer "what is installed". A test that asks what
is on this machine cannot be run against a tree where the answer is *nothing*,
and a snapshot is not a machine.

**A snapshot is a faithful copy of the files you copied, and only of those.**
For anything that reads accumulated state - installed models, a tool log, a
ledger - the copy answers a different question from the original, and the
difference reads exactly like a defect. The batch is green in the real tree:
**130 passed, 0 failed, 16.65 s**, including the startup probe.

## Four renderer defects, and a poisoned display pool I created myself (2026-10-13)

`512d4f2` consolidated four render scripts into one renderer and one driver.
**Three of the four defects below shipped in that commit and were found only by
running it**, which is this file's own rule stated the hard way.

### 1. `recycle_display` read `$num` before assigning it, and killed the sweep

```bash
recycle_display() {
    local old_pid="$START_DISPLAY" num
    ...
    sock="/run/user/$(id -u)/broadway$((num + 1)).socket"   # <-- num unbound here
    num="$(pick_display)" || return 1
```

Under `set -u` an unbound variable is **fatal**, not a warning - so the first
render that failed and reached its retry took the whole sweep down with it.
Measured: **23 of 34 panels, then nothing, and no summary printed**, because the
summary is the last thing the script does.

### 2. The stale-socket reclaim was self-defeating, and it poisoned four displays

The reclaim removed a `broadway*.socket` file it believed nobody was listening
