on. **But `ss -xl` lists a unix socket by its filesystem path**, so a live daemon
whose socket file had been unlinked is *invisible* to the check that decides
whether to unlink it. So one reclaim turned a working display into a
**permanently unusable** number: no socket left to detect, port still bound,
every future start refused with `Address already in use`.

Four numbers (`:94 :96 :109 :112`) were poisoned this way, and the result was
that a sweep with **six genuinely free numbers** in `:90-:120` printed
`no free broadway display in :90-:120` - naming a resource shortage that was
four dead files and a self-inflicted wound.

**The fix is to ask the daemon rather than predict.** Whether a number is free
is decided by `start_display` waiting for its socket, with the next number tried
on failure. The reclaim is now gated on the **port** being free as well as the
socket being present, and `BROADWAY_PORT_BASE=8080` is *measured*: `:116 -> 8196`
and `:118 -> 8198` started by hand, matching `:94 -> 8174`, `:96 -> 8176`,
`:109 -> 8189`, `:112 -> 8192`.

Proved by a planted control - a live daemon on `:90` with its socket unlinked:
the sweep skipped `:90` and took `:91`, and did **not** recreate the socket.

### 3. `py_compile` and pyflakes both pass on a `UnboundLocalError`

Narrowing the capture size for a window that chose its own size assigned
`WIDTH` inside `on_activate`. Python makes a name local for the **whole**
function the moment it is assigned anywhere in it, so every earlier read became
a read of an unassigned local and the first target raised
`UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'WIDTH'`. One `global` fixes it.

It is a **scoping** fact, not a syntax or name error, so nothing static sees it -
the same shape as the `async def` handlers this file records as having compiled
clean and never been awaited. It cost the sweep the panel I was fixing.

### And the one that was the harness's fault, not the product's

Quick Ask declares `set_default_size(460, -1)` and is a popup over somebody's
work. Forcing 1280x900 on it produced a full screen with ~730px of nothing under
it, which reads as a layout defect. **A window that sized itself now keeps its
own size**: `quick-ask` went **25,730 -> 19,047 bytes** and the artifact is
what it is in the app.

## Two product defects the render showed, both in files clean at HEAD

### `compare`: every row was a focus stop, and the first one painted a selection

`"Pick two conversations to compare."` came back **inside an orange box**. It was
not a stray style: `_row()` called `set_selectable(True)` unconditionally, and a
selectable GTK4 label is a focus stop that paints its own accent highlight once
it holds focus. `_group` built its heading, its empty `None` and its
`and 12 more` count through the same helper, so **every heading in the panel was
a Tab stop** - this file's own Diff-panel finding (content reachable by pointer
only) is the same trade the other way round.

Selectable is now opt-in and only the questions ask for it: a heading, a count
and an instruction have nothing to copy.

Two more in the same panel:

- **The sentence ended mid-clause in the source** - *"ask something twice and it
  will"* - not a wrapping problem, the string simply stopped there. It now
  completes and wraps.
- **The empty store was `STATUS_ATTENTION`** while the comment immediately below
  it said *"An empty store that was read is an answer, not a fault. Amber is for
  a panel that could not find out; this one could."* The reasoning had been
  applied to the block two lines further on. Red **"Needs attention"** for a
  machine working perfectly now reads **green "Ready"**.

### `voice`: provenance in the body text instead of the tooltip

The "Pitch, tempo and rate" row ended with a literal
`PiperTTS.timbre_description(), PiperTTS.timbre_effects(), PiperTTS.timbre_problem()`.

**The whole panel is against that**: `_row(title, detail, tooltip)` is built with
`f"...\nRead from {engine.source}"`, so every claim names the code that produced
it *in the tooltip*. This one row spliced it into the detail - and the caller
passed the detail as its own tooltip, which is why it was on screen twice and
useful in neither. `_timbre_row` now returns the provenance separately and the
caller builds the tooltip like every other row.

**Naming the code that produced a claim is the good habit here and it is kept.**
It was in the wrong place.

## Two class names with nothing behind them, and a provenance string in the wrong place (2026-10-13)

Both found by rendering, not by reading. Both are the "the code says it does
something and the screen says otherwise" shape.

### `machine-reading-table` was added by the panel and styled nowhere

`gui/surfaces/machine.py` builds a sense's reading through
`common.key_values()` - a two-column table, on purpose, because the module's own
docstring says a reading handed to a label is *"six wrapped lines of the same
weight, and the number anyone came for has to be found by reading"*. It then does
`table.add_css_class("machine-reading-table")`.

**That class name appeared nowhere else in the package.** `machine-reading` -
`ROW_CSS`, the marker a test walks to find every sense row - was the same. So
the table was built correctly and then rendered with **no container at all**,
which is why AGENTS.md had carried *"Not changed, noted: Machine's readings are
monospace blocks outside the row cards"* for a while. The reason was two class
names with no rule behind them, not a layout that could not be fixed.

The fix is an inset: a left margin ties the reading to the row above it and a
background separates data from page. The monospace is kept deliberately - these
are aligned columns read off sysfs, and the alignment is the point.

**Measured on the reading itself rather than on the picture**, because the first
probe printed a `Percept`'s `repr()` instead of its `content` and reported "1
line, 1 with a colon", which would have said `key_values` had nothing to lay
out. The content is `key: value` / indented throughout, which is exactly the
shape that helper documents it handles - so the table was right and only its
container was missing.

### `voice`: naming the code that produced a claim, in the wrong place

The "Pitch, tempo and rate" row ended with a literal
`PiperTTS.timbre_description(), PiperTTS.timbre_effects(), PiperTTS.timbre_problem()`
**in its body text**.

**The whole panel is against that.** `_row(title, detail, tooltip)` is called
with `f"...\nRead from {engine.source}"`, so every claim on the page names the
code that produced it *in the tooltip*. This one row spliced it into the detail
instead - and the caller passed the detail as its own tooltip, which is why the
string appeared twice and was useful in neither.

`_timbre_row` now returns the provenance as a third element and the caller
builds the tooltip the way the engine, speech-in and model-file rows all do.

**The habit is kept, because the habit is good.** "Name the code that produced
this" is why this page can be audited at all - `source` is a field on every
`_Engine`, and the Kokoro and Piper rows carry `kokoro-tts-enabled` and
`PiperTTS.voice_path` for the same reason. It was in the wrong place, not wrong.

## `page:` targets were rendering a window that had not finished looking like itself (2026-10-13)

The first sweep of the 29 registry-declared pages reported **8 PASS, 2 FAIL** and
every main-window page among them looked wrong in a way that had no name.

**Measured, by decoding the alpha channel rather than by looking at the picture:**
`page:main:conversation` was **96.2% fully transparent with 0.2% opaque**;
`main:panels` and `main:listening` were ~99% *partially* transparent. A
third-party viewer composites transparent PNG onto white, so `main:conversation`
**displayed as a blank page** - which is how this was found, by expecting a
conversation and getting white.

The sharpest evidence is a hash. `page:main:conversation` and
`page:main:conversations` came back **byte-identical, 24,888 bytes each, sha
`1e124f5db6d6`**. Two different pages, one photograph, both counted as passes,
because **a valid PNG is written whatever was on it**. A short capture that still
writes a file is worse than `NO NODE`, because it looks like a render.

**Cause, and it is a settle problem rather than a rendering one:** the `page:`
branch settled at **1800ms**. The main window seeds every panel's health dot on
idle after it maps - twenty-odd `systemctl`/`busctl`/`gsettings` probes, about two
seconds. `page:settings:*` came back **100% opaque from the same code** because
`SettingsWindow` does not seed panels. That asymmetry is what identified the
window's own startup cost as the thing being missed.

Raised to **3500ms**, matching what `panel:` had already been raised to for the
same reason. After the fix:

| page | before | after | alpha after |
|---|---|---|---|
| `main:conversation` | 24,888 B, 0.2% opaque | **151,142 B** | **100% opaque** |
| `main:conversations` | 24,888 B, 0.2% opaque | **150,071 B** | **100% opaque** |
| `main:listening` | 30,636 B | **147,821 B** | **100% opaque** |
| `settings:system` | **FAIL**, no file | **50,322 B** | **100% opaque** |

and the two main pages now hash **differently** (`365c4ff4a79e` vs
`58bb873cf347`), so they are two pictures again instead of one filed twice.

**A capture that photographs less than the target is a false pass**, and the
sweep's PASS column cannot see it: it is written by "a file appeared". Any future
renderer here that can settle early should be judged on **alpha coverage and
sha-distinctness across pages**, not on bytes on disk.

### Two harness bugs found on the way, one of them the *same* bug twice

- **"No free broadway display in :90-:120" on an empty pool.** `kill` is
  asynchronous: the socket file goes at once but the listening socket does not, so
  `recycle_display` reached the number it had just released, saw its port still
  held, skipped it, and repeated across neighbouring numbers while the kernel
  finished tearing down. Measured on a pool with **0 daemons, 0 ports held and
  three fresh `:90`/`:91`/`:92` starts working** - the shape of a race, not a
  shortage. `recycle_display` now waits for the port to clear first, and a number
  that will not come up costs **4s instead of 10s** so one slow number cannot eat
  a sweep that has 31 to choose from.
- **`[[ -n $VERBOSE ]]` under `set -uo pipefail`**, added while making failures
  quiet, is a **fatal unbound variable**, and this script dies on an unset name
  rather than on a false one. It is the **same defect as the `$num`-read-before-
  assignment bug this file already documents**, written a second time eight
  commits later. Caught before it ran a sweep by `bash -c 'set -u; [[ -n $VERBOSE ]]'`;
  `VERBOSE` is now declared under the `set` line and read as `${VERBOSE:-}`.
  **Both times this was found by executing, and `bash -n` passed on the broken
  version both times.**

### `page:main:quick-ask` fails in the harness and works in the product

`ChronoaWindow.show_page("quick-ask")` is implemented - it looks up and activates
`app.quick-ask` - and `ChronoaApplication` registers that action
(`app/application.py:1286`). It returns `False` in the renderer only because the
render builds a bare `Gtk.Application` that never registers it. **A FAIL here is
the harness's, not the page's**, and the renderer already has a working `quick-ask`
target that builds the real window.

## The chunk runner believed a log written against a tree that no longer existed (2026-10-13)

Ran the full suite in 10 chunks to check this session's core changes against
everything. The runner reported eight chunks **"already done"** - and every one
of those logs was from **01:00-01:09**, against a tree whose last commit was
**02:54**. So it reported a green tally for a suite that had not run since the
strip redesign, the plan-mode change and three commits' worth of everything else.

The condition was `[ -s "$log" ] && grep -qE 'passed|failed|error' "$log"` -
**existence and nothing else**. This is the stale-label failure this file records
as worse than a missing label, with the label attached to a *measurement*: a chunk
skipped on the strength of a log from a different tree reads as a chunk that
passed. Fixed to compare each log against the newest source file, and the STALE
line **names the file** so a reader can tell a harness artefact from a real
regression without opening the tree.

**A second defect behind it, found by the test I wrote for the first.** The
check asked `find ... -newer "$LOGS"`, and `$LOGS` is a **directory** - so two
logs of very different ages were judged by whichever was written last, and a
directory touched after the last code change made every log look current however
old it was. **The defect the check exists to remove, reproduced inside the fix.**
`-nt` asks the question actually being asked, one log at a time. And the same
confusion was in the test: it compared against `tmp_path.stat()`, the temp
*directory's* mtime, which is now - so it demanded a source file be newer than
the current moment and failed while the runner named files correctly.
**Comparing a log against its own directory is not a staleness check, and it is
easy to write by accident in both the gate and its witness.**

Also fixed: `CHUNKS=2` after `CHUNKS=8` iterated **four** manifests, because
`split` overwrites `chunk_aa` and leaves a previous run's higher-numbered
manifests behind. **A chunking parameter that does not change the chunks is a
parameter that lies.** `DRY_RUN=1` prints the decision and launches nothing - a
test that starts eight parallel pytest shards manufactures exactly the D-Bus
contention this file spends whole entries diagnosing.

`tests/test_suite_chunks_are_not_stale.py` (7), both directions: a log newer
than the code is skipped, **the same log back-dated is re-run**.

### And what the sweep found once it was actually measuring the current tree

**51 failures in 10 chunks; re-run serially, 11 were parallel-shard flakes that
pass alone** and the rest were real. Two were mine, and both are the same shape:

**1. The strip said "Auto", and `DONT_ASK` *refuses*.** `_AUTO`'s row carried
the word **"Auto"** - while `permissions.Mode.DONT_ASK` refuses anything it
cannot ask about, and the tooltip two lines below said *"This is not permission
to act freely"*. **The word on the chip said the opposite of the mode it
selects.** AGENTS.md already recorded the decision this reversed: *"Auto on a
mode strip reads as it may act freely, which is the opposite of this mode."* It
regressed in `3fc562b` because `test_permission_posture_chip.py` **was already
red** - looking for `_ModeStrip._PERMISSION`, which the same commit renamed to
`_AUTO` - so nothing objected. **A test that was failing when the change was
made cannot catch the change**, which is why the word is now held by a file that
is green. It is **"No questions"**.

That file was red for most of its life (**7 failed / 9 passed** at `c9ea23e`)
and it **contradicted itself**: one test asserted the strip offered
`[DEFAULT, DONT_ASK, EXPLORE]` while another asserted `EXPLORE` was *not* on it.
Two tests, one file, opposite claims - which is how a red file hides a question
nobody has to answer. The measurement settles it: explore refuses **165** of 256
tools against plan's **130**, and **50** of them are ones plan mode allows. So
the honest name is **two**, asserted, with the third's exclusion witnessed by the
measurement rather than by a comment in a table.

**Its three original assertions were three counts**, and each counted the wrong
thing: `len(_PERMISSION) + 6` failed when the strip was redesigned to five chips;
counting the strip's tables found 8 against 5 and reported a missing chip when
the missing thing was that Ambient, hands-free and reply style are drawn by
`refresh()` and reached from the palette **by design**. The property is one line
and does not go stale: **the chip is a child of the strip.** Same class as this
file's `WINDOW_TOKENS` finding - a reservation its own default exceeds, and a
count that is a claim about the whole window.

**2. My plan-mode test asserted the premise I had already disproved.** It read
*"plan mode blocks exactly the gated tools"*, and that premise is wrong for the
tools that matter most: measured when written, plan mode blocked **92** and
allowed `write_text_file` and `apply_patch`, so entering plan mode did not stop
the model writing your files. The code had already moved to
`MUTATING_TOOLS`; the test still asserted the answer it rejected. It now asserts
**the union** - `MUTATING_TOOLS | gated_by`, less `TALKS_ONLY` - because the first
version of the fix asserted only the first half and named `airplane_mode`, a
tool that changes the machine and lives in the second set. **Asserting one half
drops the other, and the half dropped is the half that was already there.**

The old assertion is **kept as a control**: `test_the_two_answers_really_do_differ`
requires `write_text_file` and `apply_patch` to still be in `blocked - gated`,
because a change that made the two sets identical would restore the premise
quietly and the 38 tools where they differ are the whole reason the answer moved.

### Three smaller ones, each a stale count

- **The empty state grew a third row.** The shortcut hints were a sibling of the
  placeholder, and `test_empty_state_names_what_to_do` failed with *"unexpected
  row in the empty state"* - its invariant is the right one (the empty state is
  the placeholder and the suggestions, and a third sibling is indistinguishable
  from a stray row a cleared transcript grew). **The sentence went into the
  placeholder instead**: one widget fewer, and the invariant survives untouched.
- **The Help window's row count was 16 and the window had 21**, because the
  *"What you can do"* section landed after it. It reads both lengths off the
  module now - **a hand-kept count of a window's contents is a claim about the
  window**, and it goes stale the moment anything is added.
- **`planmode.refused_tools()` had exactly one caller: its own test.** It read
  the **live** refusal list, which is this turn's, while the plan card is handed
  a **stored** run whose steps may be from any earlier turn. Deleted; the collapse
  moved to `task_card._what_it_would_do`, which reads `run.steps`. Two answers to
  "what would this do" is one too many, and the card is holding the run.

**And the card now says it.** It read *"3 steps, nothing has been done"* - a
count is not a plan, and approving it means saying yes to three things nobody was
shown. It names the tools, with duplicates collapsed (a model that asks for the
same write five times has described one write) and the count kept as the number
of **steps**, so three writes still reads as three.

**7 mutations, 7 caught**, and **two of them found witnesses I did not have**:
widening `tools[:3]` to `tools` left the file green, because my test asserted
"and 4 more" appears - which a row printing all seven *and then* the count also
satisfies; the assertion has to be on what is **absent**. And removing the
`if not tools:` branch was green too, so it now has a witness driven through the
helper directly - because `plan_from_refusals` does `if not tool: continue` and
*refuses* to build a nameless step, which is exactly why the guard is there.
**A guard whose only producer makes it unreachable is still a guard**, and the
row would otherwise read `goal - : , nothing has been done`.

### What was not mine, and how that was established

Six files still fail after all of the above, and **every one belongs to another
session's committed work**: `8c92258` (`delete_file` -> trash, which is why the
registry is **256** and `test_schema_caps` still expects 257), `5d17297`
(`modelfmt`, the model-card line), `1db21c4` (`tool_select`, *"explain gravity"*
still offering tools), the other session's uncommitted `README.md`, and
`model_registry.verify_digest` - which `test_no_enforcement_control_is_unwired`
names, and whose digest is **never checked**, because hashing a multi-gigabyte
model on every scan is why nothing calls it. `refused_tools` was the only
enforcement-shaped orphan in the tree, and it was **mine**.

`cultivation.py` is modified and uncommitted, carrying another session's
ladder-balanced experiment result. **Not staged and not committed** - it is their
in-flight work.

## The poisoned-display bug, reintroduced three lines below its own explanation (2026-10-13)

`acquire_display`'s comment block explains, in detail, that deleting a
`broadway*.socket` that a **live** daemon still owns makes a display number
**permanently unusable** - invisible to the socket check, held by the port check,
skipped by every future sweep. It names four numbers it poisoned doing that
(`:94 :96 :109 :112`).

**Three lines further down, the same function did exactly that on every failed
start:**

```bash
if start_display "$n" >/dev/null 2>&1; then ... fi
[[ -n $START_DISPLAY ]] && kill "$START_DISPLAY" 2>/dev/null
START_DISPLAY=""
rm -f "$sock"          # <-- deletes the socket of a daemon that may simply be slow
```

`start_display` gives a daemon **4s**. On a loaded box that is not always enough,
and a daemon arriving at 4.1s had its socket unlinked *while it was alive* -
which is the precise mechanism the comment above had already diagnosed and
recorded a fix for.

**Measured, on the first sweep of the 17 `setup:*` pages** (the last surface class
in this audit that had never once been rendered):

```
PASS  page:setup:brain        30265 bytes
FAIL  page:setup:cloud-keys   no file written     no free broadway display in :90-:120
FAIL  page:setup:done         no file written     (same, and the same for all 15 after)
```

One page, then total pool exhaustion - and the pool was **0 daemons and 0 ports
held** the moment the sweep exited. So this was not a shortage at all; **one slow
start had cascaded into all 31 numbers**, because each attempt poisoned the next
number it tried. The 16 FAILs were a single defect wearing a resource warning.

**The fix is one condition, and it is the condition the port check already
implies.** The socket is removed only once the port is *genuinely* free; if the
port never frees, the file stays and the port check keeps that number out on its
own. A live daemon is a thing to wait for, not a file to delete. `recycle_display`
now shares the same `wait_port_free()` rather than carrying its own copy of the
loop, so the two paths cannot drift - which is how the failure path ended up
without the wait the recycle path had.

Verified on the four pages that had cascaded, which are the smallest honest test
of the claim: **4 rendered, 0 not** (`brain` 30,265 B, `cloud-keys` 129,834 B,
`ears` 44,057 B, `done` 25,932 B), against 1 rendered and 3 pool-exhausted before.

**The lesson is the one this file has recorded about itself four times, in a new
costume: a fix whose explanation outlives it is a hazard.** The comment was
correct, specific and attributed to measured failures - and it sat eleven lines
above code doing the thing it warned against. **A paragraph explaining why
something is dangerous is not a control**, and the only control here was `rm -f`
being on the failure path at all.

### And a sweep that reports "no free display" is reporting a *harness* fault

Sixteen pages that "do not render" is the sentence this audit would otherwise
have written down, and `AGENTS.md` already carries the standing warning about it
(*"a page that does not render is not necessarily a broken page"*). That warning
is right and it is also **not enough**: it says don't believe the FAIL, and the
right response to "don't believe the FAIL" is to find out why, not to file it.
The cause here was a defect in the thing that produced the FAIL.

## The third false pass: `cloud-keys` writes 129KB of nothing and the sweep calls it PASS (2026-10-13)

The 17 `setup:*` pages had **never once been rendered** in this repository's
history - "0 of 17" - so the first sweep of them is the first look at any of it.
Three of four render correctly on the first attempt (`brain` 100% opaque, `ears`
100%, `done` 100%, each a real page with its title bar, body, orb mark and
`Next:` button). **One does not.**

    page:setup:cloud-keys.png   129,834 bytes   alpha: 87.1% transparent, 7.2% opaque
    page:setup:brain.png         30,265 bytes   alpha: 100% opaque
    page:setup:ears.png          44,057 bytes   alpha: 100% opaque
    page:setup:done.png          25,932 bytes   alpha: 100% opaque

**It is the largest file in the sweep and it is a photograph of almost nothing.**
What it contains is the page's own description text - *"Chronoa needs a key to talk
to a provider on your behalf..."* - rendered in the theme's foreground colour at a
default font size, on transparency, with no window chrome and no controls. So it
is not a page, and **the sweep reported `PASS` on it**, because a valid PNG was
written and that is the whole of the PASS test.

**Alpha coverage is the detector, and it has now caught all three instances.** The
first two were the main-window pages at 96.2% transparent; this one is 87.1%. A
target that settles early, or whose deepest renderable node is not the window,
produces exactly this signature, and **no byte count distinguishes it** - 129KB of
detached text outranks a real 30KB page.

### The cause is a recorded renderer trap, not a page defect

`cloud-keys` is the one wizard page holding **editable fields**, and this file
already records that shape: *"An editable widget has no surface to draw into when
snapshotted detached. Measured side by side in one mapped window: `Gtk.SearchEntry`,
`Adw.EntryRow` and `Adw.StatusPage` all return `None`, while a plain `Gtk.Entry`
and a `Gtk.Label` both return real nodes."*

The renderer walks down to the deepest node that yields one, so on this page it
walks past the unrenderable entry rows and stops on a **bare label**, captured
detached - foreground with nothing painted behind it, which is the same artifact
this file records for the task card.

**The page's layout is fine, and that is measured rather than assumed.** The
recorded cause for this page was a width overflow (struck above);
`tests/test_ui_layout_contract.py -k "scrollbar or wizard"` is **16 passed**, so
no wizard page asks for a sideways scrollbar. **Width was never why this page
did not render.**

### What a sweep of this shape has to print

The PASS column is written by "a file appeared", and that cannot see any of the
three false passes this audit has produced. A page sweep should report **opaque
percentage** beside the byte count, and treat a target under a stated floor as
**NOT RENDERED** rather than as a pass - because a capture that photographs less
than its target is worse than `NO NODE`, since it looks like a render. The floor
is not a guess: the four pages above sit at 7.2% and 100%, with nothing between.
gui: a shortcut hint that lost the app's own dim style, and two tests that wanted different shapes

The empty state carries the shortcut hints so Ctrl+K is discoverable, and I had
folded them into the placeholder's markup to satisfy `test_window_ux`'s invariant
that the empty state is the placeholder and the suggestion bar and nothing else.
That cost the hint the app's dim style - `size='small'` is not the rule every
other quiet line follows - and `test_shortcuts_are_discoverable` said so.

The fix attempted first was `<span class="dim-label">`, and **GTK refuses it**:
*"Attribute 'class' is not allowed on the <span> tag"*, and `set_markup` leaves
the label **empty** rather than falling back to plain text, so the prompt and the
shortcuts both vanished and `get_text()` answered "". Measured, not assumed - and
a reminder that a markup attribute is a guess until the library answers.

So the hint is a label with `dim-label`, and the invariant is taught the second
deliberate row rather than weakened: every row must be one of the two
class-bearing ones, which still fails on a third.

**Two of my own tests wanted incompatible shapes for the same line** - one wanted
a row of its own, one forbade a row - and the way that showed up was one of them
going red while the other was green. Neither was wrong about the property they
share (a hint must not compete with the prompt); only about the mechanism.

3 mutations on the snapshot, 3 caught: a stray row added (the invariant's whole
purpose), the hint losing `dim-label`, and the hints ceasing to name shortcuts.
Snapshot byte-identical afterwards.
