## Two more readers had the same defect, and the third of them was a person (2026-10-13)

The entry above fixed `_entries` and `dream` and said *"three of seven readers"*
- and the other four were found by sweeping the population rather than by
tripping over them again. Both new ones are worse than the three already fixed.

**`learning.load()` is the reader for training.** `train_and_save`,
`merge_models` and two more fit their models from it, so a rotation meant fitting
the outcome model on whatever had been written since. Measured on a copy of this
machine's own log through the real rotation path:

    whole history:              18,794 examples in 0.40s
    after ONE rotation:              0
    after the fix:             18,794 examples in 0.40s   (LOST: 0 of 18,794)

**`WINDOW` is 200,000 and the whole history is 18,794**, so the cap was never the
binding constraint - the file boundary was. A model fitted on nothing is reported
with a corpus the report never mentions, which is the absence-shaped wrong answer
this whole change exists to prevent, reached through the fix.

**`settings_window/activity.py::_log_tail` is the Tool Activity panel**, which is
the surface that answers *"what has Chronoa done"*. It read one generation, and
its `exists` is true and it has lines to show, so **no note fires**: a person saw
a short history with nothing saying it was short. `tail.size` renders as *"the log
weighs X"*, so a size taken from the part it read would have claimed a 19 MB log
weighs 1 KB. After: **321 rows before a rotation, 321 after**, and 18.0 MiB
reported for a log that is 18.0 MiB.

**And the over-fix was caught by a test in a file I had not read.** Reading every
chunk is only correct while a chunk that cannot be read does not take the rest
with it - so the first version `continue`d past an unreadable chunk, and
`test_an_unreadable_log_is_not_reported_as_an_empty_one` went red: a permission
error was being reported as **"The log is there and empty"**, which is *less*
honest than what shipped. The rule is now what this panel's own docstring says a
person acts on - a chunk that cannot be read contributes nothing, and a tail from
which **nothing at all** could be read is a read failure (`read_any`). The set
carries **two** over-fix mutations for the two directions, because the obvious
wrong repair is to report `unreadable` whenever any chunk failed, and no
assertion about how many rows were shown would have caught that.

### The sweep that found them, and why the obvious version of it is a crying wolf

Every shipped function that mentions a log-path resolver, and whether it routes
through `log_files()`:

    functions touching a resolver:      26
    of those, NOT routing:             21   <- a gate asserting "must route" cries wolf

**21 of 26.** They are *path resolvers* (`_log_path`, `log_dir`), *callers* that
pass a path to a reader which routes, *writers* (`_write_to_log`, `rotate`),
`stat()`-only revision markers, and `dream-*.txt` globs that are not this log at
all. Filtered to functions that **both** touch a resolver and open it, **every
remaining case is legitimate** - so there is no unrouted reader left, and the
gate's population is the six that need a documented reason rather than 26. **This
is the "a scanner that reports 54 files is worse than no scanner" conclusion
reached three times in this file**, and the honest residue is the measurement
rather than a permanent red suite.

### Two of my own mistakes, and the second is the one that would have shipped

- **The cache-revision mutation was a measured equivalent, and my first reason for
  it was a guess the run corrected.** I wrote "carrying every chunk is defence in
  depth against an archive being pruned without the active log changing, and *if
  it is caught, the reason here is wrong*". It was not caught - because **a
  rotation renames the active log away and writes a new one from empty, so its
  own `(size, mtime)` changes on every rotation, and a rotation is the only event
  that changes the archive set.** Measured over three rotations: archives 0->1->2->3
  and the active log's revision changed every time. So there is no reachable state
  the multi-chunk key would have caught, and the reason is simpler than defence in
  depth.
- **`load()`'s over-fix guard had no witness at all.** `test_one_unreadable_
  archive_does_not_blind_the_reader` drove only the panel, so the mutation
  `one unreadable archive blinds the training reader` came back a **survivor**
  while its panel twin was caught. **A witness that covers half the readers of a
  property reads as coverage of all of them** - and my own fix was what made the
  suite assert `>= 5` where the right claim was `>= 5, and not "this whole log is
  unreadable"` (the unreadable archive's records genuinely cannot be read; losing
  the readable ones is the defect).

44 tests in `tests/test_call_log_rotation.py`, 89 across it and the panel.
`tools/mutations/call_log_rotation.py`: **24 mutations, 22 caught, 0 survivors, 2
equivalent (both documented), 0 unmeasurable, 0 stale**, and no line reading "NOT
caught by". 357 passed / 1 failed across every test file touching learning, dream,
distill or the activity panel; the failure is pre-existing (`1db21c4`, "explain
gravity still offers tools") and proved by swapping my two source files for HEAD's
**in a snapshot** and getting the identical failure.

## The enum was the only schema constraint nothing was checking, and the skills already checked it in the wrong place (2026-10-13)

Asked whether the consent gate should be keyed on arguments as well as on the
tool name. It already is - **`guardrail` runs on every dispatch**, ahead of the
sandbox, checking required arguments, per-property types and
`additionalProperties: False`. So the question was not "should there be one".

**Measured what it did not check.** Across the whole registry - 682 property
nodes, 256 tools:

| constraint declared in a schema | count |
|---|---:|
| `enum` | **90**, in **73** tools |
| a numeric bound | **0** |
| a string bound | **0** |

So `enum` was the *entire* remaining gap. And it is a gap in **placement**, not
in the check: `airplane_mode` already refuses one itself -

    action = (arguments.get("action") or "status").strip().lower()
    if action not in ("status", "on", "off"): ...

- which is the right rule, **in the child**, after dispatch, after the sandbox and
after the audit origin. So the refusal existed, and read as a tool that *ran*.
The same rule one layer earlier is what `guardrail` is for.

**And the over-fix was real, not hypothetical.** Two of the 73 accept values
*outside* their declared enum through an alias table:

| tool | declares | actually accepts |
|---|---:|---:|
| `alarm` | 6 | **14** (`remove`, `cancel`, `edit`, `update`, `move`, `add`, `create`, `when`) |
| `calendar_edit` | 3 | **10** (`add`, `new`, `schedule`, `delete`, `remove`, `reschedule`, `change`) |

A gate written against the declaration alone would have refused **"remove my
alarm"** - the most natural phrasing of `delete`. So the remedy is not an
exception list in `guardrail`; it is to **declare what the skill accepts**, which
makes *"the value must be in the declared enum"* true of every tool rather than
71 of them. Offering `remove` to the model is also better selection than making
it choose between `delete` and `remove`, and `test_every_alias_a_skill_accepts_is_
declared_in_its_enum` is what makes the claim checkable - **it failed with all
15 keys named** before the schemas were widened.

**Matched with the tolerance the skills use**, because a gate stricter than the
skills refuses calls that work today: `airplane_mode` strips and lowercases, so
`action="LIST"` is legal and stays legal. Both directions are pinned - a gate
that refuses `"LIST"` and a gate that computes the check and ignores it are two
separate survivors waiting to happen, and the set carries both.

23 tests in `tests/test_guardrail.py`. **290 passed** across the dispatch,
permissions, capability and gate suites, and **150 across the workbench and
guardrail files together** after a tmp leak below was cleared. `tools/mutations/
guardrail_enum.py`: 8 mutations, including the shipped gap restored verbatim and
both over-fixes.

## The grammar is real, it is enforced, and it costs 37 points of tool choice (2026-10-13)

The three-arm experiment this file prescribed for three entries ran: **225 cases,
Qwen3-1.7B-Q4_K_M, temperature 0, one server**, ~75 minutes an arm. Arms 2 and 3
are the same two steps with the same schema in prose; **the grammar is the only
difference**, and enforcement is the only thing arm 3 drops.

| arm | acted (form) | right tool | tool+args |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `+greedy` | 210/225 | 191/225 | 186/225 |
| `+greedy+constrained` | **225/225** | 194/225 | 185/225 |
| `+greedy+request` | **121/225** | 111/225 | 101/225 |

**Arms 2 vs 3 - the experiment.** Paired, case by case, with an exact test:

| | delta | 95% CI | flipped right | flipped wrong | p |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| acted (form) | **-46.2** | -52.9 .. -39.6 | **0** | **104** | 0.000 |
| right tool | **-36.9** | -44.0 .. -30.2 | 4 | 87 | 0.000 |
| tool+args | **-37.3** | -44.4 .. -30.7 | 6 | 90 | 0.000 |

**And arms 1 vs 2, which is the other half of the question:**

| | delta | 95% CI | flipped right | flipped wrong | p |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| acted (form) | **+6.7** | +3.6 .. +10.2 | 15 | **0** | 0.000 |
| right tool | +1.3 | -3.6 .. +5.8 | 16 | 13 | **0.711** |
| tool+args | -0.4 | -5.3 .. +4.4 | 17 | 18 | **1.000** |

### What it settles, in three sentences

1. **A grammar buys form, and form is not what `task_eval` scores.** Arm 2 over
   arm 1 is +6.7 points of form with **15 cases gained and 0 lost**, and *nothing*
   measurable on choice (p=0.711) or on tool+arguments (p=1.000).
2. **Enforcement does not merely fail to improve choice - it costs it.** 104 cases
   lost and **not one** gained. That is the "superficial syntactic alignment,
   no semantic gain" of arXiv:2604.06066, reproduced here at **1.7B** with paired
   statistics, from a prediction this repo's own single-case grammar probe made
   before the run.
3. **The format request alone is the most harmful of the three arms**, and the
   grammar's only measured benefit is *rescuing form from the damage it did*: 225
   acted with enforcement against 121 without.

### The mechanism, observed rather than inferred

Without enforcement the model **answers in prose instead of calling a tool**.
`time`, `date`, `volume-get`, `mute` and `brightness` all came back classified
`reply='answer'` with no call at all. Of the 87 cases arm 2 called a tool and arm 3
did not, **85 are "no tool"**. That is arXiv:2607.18476's "a sharpener, not a
re-indexer" in a tool chooser: the model falls back to the *chat* register, and the
chat register's answer to "what time is it" is a sentence, not a call.

And a second pattern, named rather than counted - with the schema in prose and no
enforcement the model sometimes answers with **the schema echoed back as the
value**: `firmware_updates({"firmware_updates": {...}})`, `thread_activity(
{"thread_activity": {...}})`, `data_usage`, `cleanup_report`, `routing_table`,
`usb_devices`. Form satisfied; the argument is a copy of the thing it describes.

### The prediction, and being wrong about it in the direction I did not expect

This file predicted `constrained -> request`: **form -20.5, choice +2.3**.
Measured: **form -46.2, choice -36.9**. Wrong on the magnitude of form and **wrong
in sign on choice** - I expected flat-or-slightly-up and got 37 points down. The
single-case probe had already shown a model naming the one tool it was allowed to
name for a question about weather, and I read that as a caution rather than as
the size of the effect.

### What this settles for the work

**Do not ship constrained decoding.** Not because it does not work - it works
perfectly, it produced **225/225 well-formed calls** - but because the thing it
fixes is the thing nobody was asking about. The two levers the literature
supports are untouched: **schema wording** (arXiv:2604.14862 - changing only key
tokens moves accuracy, with no training run and no decoder constraint) and
**selection**, where `select` already has a measured **95.5% offered-set recall
ceiling** and 35% of what it sends shares no word with the request.

Stated limits, so the number is not read as more than it is: one 1.7B model,
greedy, one server, 225 cases, and a corpus that is half hand-written. The paired
design and the 0-gained / 104-lost asymmetry are what carry this, not the
percentages.

## The reranker was built far enough to measure it, and 17 seconds a turn says it does not ship (2026-10-13)

Asked to build the full reranker. The harness is `tools/rerank.py`; what settled
the decision was **not** training cost, which is paid once, and **not** memory,
which never bound. It was the serving cost, which is paid on **every request**.

**The stale figure first, because it was the one I would have quoted.** This file
recorded *"31.8 s per optimiser step, 15.9 GB peak, one epoch 15.5 hours"*.
Re-measured with `tools/lora_timing.py` on today's tree:

| | recorded | measured today |
|---|---:|---:|
| per optimiser step | 31.8 s | **52.5 s** |
| peak RSS | 15.9 GB | **15.7 GB** |
| one epoch | 15.5 h | **19.3 h** |

Same order of magnitude, every number moved. **A number copied into prose is a
number nobody re-measures** - the conclusion held, the digits did not.

**Memory never bound, and `lora_timing.py`'s own comment was right.** It says
*"fp32 on CPU: bf16 matmul falls back and is slower, and the whole question is
wall clock rather than memory"*, which looked stale when a 25 MB `MemAvailable`
reading suggested otherwise. That 25 MB was a transient while another session's
mutation run had the box; at rest it is **24.6 GB**, and both dtypes fit:

| | peak RSS | step | one epoch |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| fp32 | 15.7 GB | 52.5 s | 19.3 h |
| **bf16** | **10.5 GB** | 88.0 s | 31.1 h |

bf16 cuts the **weight load from 12,000 MB to 1,577 MB** - so weights were the
driver and dtype is the lever - and is 68% slower, exactly as that comment said.

### The number that decides it

A cross-encoder scores **every candidate**, so a k-candidate list costs k forward
passes in the hot path, against a selector that is a dict lookup and a sort.
Measured, one turn's real candidates, 4 threads:

| | one at a time | all 7 batched |
|---|---:|---:|
| fp32 | **16.88 s** | 13.65 s |
| bf16 | 36.46 s | 32.79 s |

**~17 seconds of selection before the model starts answering.** This box decodes a
1.7B at 6.8 tok/s, so a reply is a few seconds and a whole turn is tens - and
`tool_select` was a deliberate part of what makes a small model usable at all.
Multiplying the hot path by seven forward passes to reorder a short list is not a
trade this architecture can make.

### And the headroom, which is smaller than the number that motivated it

`tools/rerank.py --eval-baseline`, the real `ranked()` over the real schemas on
the **held-out 55**, seconds and no torch:

| | |
|---|---:|
| baseline top-1 | **49/55 = 89.1%** |
| offered-set recall at 8 | 54/55 = 98.2% |
| **reranker ceiling** (`recall_hit`) | **54/55 = 98.2%** |

**The 80% top-1 that motivated this was over all 220; on the held-out half the
selector is already at 89.1%, and a reranker cannot rank an answer into a list
that does not contain it - so the entire prize is 9.1 points.**

So the decision frame, all measured: 31.1 h/epoch unattended and reachable;
10.5 GB and comfortable; **9.1 points of ceiling**; and **17 s per request** of
serving cost on a 4-core CPU box. Three of those four say go.

**`tools/rerank.py --train` deliberately raises rather than pretending.** The
harness that would decide it exists and the numbers it needed are printed by
`--dry-run`; a training loop that has never been run is the machinery-whose-only-
purpose-is-to-report-success this file rules out.

## 2026-10-13 - Tool selection was paying 12 ms per request to re-read 256 descriptions

Asked to "fix all, make it fast, time and space". The honest first move is that
"all" is not a population I can guess at, so the instrument came first:

**`tools/profile_hot_paths.py`** - every path a turn touches, **one subprocess
each**, reporting wall time and peak RSS. Subprocess-per-item is the whole
design: `ru_maxrss` is a high-water mark, so timing ten things in one process
attributes the largest allocation to whichever ran last. Sorted by **cold**, not
warm, because a warm number is a cache reading itself back and ranking a table
by it puts the cheapest path first for the wrong reason.

The table immediately showed two of its own entries lying:

| it reported | the truth |
|---|---|
| `learning_load` 0.0001 s | `_EXAMPLE_CACHE` serving a repeat. Cold read: **0.25 s** |
| `guardrail_check` 0.566 s cold | that is **module import**, not the path. Warm: 0.0039 s |
| 4 probes `ERROR` | I had guessed four signatures. See below. |

### The one that was actually hot

**`select_tools`: 12.4 ms per request.** On the path of every single request, and
`cProfile` put 8.1 s of its 11.6 s in one chain:

```
_tool_text -> _words -> _stem     8.129 s cumulative
_tool_text called 57,344 times    = 256 per request, re-tokenising every
                                    description on every turn
_stem called 2,907,161 times      = once per word, per tool, per request
```

Every one of those numbers is a **constant per tool** being recomputed per
request. Four separate fixes, all the same mistake:

1. **`_tool_text`/`_tool_options` cached per tool** - keyed on the tool's own
   *content* (`name`, description text, enum values), not on `id()`: a schema
   edited in place keeps its identity, and an identity-keyed cache would go on
   describing the old one. 12.56 -> **5.66 ms**.
2. **`body` is a `frozenset`, not a list.** `ranked()` tests `w in body` once per
   request word per tool; against a ~200-word list that is a linear scan, in the
   one loop that has to be O(1).
3. **`df`/`option_df`/`texts`/`options` cached per tool *set*** - 2,133 and 378
   entries, **0.07 MB**, built in 0.9 ms, and they were being rebuilt on every
   request to produce numbers that only change when a schema does.
4. **`_cap_to_window` stops re-serialising the selection.** `_fits` is
   `len(json.dumps(request_tools))` and the drop loop called it once per
   candidate: **25 `json.dumps` of a ~17 KB selection per request**, to add up
   integers that were already known.

Plus two more found by re-profiling what was left: `select_tools` built the
corpus **twice** per request (512 `_tool_facts` lookups for one corpus, 42% of
the remainder), and `learned_weights()` re-derived `reliability` over every
durable record **on every request** (30% of the remainder) even though
`_durable_records` returns the *same list object* until a chunk moves.

**12.4 -> 1.80 ms per request. 6.9x. Behaviourally identical: 0 of 225 real
selections differ from HEAD**, verified by loading HEAD's module beside the new
one with `learned` pinned on both sides.

The space is a **1.86 MB** cache held for the life of the process, replacing 220
requests' worth of the same allocation churn per turn. (7 MB was my first guess,
written into the docstring before measuring; 1.86 is what `tracemalloc` says.)

### Two ways this tried to pass as done

**I measured `fn` where `_fits` measures the schema.** `{"type": "function",
"function": {...}}` - the wrapper is **34 chars per tool, 95.4% of the true
size** (180,280 of 188,984), and a selection of eight handed back ~68 tokens of a
2048 window it had already spent. Caught by `test_a_selection_fits_the_smallest_window`.

**The test I wrote for it could not have caught it.** Asserting that the new
arithmetic equals `len(json.dumps(kept))` compares the arithmetic against *the
same set the arithmetic produced* - it agrees with itself about a set it
mis-measures. So there are two pins, not one: one for the **formula** (brackets,
separators) and one for the **size** (`chars_by_name[name] == len(json.dumps(tool))`).

And the first version of the formula pin **re-derived the arithmetic inside the
test**, which proves nothing about the code. Measured: dropping the brackets
from `_selection_chars` left it **green**. So the arithmetic is now a named
function the cap calls and the test calls, and the reason is in its docstring.

### 19 mutations: 10 caught, 3 verified equivalents, 6 that change nothing observable

**Three of my mutation runs were false cleans and every one of them looked
exactly like a pass.** Worth listing, because the failure is always silent:

* an anchor that was in `tool_select.py` while I passed `learning.py` - "all
  passed", meant nothing, re-run by hand: **caught**;
* an anchor that matched **twice** - the assert fired, the mutation never
  applied, and the run reported the baseline's 53 passed. Re-run with a unique
  anchor: **caught** (5 failed);
* four mutations after a snapshot where I forgot `tests/conftest.py`, so
  `shani_chronoa` was not importable and **pytest errored at collection** - four
  rows of empty output that a careless read would have called four survivors. The
  baseline in that same batch printed nothing, which is the tell.

The equivalents were **verified by construction, not asserted**: `body` as a
list gives an identical digest across all 225 selections (2.34 vs 2.14 ms), and
`==` instead of `is` on the two caches is equivalent because equal-but-distinct
inputs produce equal answers. Six change nothing observable - three disable a
cache outright (speed only, and pinning them means a timing assertion), and one
narrows the new oracle's budget sweep from eleven budgets to one, which weakens
the test without touching the code.

### `_fits` is no longer called, so it is the oracle instead of dead code

Replacing the serialising call left `_fits` defined and unreferenced - and a
definition that documents what "fits" means stops being checked the moment it
stops being read. So it is now the **oracle**: `test_the_fast_path_agrees_with_
the_function_it_replaced` sweeps `_selection_chars` against it at eleven budgets
over all 225 real selections, because both sides do the same integer division and
an off-by-`2*k` is invisible at the one budget where the selection happens to
fit. A guard pointing at nothing is not a guard; pointing it back at the function
it replaced is what makes it one.

### The last one was invisible until the two variants were interleaved

`idf` depends on the request word and the corpus, not on the tool - and it was
being computed **inside** the per-tool loop, so each of ~10 words had its
`math.log` and its dictionary lookup done **256 times**: ~2,560 of each per
request, to produce ten numbers. Hoisting it is provably identical output and
strictly fewer operations.

Measured once against the recorded 1.68 ms: **1.66 - within noise.** So the
arithmetic said ~0.13 ms should be there and the number said it was not, and
neither of those is a measurement. Interleaving both variants, three rounds
alternating:

| | median | best |
|---|---:|---:|
| inline | 1.693 / 1.720 / 1.696 | 1.61 / 1.66 / 1.67 |
| **hoisted** | **1.624 / 1.618 / 1.579** | **1.58 / 1.56 / 1.54** |

**~4.7%, real and consistent, winning every round** - and a single before/after
against a remembered number had reported it as nothing. On a 1.6 ms measurement,
run-to-run drift is larger than the effect; only alternating the two builds
separates them. Worth saying plainly because the first measurement was
**correctly executed and useless**, which is a different failure from a wrong one.

**The headline speedup, measured both ways.** On a quiet box: 12.56 -> 1.62 ms,
**7.8x**. Mid-run the other session put `ffmpeg` at 214% and the box hit load
7.4, and a fresh reading said 2.74 ms - which would have demoted the result to
4.6x on the strength of a contended measurement. So both sides were re-measured
**interleaved under that same load**: 21.03/21.11/23.63 before against
2.72/3.07/3.29 after, **6.9x, 7.7x, 7.2x**. Both absolutes inflate; the ratio
does not, because both builds are measured in the same conditions. An absolute
number compared against one taken twenty minutes earlier is not a measurement of
anything.

### Then the space half, which found a leak of my own making

Having bounded the corpus cache I checked whether I had bounded the one above
it. **I had not.** `_TOOL_FACTS` was keyed on schema *content*, so every schema
ever edited, installed, or generated by the Workbench was a key it had never seen
- and an unbounded dict keeping all of them, ~7 KB of stemmed words each, for the
life of the process. Bounded at 1024: the live registry is 256, so normal use
never reaches it.

Two more were pre-existing and the same shape. `learning._EXAMPLE_CACHE` and
`learning._HISTORY_CACHE` are both keyed by **path** and neither was ever
evicted. Measured with real log lines: **98 KB retained per distinct path**,
one entry at a time. Production has one log so this costs nothing there, but a
test run builds thousands of temporary logs and would hold every one of them to
the end. All three bounded now, and `_HISTORY_CACHE` matters more than its size
suggests: it is the **per-request** advisory read, so its entire job is not
redoing work for a log that is not moving - which is one entry, not an unbounded
number of them.

### The fourth false clean, and it was mine again

Bounding `_HISTORY_CACHE` wrote a test that **named log paths without ever
writing the files**. `_durable_records` stats every chunk and returns `None` on
`OSError` *before* it reaches the cache, so the dict stayed empty and the
assertion passed with the bound deleted - three mutations survived it. A probe
that did write the files grew to 10 and failed, which is what found it.

That is the same failure as the three above and the same lesson: **a check on a
cache that was never written to is not a check.** The test now writes the file
and asserts the read came back non-`None`, so "nothing happened" cannot pass as
"nothing grew".

After the fix all three bounds are caught, and the mutations that survive are
`clear()` in place of `pop(next(iter(...)))` - evicting everything instead of one
entry. That is thrashing, not behaviour, so it is recorded as an equivalent
rather than pinned; pinning it would mean asserting on cache *hit rate*, which is
a timing measurement wearing a correctness costume.

### Two things measured and deliberately not changed

**The selection budget is not a hard ceiling, and my test had claimed it was.**
"Click." finishes at **1,936 tokens against a 1,536 budget**: `browse` is ~850 on
its own and is protected, because a request that cannot be answered without a
browser is sent with one. Confirmed on **HEAD, unchanged by this work**. The
honest invariant is *fits, or nothing droppable was left*, and
`protected_for()` is now a named function so the test asks the code rather than
re-deriving it. Asserting a flat "always fits" would have been red on this
machine before a line changed.

**`learning._entries()` is 117 MB for a panel refresh, and capping it would
reintroduce the rotation bug.** Its whole documented purpose is that a reader
seeing a shrinking slice of history is the failure - one rotation once made it
return 1 record of 19,111 and say nothing. Six callers train on the whole
history. Reported, not fixed.

Sparse against dense, measured with `getsizeof` and extrapolated, because the
factor is the entire argument for the sparse form: **18,796 records would be
9.86 GB dense against 5.41 MB sparse, 1,821x less.**

### The suite hangs because eight tests write into the live database

`tests/test_file_index.py` hung for 30 minutes at zero CPU and made a whole-suite
run unfinishable. Bisected to one test, then to one line:

```python
report = F.index_directory(home, embed=False)      # no db=
```

`db=None` resolves to `index_path()` - **the live index, the one the running
application reads and writes.** And `WALK_CEILING = 60000`, so that one test
built 60,005 files and wrote **60,005 rows into the person's real file index**.
It hung against the app's write lock. **Seven more tests did the same thing**,
building files under `tmp_path` and then indexing them into the live database.

Two of those then turned out to agree only because of it: `test_it_counts_what_
was_indexed` indexed with `_three()` and read `F.status()` with **no `db=`** -
so the writer and the reader were both the live index, and the test passed
because it had polluted the state it read. Give the writer its own database and
they stop agreeing, which is the fix, not the regression.

**54 passed in 348 s** (was: never), and the live index is **byte-identical**
before and after by `md5sum`.

The guard for the guard is a source scan, because the failure is invisible at
runtime - a test that writes to the live index still passes. It found **three
more** call sites on its first run that a `grep` had missed. Mutation-checked
three ways; all three caught.

### `_entries_of` held the file, every line, and every record at once

`_entries()` is 117 MB per panel refresh and stays uncapped, because capping it
reintroduces the rotation bug it exists to prevent. But the *transient* was
avoidable. `read_text()` then `splitlines()` means the file's text, every line of
it, and every parsed dict are live simultaneously. Measured on this machine's own
archive: **76.1 MB peak against a 37.3 MB result.**

Streamed one line at a time: **peak 76.1 -> 37.5 MB**, result unchanged, and
**byte-identical** on every input including a missing file, a directory, and an
empty one. The `OSError` still returns `[]` from anywhere in the file, not the
records read so far - a reader that reports a half-read file as a short file is
the shape of quiet wrongness already in this file.

### The same streaming, applied to `dream.read_log`, was reverted

`dream.read_log` had the identical shape - `handle.read()`, decode the whole
payload, `splitlines()` it - and **57.7 MB peak against 0 MB retained**, three
live copies of an 18.9 MB chunk to count records it does not keep. Streaming it
gave **27.4 MB** and an identical `Reading(records=19112, unreadable=0)`.

**Then the A/B said it was slower: +23%, and it lost all three interleaved
rounds.** Iterating a binary handle costs Python-level work per line that one
`read()` plus a C-level `splitlines()` does not. So it is 30 MB for 50 ms on a
**background consolidation pass**, on a machine with 24.6 GB available - and
this file's own rule is that a trade has to say which side binds. Neither does.
**Reverted.**

Which leaves the difference that made it worth doing at all:

| | time | peak |
|---|---|---:|
| `_entries_of`, `read_text` -> streamed | 0.282 -> **0.288 s** (unchanged) | 76.1 -> **37.5 MB** |
| `dream.read_log`, `read_text` -> streamed | 0.206 -> **0.254 s** (+23%) | 57.7 -> 27.4 MB |

Same technique, opposite verdicts, and the only reason to tell them apart is
that the second one was measured both ways. **Half the peak for free** is worth
having; **half the peak for a quarter more time** is not, and I would have
written up the second one as a win on the strength of the memory number alone.

### And the 0600-directory leak I had recorded was the wrong file

The note in this file said `test_skill_workbench.py` leaks mode-600 directories
that block pytest's `rm_rf`. It does not: the leaked `logs.2` / `logs.3` are
**directories**, from `test_call_log_rotation.py`, and they do not reproduce -
`rotate()` refuses a directory, `test_a_log_directory_is_refused_rather_than_
renamed` pins it, and the file now leaves **44 passed and no garbage behind**.
The leaked directories were from before that guard landed.

### The blast radius, and a suite that hangs

`pytest tests/` as one process **hung for 30 minutes at zero CPU** and reported
nothing, so it was killed by PID and replaced by 25 chunks with a per-chunk cap.
That run: **9,100 passed**, 53 failed or errored across 17 files, 1 chunk hung.

The hung chunk bisected to a single file: **`tests/test_file_index.py`, which
hangs on its own** - 24 of the other 24 files finish in 1-39 s each. Run against
HEAD's `tool_select.py` and `learning.py` instead of mine it **still hangs**
(rc=124 either way), so it is pre-existing and it is what makes a whole-suite run
unfinishable on this machine.

**Then the 53 failures refused to be attributed at all.** Running them in one
batch, swapping only my two files for HEAD's, gave totals of **32/31, then
21/32, then 31/21** across three alternating rounds - the same code producing 21
or 32 failures depending on the run. "Fails only with mine" went 5, 0, 10. So
batch results measure the batch, and the fix was what this file already records
for `test_skill_workbench.py`: **one process per node**, no shared tmp, no
module-level GTK state carried between tests.

One process per node: **16 fail with this change, 22 with HEAD.** Fourteen fail
under both. The remaining two looked like mine until they were run five times
each side - `test_silence_is_not_a_request` and
`test_voice_styles_measured[assistant]` - and they fail **5 of 5 with HEAD too**,
so the solo run's "passes with HEAD" was itself the flake.

**Every failure under this change also fails without it: 0 attributable.** And
HEAD shows six *more* failures than the branch does, which is the wrong direction
for a regression and the reason the 32/31, 21/32, 31/31 spread could not have been
read as one.

## Ctrl+K built a palette that was never in the window, and a ceiling that crushed it (2026-10-13)

Three things were asked for: make the command palette appear, make it and the
model picker scrollable, and put a searchable list of cloud providers and models
in both. **The first was a layout defect and the second was a GTK-semantics
defect, and the second would have shipped looking fixed.**

### The palette reported success and drew nothing

`_on_palette_key` set the palette visible, returned `True`, and Ctrl+K "worked".
Measured on the built window: after the press `visible=True` and **`parent=None`**,
`in_subtree=False`, `mapped=False` - 50 entries built and **0 containers**. A
`Gtk.Box` with no parent is not a popover, a popup or a layer; it is a widget with
nothing to draw on.

Parented to the chat column, inline, directly under the transcript - the
transcript is `vexpand`, so showing the palette takes its height from the
conversation rather than from the window. The same idiom as `_question_row`.

**And "somewhere in the window" was too weak an assertion to pin any of this.**
A palette nested inside any hidden box *is* a descendant of the window and is
mapped never, because a hidden ancestor takes its children with it. So the test
asserts the **specific parent**, which is also what makes a mutation for the
placement measurable at all: `self.set_child(self._palette)` was the original
mutation and it was **UNMEASURABLE**, because replacing an `ApplicationWindow`'s
only child aborts the window build and pytest printed no summary. The mutation
that replaced it parents the palette **inside `_question_row`** - which is
itself hidden, and which a "is it a descendant" test passes.

### `set_max_content_height` alone is a crush, not a cap

This is the half worth reading, because **the ceiling tests passed the whole time
the surfaces were broken.** `set_max_content_height(420)` bounds the scroller's
*request*. It does not make the scroller **ask** for that height, and a
`Gtk.ScrolledWindow` asks for very little by default - so both surfaces came back
at their own **58px**, about one row, and the 3-entry palette drew a scrollbar
over content that fits.

Measured in a presented 320x900 window, identical widgets, only
`set_propagate_natural_height` differing:

| | flag off | flag on |
|---|---|---|
| picker, 6 tiers + 848 models | **58px** | **420px** (upper 47,666) |
| palette, 50 entries | **58px**, scrolls | **420px**, scrolls |
| palette, 3 entries | **58px** + **scrollbar** | **126px, no scrollbar** |

`test_the_picker_has_a_scroller_with_a_ceiling` **passes with the flag deleted**
- measured, it did - so the two are separate mutations and the new test asserts
the *flag*, not the ceiling.

**Three instruments could not see this, and each was wrong for a reason this
file already records.** An **unallocated** scroller reports `upper == page_size
== 0`, so a probe reading the adjustment said "does not overflow" for every case
including an 848-row list. Offering a **presented** widget 2000px returned
`page=2000`, because `max-content-height` bounds a request and not an
allocation - so the cap's own number had to be measured twice, from two
directions, before either was believable. And a `Gtk.Popover` does not lay out
its child until it is popped up, so the picker reads `upper=0 page=0` whatever the
model count: **the height the picker produces in a real popover is not
established, and is not claimed.** The flag is asserted; the resulting height is
not.

### One shared cache, because two surfaces could otherwise disagree

`cloud_llm._MODEL_CACHE` is read by the picker and the palette, so they cannot
answer "which models exist" differently. `cached_models()` returns `([], "")`
when nothing has been fetched - deliberately ambiguous, which is why
`models_asked()` exists to separate *"nobody looked"* from *"there are none"*.
A refusal is cached **with its reason**, and `forget_models()` drops the cache
on a key change. Fetching runs on a worker with `GLib.idle_add` rebuilding per
provider, so opening either surface never blocks on HTTP and the list fills as
answers arrive.

`app.answer-cloud-model` takes `(ss)` rather than being a stateful chip, and is
refused **by name** for an unknown provider, a blank model, or a provider with no
`MODEL_SETTINGS` entry - the last of which happens *with* a rebuild so a refused
choice still saves what the person had before it.

### Four of my own witnesses could not fail, and the mutation run said so

| mutation | what the run reported | why |
|---|---|---|
| an unregistered provider is accepted | **survivor**, 7 failed | the witness is caught by *both* provider guards, so removing either leaves it green - the test has to put the name in `MODEL_SETTINGS` **alone** |
| the model name is saved with its spaces | **mis-named**, 1 failed | `expect` named `test_a_choice_is_written`, which passes an already-trimmed name; the run named the padded test that bit. Correct the name - do not write a test |
| the palette is parented off the chat column | **unmeasurable** | replacing the window's only child aborts the build |
| the scroller has no ceiling | **passed with the flag deleted** | `assert cap` is truthy, because GTK's default `max-content-height` is `-1` |

The first two are the same failure this file has recorded several times: **a
witness list that names tests passing either way reads as coverage while the
mutation is covered by a different one.** The runner reporting "failed for
another reason" is the only reason either was noticed.

### And the flake was concurrency, which is the fourth time it has been the answer

The palette probe's original fixed 1200ms deadline became **30 seconds of
retries** for a window that was never coming, and it failed 1 batch in 7. The
cause is the bus, not the clock: `ChronoaApplication` hardcodes
`dev.shani.chronoa`, and `tests/test_slash_menu_opens.py` in the same batch
registers it, so activation is **forwarded to that owner**. It now builds the
window the way `do_activate` builds it - one call, the same constructor - and
presents directly. With `test_slash_menu_opens.py` in the batch: **29 passed**.

**And the mutation run's first two attempts reported 6 of 25 UNMEASURABLE**,
because a regression batch of mine was hitting the **same broadway display**
concurrently. Measured rather than assumed: 22 consecutive runs of that one test
alone, **22 clean**. So the tally is only real when nothing else is on the
display - the same "concurrency manufactures failures that look exactly like
defects" this file records for `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, `GSETTINGS_BACKEND`,
`fake_bin`'s `PATH` and the D-Bus name, now in a fifth costume.

`tests/test_cloud_models_are_chooseable.py` (31),
`tools/mutations/cloud_models.py` (25 mutations, 25 anchors; measured run 5:
**25 mutations, 25 caught, 0 survivors, 0 equivalent, 0 unmeasurable**, 251s on a
display of its own - the six UNMEASURABLE of run 4 were display contention, as
the re-pointed witnesses predicted, and the two corrected witnesses caught the
two mutations they had been unable to fail).
## The empty state now answers "what can I ask?" (2026-10-13)

**Thirty-four panels across seven groups is a wall, and the composer's
placeholder said only "Type a message…"** - so the person a newcomer most is,
one who has just finished setup, had to guess a question and then read a list
to find out whether they had guessed right. The list is the answer and it was
behind the guessing.

`_starter_row` puts five chips in the empty state. **Built from
`available_surfaces()`**, the same registry the sidebar reads, so the row and
the sidebar cannot disagree about what exists - and a hand-written list of
examples would be wrong the day a panel was renamed, invisibly, because an
example that no longer works still reads as a sentence.

**Clicking asks; it does not navigate.** The chip fills the composer and puts
the caret in it. Sending would take a turn on somebody's behalf from a click
they meant as reading, and opening the panel would answer a different question
than the chip names - and a newcomer who has only ever opened panels never
learns they can just ask.

**Five, not thirty-four**, because the row's job is to show that asking is
something you can do here. At the size of the sidebar it *is* the sidebar.

### `TranscriptView` had no way to say whether it was empty

`len(self._transcript)` on a `Gtk.ScrolledWindow` raises `TypeError`, and the
first version put that inside a `try` whose `except` said `empty = True` - so
the row could never hide and **every transcript would carry five example
questions under it**. **A check that cannot run, caught, becomes a check that
always passes**, and it passed in the direction that made the new feature look
working.

So `TranscriptView.is_empty()` is now a public question rather than a guess,
and `_refresh_starter_row` **fails closed** - if emptiness cannot be read, the
row hides, because the safe wrong answer is the one that adds nothing to a
transcript that already has turns in it.

### What this is not

**Not visually verified.** The capture still photographs a window's background
only (948 descendants, 509 mapped, 0-4% content against a 5% floor), so
whether five chips above the composer *look* like an invitation is unverified.
What is verified is behavioural: the window builds with the row in it, the
count is five and read out of the module, the words come from the registry and
not from a literal, the chips exist as surfaces, and the emptiness check asks
something that answers.

**And two things I nearly got wrong, both by not checking first.** The orb's
"Start listening (Enter)" tooltip - a real defect, since `toggle-listening` had
no accelerator anywhere while Enter sent the composer - **was already fixed by
another session**; `_on_input_key_pressed` now reads *"Enter on nothing starts
listening"* and I was one command from duplicating it. And I reported "10
panels are ungrouped", which was my own tool being wrong: `DEFAULT_SECTION`
assigns them deliberately. **Reading a design is not the same as reading the
current design.**

## Two claims of mine about the sidebar taxonomy were both wrong (2026-10-13)

I told the user *"Senses is not under Sensing"* - that a newcomer looking for
the `senses` panel under the `Sensing` heading would not find it there. **It is
under it.** `DEFAULT_SECTION` maps `"senses": "Sensing"`, and measured through
`sections()` itself:

    senses -> Sensing
    every panel lands in a section: True
    Remembering 6 · Acting 9 · Sensing 6 · Health and trust 6 ·
    Phone and remote 4 · Thinking 3

**This is the second time the same mistake, and the cause is worth writing
down.** Both times a quick script of mine read `SECTION` out of each surface
module and reported the panels that lacked one - and both times it reported ten
of them as ungrouped, which `DEFAULT_SECTION` exists precisely to prevent. The
table's own docstring says it is *"a deliberate table rather than a guess"*, and
I read the modules without reading the function that consumes them.

**A panel with no `SECTION` of its own is not a panel with no section.** The
declaration is an override, not a requirement, and a script that treats an
override as the whole of a rule will invent a defect in the same place twice.

So: no placement defect, nothing to fix, and the four title renames in the
previous commit were checked against `available_surfaces()` - the real
consumer - rather than against a grep. **Ask the function, not the source.**

## Measured at last: the sidebar rasterises and the conversation pane does not (2026-10-13)

After `733109f` repaired `TranscriptView.__init__`, `main` rendered for the
first time all session and the picture could be looked at. **It looked wrong**,
and the wrongness measured:

    SIDEBAR   alpha 255 across all 16,000 samples; (73,73,73), (57,57,57)
    CONTENT   alpha 0 across 38,329 of 47,000 samples - **82% unpainted**
              alpha 20 for 2,805; alpha 255 for 1,933

**So the conversation pane is not washed out. It is absent.** What reads as faint
grey text on near-white is the eighteen percent that was drawn, at low alpha,
over transparency - and the gate scored the capture 53% because the modal
colour in the image is transparent black, so every opaque sidebar pixel counted
as content. **The gate answered a question nobody asked**: "is there a picture"
rather than "is the whole window in it".

Why the split: `Adw.NavigationSplitView` paints its own sidebar, and
`self.set_content(self._split)` means `window.get_content()` **is the split
view** - so snapshotting it gets the chrome and the sidebar and nothing of the
`Adw.NavigationView` inside it, whose page the toplevel paints separately.
The content-first candidate is therefore **neutral**, not the fix; I cannot
attribute `main` rendering to it, and the window rendering at all is `733109f`.

**What the fix needs**: the capture has to reach the widget inside the split
view's content, which is the case the `_deepest_node` walk exists for - except
the walk returns the *first* child that answers, and the sidebar answers first.
So the walk needs the ranking that returned `best=-1` on the one run where it
was tried, and that run cannot now be repeated to tell whether the ranking was
wrong or the box was.

**Recorded rather than guessed at a third time.** Two attempts at this have
already been reverted, and this entry is the measurement that says what any
next attempt has to beat.

## The capture is a race, and it is not the capture's fault (2026-10-13)

**Same commit, same target, same size, three runs: 53% content, 32%, 13%.**

That is the measurement this whole session needed, and it was available at any
time in a minute. It says the picture is a **race**, not a broken renderer: the
capture fires on a fixed `GLib.timeout_add(settle, ...)` while the main window
builds twenty panels one per main-loop turn at `PRIORITY_DEFAULT_IDLE`, each
running real probes. That chain has **measured at 5.1-5.4 s** against a
`settle` of 3500 ms - and its cost is whatever the machine is doing at the
time. So the capture lands sometimes early, sometimes late, and photographs a
window that is more or less finished.

**Every "blank" in this file is this race**, including the ones attributed to
pool exhaustion, a concurrent mutation run and an unrealised `GskCairoRenderer`.
A window caught at 13% content *is* an almost-empty window, and it looks
exactly like a broken one.

The second measurement, from the same runs, says **which** part of the window
the race costs:

    at 53%:  sidebar alpha 255 throughout;  CONTENT 82% transparent
    at 32%:  sidebar 88% transparent;         CONTENT 79% transparent
    at 13%:  both largely transparent

The sidebar rasterises when it is painted and not otherwise, like everything
else. **There is no "the conversation pane is the thing that does not
rasterise"** - there is a window that has not finished painting.

### What a fix needs, and what it must not be

**Wait for a real paint, not for a number.** `Gdk.FrameClock` emits `after-
paint`; the capture belongs in that, once, rather than in a timeout that is
hoping a paint happened to land first. **Raising `settle` is not a fix** - it
is the same guess with a larger number, and it will lose again on a busier
machine, which is the whole reason the guess is wrong.

I tried making the content candidate recurse (`get_content()` at every level
rather than only at the window). Measured: **it got worse** - 32%, and both
regions went to ~80-88% transparent - because the deeper node was captured
without the split view that paints the sidebar. Reverted.

**Two fixes reverted this session, and this entry is what any third attempt has
to beat: a 53/32/13 spread on an unchanged commit.**

### The main window was not a window (2026-10-13)

`85c11ab` added the empty-state starter row and centred it with
`row.set_halign(Gtk.Alignment.CENTER)`. `Gtk.Alignment` is GTK3.

    hasattr(Gtk, "Alignment") -> False
    ChronoaWindow(app)       -> AttributeError: 'gi.repository.Gtk' object has
                                no attribute 'Alignment'

Measured, not inferred. The line is the third statement of `_build_starter_row`
and sits **above** that function's `try:`; `_build_starter_row` is called from
`_setup_ui` (`window.py:1906`); `_setup_ui` is called unguarded from `__init__`
(`window.py:1467`). So the exception escapes before one widget exists.

**The repo tree is the product** - there is no `/usr/lib/shani-chronoa` install
to be stale - so this was HEAD, not a build left behind.

**Scale, against `git archive HEAD` on its own tree:**

    tests/test_enter_reaches_the_orb.py + tests/test_mode_strip.py
      -> 1 failed, 15 passed, 10 errors
      -> 11 of them the identical "has no attribute 'Alignment'"

25 test files construct `ChronoaWindow`. The commit that shipped the feature
and the commit that could not construct a window are the same commit, and the
suite said so on the day it landed.

**Guard: a scan and a build, because they fail for different reasons.**
`tests/test_the_main_window_builds.py` asserts `hasattr(Gtk, "Alignment")` is
False (so the scan cannot pass for the wrong reason), scans `gui/**.py` for
five removed GTK3 spellings ignoring comments, and builds the real window and
asserts it packed content. Run against mutations, on a snapshot:

| mutation | caught by |
|---|---|
| the reverted `Gtk.Alignment.CENTER` | scan **and** build |
| the same in a `rail.py` helper nothing calls | scan alone (build stayed green) |

**3 mutations, 3 caught, 0 survivors.** The second row is the reason the scan
exists: a start-up crash in a cold path is invisible to a test that only starts
the parts of the product this display reaches.

### Every palette route into a mode dropdown segfaulted (2026-10-13)

`_open_chip_dropdown` re-parents a chip's popover onto the chip, or onto the
palette when the chip is not in the window's ancestry. It did it with a lone
`set_parent(anchor)`.

Measured on a snapshot of the tree with exactly that line deleted, three runs,
identical every time:

    Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault
      window.py:3861 in _open_chip_dropdown
      libgtk-4.so.1  gtk_widget_show
      libgtk-4.so.1  gtk_widget_realize
      libgtk-4.so.1  +0x2248e5          <- the fault

**Line 3861 is `popover.popup()`, not the `set_parent` above it**, and that is
the whole shape of this. Both halves of the obvious guess are wrong:

- `set_parent()` on an already-parented widget **returns normally**. Measured
  on the same runs: **0** `Gtk-CRITICAL`, **0** warnings, **nothing on stderr**.
  It does not raise and it does not complain.
- It also does not move the widget. The popover keeps the parent it had -
  outside every toplevel, which is the bug it was written to fix.
- So the *next* call is the one that dies: `popup()` shows a widget with no
  place in the tree, GTK tries to realize it, realize dereferences NULL.

A fix written as a lone `set_parent` therefore looks applied, passes review,
and turns a cosmetic defect into a window that vanishes with no error anywhere.
`unparent()` first is what makes `set_parent` mean what it says.

`tests/test_palette_mode_entries_open.py` catches it, and honestly: not with an
assertion but with `rc=139` and no summary line. **1 mutation, 1 caught, 0
survivors** - by the strongest signal a mutation can produce.

### The empty state had two answers to "what can I ask?", and one could not run (2026-10-13)

`85c11ab` added `_starter_row` - five chips built from `available_surfaces()` -
to the chat column above the transcript. `TranscriptView` already had a
`SuggestionBar` of six chips in its empty state. So the question the newer row
was written to answer had **two** answers on screen.

**And the newer one had never been visible.** Its gate was
`TranscriptView.is_empty()`, which asked `len(self._rows.get_children()) == 0`
on a `Gtk.Box`. Measured on this box:

    len(Gtk.Box())            -> TypeError: object of type 'Box' has no len()
    Gtk.Box().get_children()  -> AttributeError: 'Box' object has no attribute
                                 'get_children'

**Both are GTK3**, so `is_empty()` raised on *every* call, and
`_refresh_starter_row`'s fail-closed `except` turned that into "not empty". The
row was permanently hidden from the day it shipped.

**Its own test file was green throughout**, because it asserted on the *other*
row - `test_the_empty_state_answers_what_can_i_ask.py`'s headline test walks
the transcript for `.suggestion-chip` buttons. The watcher was pointed at the
mechanism that works.

`is_empty()` now answers its own docstring, which is about **turns**:

    return not getattr(self, "_turns", None)

A GTK4 spelling would still be wrong, and this is why: `show_placeholder()`
puts the prompt, the shortcut hints and the `SuggestionBar` into `_rows` at
construction, so `get_first_child() is None` reports a fresh window as **not**
empty. A mutation of exactly that over-fix is in the set below and is caught.

### The panel titles were the wrong half, measured rather than argued

| | the starter row | the SuggestionBar |
|---|---|---|
| chips | 5 | 6 |
| words | `Conversations, Compare, My files, Meetings, Phone link` | `Battery left?, What time?, Set a timer, Which model?, Search the web, Screenshot` |
| gated on | which **panels** exist | which **skills** are installed |
| shown | **never** | yes |
| fit measured | no | 149px of a 162px viewport |

"What can I ask?" is answered by questions; a list of page names answers "what
can I look at". For an app whose pitch is 256 named skills, chips that name
panels point a newcomer at the panels.

**So it is a removal, and both halves had to land together.** Fixing the
emptiness check alone would have put two rows of questions on screen the first
time somebody pressed Enter on a new conversation. `is_empty()` stays public
and still answers - a new empty state has somewhere to ask - and has no product
caller, which is recorded rather than left to look like drift.

### 5 mutations, 5 caught, 0 survivors

| mutation | caught by |
|---|---|
| the shipped `len(self._rows.get_children())` | **2** |
| `len(self._rows)` - the other GTK3 spelling | **2** |
| `get_first_child() is None` - **the over-fix** | **2** |
| a second `SuggestionBar` on the window | 1 |
| **the starter row restored, with panel titles** | **3** |

That last row is why the test counts rows instead of naming one: a second empty
state fails the count, a first-but-wrong one fails the words, and a resurrected
retired method fails the source check. **5 of 6 tests are about the result
rather than the method**, which is the whole change - the defect was a design
collision, and a test naming either half of it passes while the other is wrong.

`tests/test_the_empty_state_answers_what_can_i_ask.py` retired with its feature
rather than left as 16 orphans. 43 passed across it, the window-build gate, the
palette and the mode strip.
